Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The government will save more than it spends, says Jim Chalmers, but it won’t be a “slash and burn” budget update.

Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo).

There’s still a fair bit of work to do to finalise it all, but we’ve made enough progress to be confident that at this stage there will be a modest net save in the budget.

We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. But we haven’t focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update. They will be substantial, as I said. These are serious times.

You can see in the quite extraordinary reaction on the stock market just how volatile global markets are right now. I think it’s a bit of a symbol of the quite extraordinary volatility, unpredictability that we’re seeing play out in markets in the AI sector, but more broadly as well.

articles.title: A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis? | Bill McGuire
articles.summary:
Fossil fuel producers are choking off progress while we reap the whirlwind of our inaction. This is what sleepwalking to disaster looks like

It’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe. But the reality is that we are walking into it with our eyes wide open, in the full knowledge that we are dooming the lives of our children, and countless generations down the line, to hell on Earth. In the UK, summer temperatures could hit the mid-40s within decades, making extreme drought and harvest failures the norm, and leaving people camping in the streets as houses become overheated death traps. Across Europe, the fastest-heating continent on the planet, the 50C temperature record could be broken as soon as next year. Elsewhere, by 2050, humid heatwaves could take many thousands of lives in a single day in parts of China, South Asia and the Gulf region.

We continue to pump out the CO2 weight-equivalent of 800,000 Titanics every year, with no end in sight. Meanwhile the latest climate Cop – the only global initiative with the potential to turn things around – has just collapsed in disarray, unable to get its act together even to agree on a vague form of words about the need to transition away from fossil fuels.

articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
articles.summary:
Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action

In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.

Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive.

articles.title: Back with a Huang: Jensen reinstated as Nvidia chief exec after Trump call
articles.summary:
Stock markets were stunned on Monday after one of the best-known tech executives on the planet staged a shock return following a direct intervention from the US president. 

Billionaire Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of chipmaker Nvidia earlier this month following reports of multiple extra-marital relationships with colleagues and an alleged Chinese spy, was reinstated just days later despite his actions triggering an internal investigation and an external probe by the US FBI.

In a stock exchange statement on Monday afternoon, the board of Nvidia said it had decided “unanimously” to reappoint Huang immediately following assurances from “senior levels” of the US government that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

US President Donald Trump, who appeared to take credit for the decision and reportedly joined an Nvidia boardroom call ahead of the announcement, said it was “the correct and proper decision,” adding that the US government “did not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.

“I’m doing it for the country…. if I didn’t get involved you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” he said in a lengthy interview with CNBC.

Huang ‘honoured’ to return to Nvidia

Huang, famed for his avant-garde leather jackets, said he was “honoured” to return to the company.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process… I can’t wait to get back to work,” he said.

Nvidia shares rocketed as much as 32 per cent following the announcement, clawing back most of the more than $1 trillion in market value the tech firm had haemorrhaged since Huang’s sudden exit in one of the most dramatic comebacks in corporate history. Chipmaker peers joined in on the rally, with Intel shares jumping 13 per cent and UK-based Arm soaring 17 per cent. 

“Jensen Huang is the Rocky Balboa of the stock market. He’s taken a huge hit, been knocked down, and then climbed straight back into the ring,” says Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

“This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world’s most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable.”

Huang’s return to Nvidia’s board comes despite repeated reports that board members had ruled out the possibility of any immediate return, alongside beginning a formal search for a new chief executive. Arm boss Rene Haas had been widely seen as a front-runner for the role.

Tech chiefs rallied round

But an online petition which attracted hundreds of thousands of signatories including from the likes of Tesla boss Elon Musk, alongside Trump’s intervention and a public plea from Huang for a quick reinstatement, appear to have tilted the odds back in his favour.

Huang’s shock return to Nvidia, which echoed a similar move to bring Sam Altman back to run Open AI in 2024, are likely to cement the dominance over the company by the firm’s co-founder for the foreseeable future, raising questions over standards of corporate governance in the world’s biggest tech businesses.

The move “shows everything rotten in Silicon Valley’s leadership and culture,” former Mark Zuckerberg adviser, Dex Hunter-Torricke, said. “Lying to the board should be a dealbreaker for any board, but normal rules don’t apply.”

articles.title: Professional services firms in legal crosshairs over collapsed private credit lenders
articles.summary:
Professional services firms that have advised collapsed private credit lenders are in the firing line as they risk facing a wave of legal claims themselves, lawyers have warned.

In October, an intermediary of the collapsed bridging lender, Market Financial Solutions (MFS), filed a legal claim against the solicitors which had advised it before MFS’ collapse in February.

The collapse of MFS triggered the City’s financial watchdog, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), to initiate an enforcement investigation, and also highlighted concerns about the risks associated with unregulated lending for both consumers and markets.

In July, the FCA agreed to toughen up its scrutiny of unregulated lenders, and in August the watchdog warned investors could lose their life savings if they pump cash into high-risk, unregulated investment services.

However, firms that advised these lenders may now come under scrutiny. A wave of secondary disputes are appearing where insolvency practitioners start to comb through the conduct of these firms to help recover losses for creditors.

The accountancy watchdog, the Financial Reporting Council (FRC), opened a probe in June into the conduct of three audit firms and individual accountants involved in auditing the accounts of MFS.

An uptick in claims

Jessica Wicker and Mark Wilson, both partners at Pinsent Masons, told City AM they are both seeing an uptick in a wave of claims against firms who advised fallen lenders, putting them squarely in the firing line of disgruntled investors and regulators.

Wicker said there is “a steady indication that due to geopolitics and various other market volatilities, it is quite easy for one piece of the ecosystem to fall over”, leading to the possible downfall of many of these high-risk investment firms, creating knock-on effects for the firms involved in providing advisory services to them.

“If something goes wrong somewhere in the ecosystem, there will most likely be a contagion effect, and it will ripple out towards the other parties,” she said.

Wicker said the professional services firms which have advised collapsed – and often unregulated – private credit lenders face “serious reputational damage”.

She added that for those advising companies in this market, “a healthy amount of scepticism is probably a good idea” to avoid being impacted further down the line if the lender collapses and is found to have breached regulatory rules.

Trouble comes when the music stops

Alongside MFS, there have been other recent high-profile collapses of lending firms, such as litigation funder Woodville Consultants.

The funder entered administration in July following a High Court order after raising £300m by selling high-yield unsecured loan notes to retail investors to fund law firms handling thousands of consumer claims, primarily in the motor finance scandal.

Mark Wilson, partner and head of insolvency litigation at Pinsent Masons, said fraud-related problems are often the catalyst causing liquidators and administrators to try and work out who is “culpable”.

“When there’s stress or distress, that’s when these problems become apparent,” Wilson said, adding that “when there’s lots of money pumping around the system, it’s less obvious. It’s when the music stops that it becomes more obvious.”

“Quite often, the people that originally caused the problem may have disappeared,” Wilson said.

“Fraud doesn’t really respect country boundaries, so then you are spinning around looking at who else may have participated in that, which may involve looking at what lawyers have done, what they knew, and whether they’ve turned a blind eye to what’s going on,” he added.

Far-reaching implications for professional services firms

For embroiled professional services firms, the implications can be far-reaching.

“If a law firm has overlooked the obvious, and it’s got some form of blind eye knowledge of what was going on, then it could be culpable for dishonest assistance, in which case they would be liable for the whole of the loss potentially,” Wilson said.

Wilson added, however, that “the vast majority” of professional services firms “are looking to do the right thing.”

“It’s really circumstantial where they haven’t realised what is going on, rather than having cut corners,” Wilson said.

articles.title: It’s not Arteta’s job to answer for the Arsenal boardroom
articles.summary:
Mikel Arteta should not have to defend Arsenal’s boardroom. Club owners must face fans over ticket prices, redundancies and Super League plans, writes Freddie Barber

In this world nothing is certain, except death, taxes and everyone hating Arsenal. As a long-suffering supporter since 1997, I accept that, and I’ve been particularly gracious about this fact since May. What I cannot accept as a communications professional is the way Mikel Arteta has to speak about topics far beyond his remit. These include recent redundancies at the club, and most pertinently, the unbelievable decision to enter the doomed European Super League. In the words of Roy Keane, “it’s NOT his job”.

Josh Kroenke, the Arsenal co-chairman, is far from the worst Premier League owner at not fronting up to boardroom decisions, but a listed company generally publishes results and speaks to investors four times a year in this country. In an H/Advisors event this week on business and football, I kicked it off with two requests:

Raise your hand if you support a football club (a sea of raised hands)

Keep your hand raised if you trust the people that run your football club (three hands stayed up, sheepishly)

I’m not saying a football club should be run like a FTSE 100 company. Please no, the corporate speak would ruin the beautiful game. But the chasm in trust between the boardroom and the stands is something that every club would want to improve. By the way, the disconnect between what those with authority (the board) talk about and what those with responsibility, but less authority (managers) are expected to explain to fans is not universal in football, but it’s certainly not the manager’s job to defend the owners for signing up to a breakaway league with no relegation.

Arsenal execs should answer for ticket prices

As Oscar Wilde’s character Lord Henry said in The Picture of Dorian Gray, “people know the price of everything and the value of nothing”, which is an apt summary of the constant ticket price raises and increase of corporate hospitality that many clubs around the country have seen. Football is now big business. The Premier League is one of the UK’s last world-leading, global exports. You could be trekking in the jungles of Borneo and still find locals eager to discuss the bend on Declan Rice’s set-piece delivery. Football is the playground of billionaires, sovereign wealth funds and private investors, with no fewer than 11 Premier League clubs owned by Americans. Since 1992, average Premier League club revenues have grown over 30 times. UK GDP only increased by three times over the same period.

What can be done about it? With the vast sums of money swilling around the game, it’s hard to see this changing any time soon, but it doesn’t have to be this way. In Germany, sporting directors and board members routinely explain the big decisions. English clubs could do the same, and it wouldn’t cost them anything. The manager talks about the football. The sporting director talks about transfers. The chief executive or owner answers for ticket prices, redundancies, changes to the stadium and anything else decided in the boardroom. Clubs already publish accounts. They should explain them, in person, at least once a year, to the fans who fund them.

The irony is that fans are not asking for much. They will keep turning up whatever happens, which is precisely why clubs have got away with saying so little for so long. But loyalty is not the same as trust, and the show of hands in our room suggests most clubs have far more loyalty than trust.

So, the next time Arteta is asked about the Arsenal boardroom, spare a thought for him, and thank your lucky stars you don’t support a team from Manchester. Then again, this being a London paper, plenty of you probably do.

Freddie Barber is an associate partner at H/Advisors

articles.title: Good riddance to Natural England – the country’s most toxic quango
articles.summary:
Louise Haigh has hinted she might abolish Natural England, an organisation that has spent two decades making it harder to build, harder to grow, and harder to end decline, says Tom Willerton-Gartside

I was three years old when the government established a quango called “Natural England”. The England football team had just been knocked out of the World Cup on penalties, and the BBC had aired its final regular episode of Top of the Pops. WikiLeaks would be launched days later.

Much of Britain is now numb from decades of decline. Yet we could finally bid farewell to what is surely the country’s most anti-growth organisation – as Louise Haigh has hinted she may abolish it. It follows Kemi Badenoch’s pledge to bin both the Environment Agency as well as Natural England.

Since its creation, this unelected quango has wielded a de facto veto over our jobs, industries, energy prices, homes and living standards. From new power stations, roads and homes to theme parks and kite festivals, Natural England has objected to, blocked, delayed and banned almost everything you can think of – and plenty you couldn’t, including the construction of its own office in Cornwall.

They spent over 1,000 days blocking 20,000 new homes because the people living there may damage the habitat of a snail, blocked 74 local planning authorities from granting permission until they could achieve “nutrient neutrality”, and shut down a paintballing centre in Exeter that had been in operation for over a decade.

Today, across much of Britain, projects effectively need the quango’s permission to become reality. If those in Natural England object, proposals face years of legal battles, costly new conditions and even cancellation.  

The most infamous example is not the £100m HS2 bat tunnel, but the £700m fish disco at Hinkley Point C. This saga has held up Britain’s first nuclear power station this century for nearly a decade – and there’s still no guarantee Natural England will sign off. Earlier this year, reports emerged that the 2030 start date could slip yet again, after the quango decided that the “fish deterrent” system was no longer adequate.

You don’t need to be a cynic to believe that Natural England just opposes nuclear energy altogether.

A threat to Britain’s energy system

Certainly its chair, Tony Juniper, has made no secret of his views. As Executive Director of Friends of the Earth, he wrote ‘Say no to Labour’s nuclear nightmare’ in Socialist Worker, a “revolutionary socialist newspaper”, arguing that new nuclear power stations were not “justified” and “would greatly increase the risk of nuclear proliferation” (Britain already had a nuclear weapon). At the 2010 General Election, he stood as the Green Party candidate in Cambridge, pledging to “phase out nuclear power and resolutely oppose any new nuclear power stations”.

Although Tony lost, his activism continued. In 2013, he told followers that nuclear “simply does not work in the context of modern energy economics”. Three years later, he echoed Nick Clegg’s theory of nuclear power, calling it a “dead end”. Most interestingly, however, he promoted articles opposing Hinkley Point C on social media, and even boasted about signing a petition that opposed it.

In 2019, the Conservative government made the former Green Party candidate and anti-nuclear activist the new chair of Natural England. He was reappointed in 2021, again by the Tories, and in 2025 by the Labour government. Since then, Natural England has continued to obstruct, delay, block, and ban improvements to the lives of the British people. Hinkley Point C – the very project that Juniper campaigned against before taking the job – has been repeatedly delayed by the quango’s veto.

Natural England has become a threat to Britain’s energy system. It is holding back the cheap, secure, and reliable nuclear power that, according to a report by think tank Onward, could save us more than £320bn by 2050 – around £540 for every household, every year.

Instead of tinkering around the edges, Andy Burnham must begin to take the radical action required to rescue Britain. Natural England has spent two decades making it harder to build, harder to grow, and harder to end decline. There should be no more reviews or consultations about what to do, no more waiting for “ten-year plans”. The Government must act now and abolish Natural England.

Tom Willerton-Gartside is the Head of Communications at Looking for Growth, the political movement to end decline and save Britain.

articles.title: The 12 best City of London bars, from a hidden speakeasy to a wine bar in a crypt
articles.summary:
These are the City of London bars our Toast the City writers rate most, from subterranean cocktail dens to historic wine bars and sky-high terraces, with each pick taken from our original reviews and features.

Cocktail bars in the City of London worth seeking out

The Discount Suit Company

If you are searching for a bar that does things a little differently then the Discount Suit Company is a place to discover. And discover it you will have to – this is a hidden, subterranean speak-easy style cocktail bar that the commuters walking past Liverpool Street Station would never realise was there. 

Read the full piece

Martini Bar at the Barbican

Tucked away on the first floor of the main building, it is a dark and atmospheric space. Ninety percent of the conversations are about what people have seen that day, be that art or theatre. You can go in the afternoon but savouring a late-night drink is best.

Read the full piece

The Pregnant Man

The Pregnant Man is as unique as its name. Part owned by Saatchi & Saatchi and originally an agency-only pub in a car park, it’s now a fully-fledged bar and restaurant open to the public on Chancery Lane. It takes its title from one of Saatchi & Saatchi’s most successful advertising campaigns from the 1970s, promoting safe sex, and there’s a tongue-in-cheek vibe to everything here.

Read the full piece

The best wine bars in the Square Mile

El Vino Fleet Street

Journalists still frequent El Vino today – but it is also popular with lawyers and city types seeking a spot for a relaxed business lunch. With its dark mahogany bar and sherry casks, there is a classic charm to the interior, which retains the feel of an Edwardian wine merchant blended with an old-school gentleman’s club. El Vino is a little slice of history, a place to soak in ‘old’ London and enjoy a bottle of wine in a spot where political intrigue has been discussed, novels plotted and gossip columns written. 

Read the full piece

Dave’s Wine Bar

It strikes me as a partially hidden oasis in the middle of the frantic financial district – one that serves great wines ranging from Burgundian Pinot Noirs to premium English sparkling and an exceptionally quaffable Gavi that remains a best seller. There’s also half price food on Fridays and up to a quarter off the drink-in price for any bottles you want to take home. 

Read the full piece

Humble Grape Bow Lane

Now there are seven venues across London, with Humble Grape Bow Lane being a Toast the City finalist for Best Bar and Best New Opening this year. A wine bar and restaurant in a cool crypt below St Mary-le-Bow Church offering over 500 wines by independent winemakers, it’s a real piece of City history best enjoyed with a great glass in hand. 

Read the full piece

Terra at Eataly

For the Italian wine lover there is no better City of London spot than Eataly, which boasts the largest selection of Italian wines in the UK. Terra is the beating heart of this ode to Italophilia, focusing on simple Italian dishes cooked with flair and fire in their wood-burning grill.  

Read the full piece

The best rooftop bars in the City of London

Bread Street Kitchen, 22 Bishopsgate

It’s very high. From up here, the Walkie-Talkie looks like a toy. Planes fly past at what feels like a similar height, which is mildly terrifying. 

Read the full piece

Wagtail

During some months there are more Google searches for ‘London rooftop bars’ than ‘new London bars’ – and that’s true even in winter. It’s just one sign that the capital’s intense love-in with sky-high hedonism shows no signs of slowing. It’s a love affair that continues with Wagtail, the rooftop spot near Monument that’s about to celebrate its first year of existence – and I reckon it’s smarter than a lot of the competition.

Read the full piece

Florattica

Florattica is on the 11th floor of the Canopy by Hilton London City hotel in Aldgate and boasts incredible views across the Square Mile.

Read the full piece

Coq d’Argent

From ground level (fun fact: Putt Shack in the basement is built on what would have been the ground floor in Roman Londinium), Coq d’Argent is accessed by a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it lift, which beams you up to the 6th floor, where you can pick between the sprawling restaurant and a terrace that wraps around the central atrium.

Read the full piece

Sky Garden

Sky Garden offers something rare in London: a beautifully landscaped public garden 37 floors above the city. Designed by Gillespies, the space is home to two restaurants, Fenchurch Restaurant and Darwin Brasserie, alongside bars, live music and panoramic views across the capital. Whether visiting for drinks, dinner or simply to take in the view, it’s the combination of setting and atmosphere that makes Sky Garden so unique.

Read the full piece

articles.title: Public control of utilities: What Britain can learn from Australia and France
articles.summary:
Louise Haigh wants public control of Britain’s utilities. Australia, the US and France show why who owns the pipes and wires really matters, says Helen Thomas

Louise Haigh used her address to the CBI annual conference on Monday to make the case for greater public control of Britain’s utilities. Before this descends into the familiar argument about the merits of privatisation, it’s worth looking at the economics of utilities and what other countries have actually chosen to do.

When it comes to something we all need, like water, once someone has dug up the street and laid the pipes, it is generally cheaper to connect another house to the same network than to build a rival one. Economists call this a natural monopoly. If the owner puts up the price or skimps on maintenance, where exactly is the customer supposed to go?

Governments can run these networks themselves or give regulators powers over what companies can charge and what they must deliver. Both arrangements have their difficulties. A minister can keep bills down before an election and leave a successor to pay for the maintenance. A regulated company can know far more about the condition of its pipes than the people deciding what it ought to spend. And whoever owns it has to find the money for work today whose chief benefit may be that, 20 years from now, nothing goes wrong.

Australia shows how a country can bring in private capital and still draw a line around a particular asset. In 2016, New South Wales sought to lease a majority interest in Ausgrid, the electricity network serving Sydney and surrounding areas, for 99 years. The federal treasurer rejected two foreign bids on national security grounds. The lease went to Australian retirement savings investors, while the state kept just under half. Australia generally requires foreign government investors to seek approval for a direct interest in a business, typically a stake of at least 10 per cent. That gives Canberra a chance to examine what powers come with the investment before the deal goes through.

Decisions about who pays for new infrastructure can determine whether it gets built at all

The United States has a mix of investor-owned utilities, municipal providers and co-operatives. Certain foreign investments in critical infrastructure face federal security scrutiny, while utility regulators consider what a takeover could mean for customers. This month’s midterms showed just how political those customer interests can become. Voters in 10 states backed restrictions on data centres or rejected proposals to build them. Behind some of that opposition was a question about electricity bills. If the tech companies need more power plants and bigger grids, who pays for them? The row went straight to the heart of utility regulation. Decisions about who pays for new infrastructure can determine whether it gets built at all.

France made a different choice. It already controlled EDF when it bought out the remaining shareholders in 2023, after President Macron announced a new nuclear construction programme. There is a financial logic to full ownership when ministers want a company to commit billions to power stations that will take years to sell their first unit of electricity. The state can set the timetable and accept risks that outside shareholders might baulk at. French taxpayers carry the risk if costs overrun. And the company France regards as central to its own energy security also operates nuclear power stations in Britain.

An electricity grid or a water network will outlast most governments and quite possibly some alliances. A country we trust today may have very different interests in 30 years. So when a foreign government buys into a British utility, it is worth asking what it could do if relations sour. Does its stake mainly earn it a dividend, or does it give it influence over the people who run the network or access to sensitive systems? Could Britain keep the service running if the owner stopped co-operating? The percentage on the share register only gets you so far.

Britain also needs investors prepared to put money into assets that take decades to pay for themselves. Ofwat’s latest price review provided for £104bn of investment over five years. Pension funds and insurers can be natural investors in that sort of infrastructure because they have pension and insurance promises to meet decades from now. They can price a clear set of rules about what they may own and what return they can earn. If they think those rules could change whenever bills become politically awkward, they will ask for a higher return. Customers can end up paying for that uncertainty.

Team Burnham is looking at this thorny topic at a pivotal moment. Governments are looking to secure supplies of energy, water and other essential resources just as new industries are making greater demands on the networks that deliver them. Britain will need to raise capital on terms households can afford while retaining the ability to keep those services running in a crisis. That is the debate Haigh has opened up. Who owns the pipes and wires matters because of the decisions they get to make and the risks the rest of us are left to carry.

Helen Thomas is founder and CEO of Blonde Money

articles.title: Compass US listing move is a wake-up call for UK capital markets
articles.summary:
Compass’s move of its primary listing to the US should be a wake-up call for anyone who cares about UK capital markets, says Charles Hall

Crisis, what crisis? Compass is expected to announce tomorrow that it intends to move its primary listing to the US. This may not seem a big event for many – after all you will still be able to buy the shares in London and the shape of the business will not change materially. However, this should be a serious wake-up call for anyone that cares about UK capital markets and the health of the UK economy. Do we want to be an incubator economy or a country where companies start, scale and stay?

As an outsourced foodservice company, Compass may not operate in the most glamorous of sectors. However, it has been a great British success story. The company was founded in Croydon in 1941 and listed its shares on the London Stock Exchange in 1988 at a market cap of around £200m. The company has successfully accessed the equity market numerous times to fund growth and most recently raised £2bn to ensure the business was well funded through Covid. Shareholders have nothing to complain about, with the shares close to an all-time high, up >10x since IPO and 2.5x since the mega 2020 placing. The business now has revenues of £38bn, a market cap of £42bn, over 600,000 employees, operates in 25 countries and is the world leader in its sector.

We will find out tomorrow some of the rationale for the switch to the US. The key drivers are likely to be that over two thirds of its business is in North America and that Compass will be eligible for US indices and so of greater interest for US institutions that have a domestic focus as well as passive funds. Inevitably executive remuneration is a contributing factor for many as well as differences in board structures and focus.

The grass is not always greener

In reality, the grass is often not greener on the other side of the pond. Eligibility for the key indices is not a given, valuation may not improve and legal risk is far higher. There are plenty of examples where experience is a distance from expectations – just look at the trajectories of Flutter and Wise since they moved stateside. However, this reality is not stemming the tide with the market value of companies leaving the UK over the last five years now totting up to an eye-watering £300bn, which is close to 10 per cent of the total market cap of the UK equity market.

The UK capital market should be seen as a core national asset. It provides permanent capital for companies to invest and grow as well as to navigate challenging markets (not least Compass in Covid!). It enables companies to raise their profile, to highlight their core strengths and to reward employees. It connects companies with investors and allows everyone to have a stake in the growth of UK based companies. It enables companies like Compass to be global market leaders. It also drives economic growth and tax revenues. Furthermore there is a broad ecosystem that surrounds each business including banks, financial advisors, lawyers, accountants and other suppliers. When the business changes its listing venue, inevitably the focus of the company shifts with it. Key leadership roles move, the ecosystem fades, tax revenue reduces and investment decisions are made elsewhere. Every time a company leaves there is a hole in our economy, investment and growth.

So what can be done? There has already been a regulatory revolution that has made the UK highly attractive as a listing venue and attitudes to compensation have shifted materially. There is also plenty of evidence and reasoning to show that the rationale for the shift is far from compelling. But this is nowhere near enough in a world that is becoming increasingly competitive for capital, companies and talent. We must have policies that make the UK not just competitive, but the best market to be listed in. Clearly stamp duty has to be the first thing to go. Having a tax that says please invest elsewhere is economic suicide. Providing nearly £100bn of tax incentives every year to pensions and ISAs only to see the capital fund growth overseas is bizarre. Encouraging successful founders to leave the UK due to tax is extraordinarily inept. If we make the necessary changes, we can have a capital market that drives economic growth across the UK, substantially increases tax revenues and enables individuals to increase their savings. There is no time to be lost.

Charles Hall is head of research at Peel Hunt

articles.title: Price controls have failed for 4,800 years yet politicians never learn
articles.summary:
Price controls have a 4,800-year record of failure. From Turkey’s rent caps to Hungary’s fuel limits, they bring shortages, not lower prices, says Rainer Zitelmann

As inflation has risen again in many countries, calls for price controls have grown louder. There are numerous examples around the world of governments trying to bring inflation under control through price controls. In Turkey, the government attempted to limit rent increases to 25 per cent a year, even though inflation temporarily reached almost 70 per cent. It also took action against allegedly excessive food prices, imposed fines on supermarkets, and blamed retailers for inflation. But none of this stopped inflation.

In Hungary, the government capped gasoline prices at 480 forints per litre in 2021 and 2022. The consequences were shortages, panic buying, and gas station closures. Eventually, the government had to abolish the price cap. Nevertheless, in March 2026, it once again introduced maximum prices for gasoline and diesel. Smaller gas stations became unprofitable, forcing the government to provide discounted fuel from strategic reserves.

Since April 2026, gas stations in Germany have been allowed to raise their gasoline and diesel prices only once a day. However, a study found that the regulation did not lower gasoline prices but often had exactly the opposite effect.

In 2025, Donald Trump threatened major pharmaceutical companies with government intervention in their pricing policies. He demanded that they drastically reduce their drug prices in the United States. He gave 17 major pharmaceutical companies a deadline of 60 days and threatened that the pharmaceutical industry would either lower prices voluntarily or he would force it to do so. Absurdly, he repeatedly boasted that he had reduced pharmaceutical prices by more than 1,000 per cent, which is, of course, mathematically impossible.

Attempts to bring inflation and rising prices under control through government price controls are much older, however, as British economist Eamonn Butler shows in his contribution to the book “The War on Prices” (Cato Institute), edited by Ryan A Bourne. He has compiled hundreds of examples of price controls dating back to 2800 BC. His conclusion: “…no economic policy has been tested so long, so often, among so many peoples, and in so many places. Nor does any have such a uniform record of failure”.

Lessons from history?

In his lectures on the philosophy of history, the German philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel argued that peoples and governments had never learned anything from history or acted on the lessons that could have been drawn from it. Price controls are an excellent example of this.

Price controls are popular because they are based on explanations for rising prices that are as simplistic as they are wrong, as American economist Brian C Albrecht shows in his contribution to the volume. Corporate greed is seen as the cause of inflation – a popular tactic used by politicians to distract attention from their own failures. In a 2023 YouGov survey, Americans agreed with no explanation for inflation more frequently than “large corporations seeking maximum profits”. Absurdly, only a few respondents believed that raising interest rates could be a way to combat inflation. They even believed that higher interest rates would cause inflation to rise.

According to Bourne, inflation is always the result of misguided monetary policy by central banks that expand the money supply too much. But, of course, rising prices for certain goods are not evidence of inflation, but of scarcity. And they serve an important function. For economist Ludwig von Mises, prices perform an indispensable function because they convey information about the scarcity of goods and consumers’ preferences. Prices emerge from the interaction of supply and demand and show entrepreneurs which goods are particularly sought after and which are less in demand. In this way, prices coordinate the decisions of millions of people without a central authority having to tell them what to produce or consume. Only market prices expressed in money make economic calculation possible.

This is demonstrated in practice by the contribution “Under Rent Controls, Everyone Pays” by economists Jeffrey Miron and Pedro Aldighieri. They demonstrate that where rent controls were introduced, landlords eventually withdrew apartments from the rental market and preferred to sell them as condominiums. They also cut back on maintenance, which reduced the quality of buildings. Conversely, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for example, annual investment in housing doubled after rent control was abolished. On the other hand, studies show that tenants living in apartments with artificially suppressed rents are understandably less likely to move because apartments on the free market are more expensive. This has negative consequences for society because it reduces mobility. Studies also show that poor people in particular benefit less from rent controls. In San Jose, California, 62 per cent of rent-controlled apartments were occupied by middle- and high-income households.

Price freezes therefore achieve the desired result at best for a very short time. Much more often, they produce unintended consequences and even bring about exactly the opposite of what was intended.

Rainer Zitelmann is author of the book In Defense of Capitalism https://in-defence-of-capitalism.com/

articles.title: Did you even notice Apple has a new CEO?
articles.summary:
John Ternus has launched a foldable iPhone, but former Apple music chief Neil West says the new boss is working hard to feel familiar in today’s Notebook

Apple’s new CEO has had a busy three months. So why does so little feel different?

Three months into his tenure as Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus has overseen the launch of a foldable iPhone, a smart home display and a touchscreen Macbook Pro. After years of criticism that Apple had lost its appetite for bold moves, the company seems ready to be more adventurous.

And yet, watching Ternus on stage, giving interviews and posing for selfies with customers in Apple Stores, I’ve been struck by how little seems to have changed. He looks and sounds like an Apple executive, talks about the same values and appears perfectly at home in the rituals of an Apple product launch.

I suspect that’s no accident. Apple wants to excite customers with new products while reassuring them that the company they trust isn’t about to become something unrecognisable.

During my 16 years at Apple, I learned that the company pays enormous attention to how its products and experiences feel, not just how they work. There’s a psychological principle called cognitive fluency: our brains respond more positively to things that are easy to process. It helps explain Apple’s simple product designs, its consistent typography and why Apple Stores feel familiar everywhere.

And I think Apple is applying the same thinking to its new CEO.

Ternus’s first keynote emphasised continuity rather than a grand new vision. He talks about excellence, simplicity and making great products, just as his predecessors did. He dresses the part. Most of us have just met him, yet somehow he feels familiar. And familiarity makes us more comfortable, confident and trusting.

It’s too early to judge his leadership, but there’s a lesson for leaders managing change. The more adventurous the future you’re asking people to embrace, the harder you should work to make everything around it feel familiar.

Great organisations don’t just make change happen. They make change feel like a natural next step.

Is Homeview a miss for Apple?

Steve Jobs once failed to catch five paper balls thrown at him simultaneously. It was a clever demonstration of why great advertising should communicate one clear message, not five. I think of that story when contemplating Apple’s new Homeview. Music, Facetime, home security, smart home controls: there’s plenty to love, but no single message as compelling as iPod’s “1,000 songs in your pocket” or Macbook Neo’s “the magic of Mac at a surprising price”.

I’ve no doubt Homeview’s a fantastic product. But Apple needs to give us one compelling reason to fall in love with it. One ball, not five.

Are the Spanish right about the clocks?

I split my time between London and Madrid, so Spain’s upcoming general election has my attention. Among the weightier issues, Pedro Sanchez wants to abolish the twice-yearly clock changes.

But which time should Spain keep? Sleep specialists favour winter time, while two-thirds of Spaniards prefer summer time and lighter winter evenings. Having spent the last fortnight in London, I know whose side I’m on. The Spanish have already convinced me of the merits of leisurely lunches and beer served in ice-cold glasses. Perhaps they’re onto something with the clocks, too.

A cracking business

Almost seven years after Covid derailed the careers of a Welsh lobster fisherman and a London-based photographer, their unlikely venture, Lockdownlobsters.co.uk, is still going strong, delivering some of the UK’s finest seafood to homes and restaurants across London. Sustainably caught, superb quality and run by genuinely good people. A cracking business, in more ways than one.

Quote of the week

“Simplicity is really hard!”

Jony Ive in Objectified, a documentary directed by Gary Hustwit, 2009.

Sixteen years at Apple taught me he was right. But I can report that helping other businesses discover how the hard work pays off is a lot of fun.

A podcast recommendation: My Favourite Beatles Song

With a new Rubber Soul box set just released and four Sam Mendes films on the way, it’s a good time to be a Beatles fan. Not that I’ve ever needed much encouragement.

During my years running the music team for iTunes, I regularly visited Abbey Road Studios and never missed a chance to stand in Studio Two, where the Beatles recorded so much of their music, and just breathe it all in.

These days my favourite regular Beatles fix is Tim Tucker’s podcast, My Favourite Beatles Song. Tim has a remarkable musical brain, but it’s his infectious, wide-eyed enthusiasm that makes the podcast so wonderful. Every week he reveals something new in songs I’ve known all my life. A splendid time is guaranteed for all.

Neil West is the former head of music for Apple in the UK and Europe, where he helped grow iTunes into the world’s largest music retailer. Now a keynote speaker, he is the author of It Just Works: The Nine Simple Rules of Apple’s Success.

articles.title: CBI conference turns into a feisty battle of ideas
articles.summary:
The annual CBI conference isn’t always associated with a feisty battle of ideas. This isn’t the fault of the CBI; the event has tended to reflect the stodgy consensus of our political debates. Yesterday, that consensus was shattered as heavyweights from Labour, the Tories, Reform and the Liberal Democrats used the platform to argue for radically different policies.

Louise Haigh, Andy Burnham’s deputy, began by acknowledging that “opening the CBI Annual Conference with a keynote speech on public control may feel somewhat counterintuitive.” Frankly, it was somewhat counterintuitive to see Haigh addressing the CBI at all, given her solidly left-wing credentials.

But she was there to convey the Prime Minister’s message, and to convince a hall full of capitalist go-getters that “collaboration between public and private sectors is the only way to rewire our economy.” Well, it’s one way.

Reassurance came from the fact that the government’s plans for ‘public control’ over key sectors remain pretty thin, so far amounting to more local bureaucracy.

The First Secretary of State was on firmer ground with her critique of regulators and quangos, but don’t confuse her hostility to Natural England for some sort of libertarian conversion; ministers want the finger-wagging powers of these bodies transferred to local government, instead.

Badenoch warns business chiefs to ‘be alarmed’

Meanwhile, Kemi Badenoch painted Burnham’s focus on EU relations as outdated nostalgia. The Tory leader is opposed to Burnham’s EU reset on the grounds that – among other things – it binds the UK to future rules over which we will have no say whatsoever. This is not an unreasonable position.

More dividing ground opened up on the issue of public control, where Badenoch suggested that business leaders should reject Haigh’s overtures. Her message was simple: you can’t trust this lot. “These are the same Labour politicians who didn’t know that putting up National Insurance would make it more expensive to hire people,” she said, adding: “I would be alarmed if politicians with that level of ignorance were coming for your business.”

Badenoch, unlike Haigh, also made the unfashionable case for cutting public spending and reducing the deficit. Every single business leader I speak to understands the importance of getting the public finances under control, and I suspect it was a line that resonated more than anything Haigh had to say on the merits of public control or the delights of partnering with government.

articles.title: What do a wind-up radio, the Microsoft outage and bank resilience have to do with each other?
articles.summary:
The Microsoft outage was a reminder that City firms must plan for disruption, and the operational resilience rules expect them to, says Omar Salem

If you are ever lost for conversation with a stranger, there is now a third option. Once you have exhausted the weather and how you each travelled there, ask what they keep in their emergency stores. The last person I discussed this with had bought a gas canister to warm up his food when the world shut down.

The government has been criticised for asking the public to prepare while not having its house in order. But the point is not that nothing ever fails; it is to be prepared when a crisis hits. This month’s Microsoft outage put that lesson to the City. So, we’ve got a carefully chosen wind-up radio and are building out the stores.

The pain of preparation

The instinct to skip the preparation is understandable. In The Ostrich Paradox, Wharton professors Robert Meyer and Howard Kunreuther trace under-preparation to six biases, including myopia (the cost is today, the benefit long-term) and optimism (disasters happen to other people). We also dislike dwelling on unpleasant events. And no-one likes seeing their work go to waste: preparation for something that never happens looks like wasted effort. A radio never wound looks like money thrown away. So does a business continuity plan nobody ever opens.

However, with all these things, it doesn’t matter until it matters. When something goes wrong and there isn’t a plan, that’s a problem. Suddenly, it seems obvious that there should have been a plan, and people look for who to blame.

That is why governance and compliance systems exist. Left to instinct, there is always something more urgent to do. Governance and compliance can bridge that gap, where otherwise the risks of a future crisis, perhaps years away, could be discounted.

Twenty-four hours

For some, the recent Microsoft 365 outage was a welcome relief from a bulging inbox. It was also a reminder of how fragile and vulnerable the modern world can be.

City firms might fairly ask what they were supposed to do about it. The whole country, nay, the whole world was affected. The cause was a latent defect in Microsoft’s own gateway servers. No compliance officer could have patched it.

But the rules never asked them to. The operational resilience regime assumes disruption will happen. Firms must identify their important business services and set an impact tolerance for each: the maximum disruption that can be tolerated before customers or markets suffer intolerable harm. The test is not whether Outlook failed. It is whether firms can keep carrying out their key functions, such as executing a payment, making a trade or giving someone a mortgage offer.

Hindsight isn’t needed

Nor was any of this unforeseeable. The critical third parties regime, created by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, lets HM Treasury designate suppliers whose failure could threaten the stability of the financial system. Nine firms have been designated by HM Treasury so far. Once designated, the Bank of England, the PRA and the FCA oversee the services those suppliers provide to the sector and hold them to resilience rules..

The new regime should increase systemic resilience but it does not remove responsibility from City firms. Designation, the authorities made clear, does not diminish the accountability of regulated firms. The Microsoft outage may be a nudge for firms to take another look at their operational resilience and business continuity plans.

I hope never to wind my radio in anger. But if you find yourself beside a bank chief executive and the weather runs dry, you know what to ask.

Omar Salem is a Partner Consultant at Pierson Ferdinand UK LLP

articles.title: After its shares tumbled on Monday, Capita has one final roll of the dice
articles.summary:
Over the past few years, Capita has had almost as many bosses as Manchester United. And, like Manchester United, nothing seems to do the trick.

Since 2014, the British outsourcing firm has worked its way through some five separate chief executives. On Monday, it welcomed its sixth.

Capita’s market cap collapsed a jaw-dropping 99 per cent during that time, positioning it near the bottom of the corporate league table. At its peak it had once been worth £8bn – it has since sunk to less than £80m. The firm’s new boss, the Pochettino of procurement executives, must feel this is the last chance to revive Capita’s fortunes, before it’s all over.

Pablo Andres, who was Capita’s chief financial officer for two years before his promotion yesterday, will sense the scale of the task that lies ahead. The firm’s shares plunged an eye-watering 70 per cent within minutes following the sudden departure of his predecessor on Monday.

Capita said it was seeking to raise more than £100m in additional cash from shareholders to shore up its finances. The company admitted it would have to renegotiate its covenants with lenders to get the raise over the line. Amid all of this, the firm’s botched handling of a major government contract means profitability next year is already well-behind market expectations.

Capita is no stranger to corporate scandals, having coughed up for a host of regulatory fines over the past two decades. And for Andres, whose CV includes Arthur Andersen and G4S, reassuring shareholders that another is not round the corner will be a top priority.

The company’s latest setback relates to its management of the Civil Service Pension Scheme, a contract it was awarded back in 2023, and which it took over in 2025.

Beneficiaries of the scheme reported trouble pretty soon after the handover. Payments were missed or delayed, and users reported being unable to access the online portal.

Arguably, what made matters worse for Capita, was that they were running the pension schemes of some of the most powerful people in government: well-connected individuals who knew which levers to pull if anything went awry. And pull levers they did.

In the summer, the National Audit Office said it had begun a probe into Capita’s handling of the scheme, while earlier this month, Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee joined in on the action, launching its own inquiry. Neither has minced their words.

The NAO said: “Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for taking over the scheme, Capita has struggled to administer the scheme effectively following the transfer. Key service levels have been repeatedly missed, leaving many members struggling to access the information they need to plan for their retirement.”

Meanwhile, PAC chair Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown spoke of the “alarming reports of hard-working civil servants being thrown into financial uncertainty following Capita’s takeover of the CSPS.”

“Over and over again, promises have been made and broken by Capita, to our faces in formal evidence sessions, that they will get a grip on what has gone wrong,” Clifton-Brown said.

For the time being, Capita is still in charge of running the scheme, and says putting things right for beneficiaries “is our number one priority alongside rebuilding trust with the government.”

But even if it is able to do both of these things, it may be too little, too late. Andy Burnham has already made plain his desire to “end neoliberalism” and absorb more functions of the state into Westminster, away from private hands. A tale such as this will put wind in his sails.

articles.title: Yerevan: The pink-stone capital older than Rome, with hotel rooms from £40
articles.summary:
Every capital has open spaces, but Yerevan’s Republic Square is arguably the most beautiful, thanks to the local building stone: volcanic tuff in shades of pink, orange, and yellow. Easy to carve, Armenian motifs of grapevines and wheat soften the imposing façades. I took a walking tour with Ioanna, learning how to interpret the different buildings, both Imperial Russian and Soviet, then moving into traditional Yerevan courtyards where families shared the cool shade. We paused at the humble flower bed where a statue of Lenin once stood; and gazed up at the enormous Mother Armenia, a replacement for Stalin. Yerevan’s foundation stone is dated 782 BC: this city is older than Rome.

Republic Square, Yerevan, built from pink and orange volcanic tuff (Maximum Exposure)

Sunsets over Yerevan and Mount Ararat

For each sunset, I chose a different vantage point over the city. One was achingly reflective: the platform beside the Genocide Memorial, contemplating how appalling humans can be. The next was at the highest terrace of the Cascade Complex, an artwork in its own right with about 570 steps and a sculpture‑and‑art museum threaded through its levels. Ararat glowed above the rose-tinted city, and whether Armenia ever regains that mountain or not, nothing can block its spirit.

The Cascade Complex, where the highest terrace gives one of the best sunset views over Yerevan (Armenia.Travel)

Day trips from Yerevan: Garni, Geghard and Khor Virap

A 40-minute drive from central Yerevan is Garni Temple, a Greek-style Parthenon perched above a basalt-cliff gorge. The temple is thought to have been dedicated to Mihr, an ancient Armenian fire god, but mythology fans can also spot statues of Atlas, the Titan condemned by Zeus to hold up the sky for eternity. Geghard Monastery, a UNESCO World Heritage Site founded by Gregory the Illuminator in the 4th century, until recently housed the spear said to have wounded Jesus at the crucifixion. It has now been moved to the museum in Vagharshapat, seat of the Catholicos (Pope) of the Armenian Apostolic Church. Gregory the Illuminator, the founder of the Armenian Church, is also connected with nearby Khor Virap Monastery. Here, he was imprisoned in a snake-infested underground cell for 13 years.

Garni Temple, a Greek-style temple a 40-minute drive from Yerevan (Maximum Exposure)

Geghard Monastery, a UNESCO World Heritage Site within easy reach of Yerevan (Maximum Exposure)

The birthplace of wine

In the Bird Cave (Areni-1 Cave) above the Areni River there is compelling evidence – carbon-dated grape pips alongside sunken wine vessels – that Armenians are the inventors of wine. UNESCO dates the site to the late 5th millennium BC. Georgians across the border disagree, but that goes with the territory. Needless to say, any day trip to Areni should include a tasting at a vineyard. Armenian wines are very good.

Dilijan and a jeep ride to the clifftops

Another day, head north from Yerevan. Passing through a tunnel on the road towards Georgia, the scenery dramatically changes. Suddenly, we were in forests with alpine meadows and craggy peaks. Then came Dilijan, a place with more than a passing resemblance to a Swiss village, with a sandstone cliff extending high. We transferred to a jeep capable of handling anything a mountain could throw at it. About 90 minutes later, we were, indeed, perched atop that cliff, my hair tousled by the wind and raised by the exhilaration.

By jeep to the clifftops above Dilijan, north of Yerevan (Maximum Exposure)

Where to stay in Yerevan

The Imperial Palace Hotel (hotelimperial.am; rooms from £40) in Yerevan’s University Quarter is not as grand as its name suggests, but the rooms are of excellent value.

Need to know

Wizz Air (wizzair.com) flies direct from London Luton every Monday and Friday. Yerevan-based tour operator Phoenix Tour (phoenixtour.org) offers the four-night Armenia City Break from £513.

articles.title: Wasps team up with Uefa’s Champions League marketing firm
articles.summary:
Rugby club Wasps will this week ramp up their hopes of returning to Prem Rugby by announcing a partnership with Uefa’s marketing firm Team, City AM understands.

The deal will see the agency that helped turn the Champions League into a €50bn behemoth partner with the former two-time Champions Cup winners as they seek to return to competitive rugby following their administration in 2022.

Wasps, who formerly played at QPR’s Loftus Road and High Wycombe’s Adams Park, became one of three top flight Prem Rugby clubs — alongside London Irish and Worcester Warriors — to cease playing due to financial problems.

Wasps, then playing in Coventry City’s Coventry Building Society Arena, had issues refinancing a £35m bond — secured at 6.5 per cent — before it matured in 2022.

But under Christopher Holland – who also owns Worcester Warriors – the club this month announced plans to build facilities in Kent in the hope of capturing the talent pool in England’s south east.

Team Marketing’s contract with Uefa is coming to an end after more than three decades and the organisation – headquartered in Lucerne but with a London hub – is set to use Wasps as part of a broader advance into rugby.

The Wasps deal is likely to be followed by others in the sport and mark the first of a number of strategic moves to shift beyond Uefa. Team Marketing develops rights by building value, sells rights and then delivers packages for clients.

Wasps comeback offers hope of Prem Rugby return

The move comes as Prem Rugby seeks to expand the English top flight from 10 to 12 teams from the 2029-30 season. It is understood that Welsh regions will express an interest in joining the expanded league, while Worcester Warriors, Wasps and London Irish are also likely to be keen. A number of Champ Rugby clubs, too, are set to express their interest in joining the league before an official tender opens next year.

If Holland is successful in returning Wasps to the top flight, he would not be able to own Worcester Warriors in the same league. City AM understands that a pitch deck for the sale of Warriors is making its way around potential buyers, alongside similar documents from a number of other clubs seeking a full or partial sale as investment sweeps into English rugby.

Upon submitting plans for the Wasps community and academy training ground last week, Holland said that the move was an “important moment in our journey to return Wasps to the professional game”.

He added: “We recognise what this club means to its supporters, its former players and the communities with which it has been connected for generations.

“Our ambition is to build a sustainable and resilient future that honours that history while creating a strong foundation for the years ahead. We know there is still work to do, but this is a meaningful step forward.”

Both Wasps and Team Marketing were approached for comment.

articles.title: Poundland bidders locked in four horse race as deal deadline looms
articles.summary:
Four bidders are racing to snap up Poundland with the discount retailer just days away from collapse. 

Newcomers Premier Quality Foods and Zachert Private Equity have held crunch talks with the management of Poundland’s owner Gordon Brothers in recent days, sources close to the matter said, hoping to thwart the two bidders who were already circling the retailer.

Those are Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG) and little-known investment vehicle Xyra Group Holdings, who have been in talks with Gordon Brothers for a number of weeks. 

The parties hoping to buy Poundland as a going concern have until Wednesday night to win over Gordon Brothers. On Thursday, the retailer will collapse into administration. 

Xyra Group, which is led by 23-year-old Manvedeep Singh, had previously been positioned as the frontrunner to acquire Poundland because of its pledge to pay more than MPG towards a loan attached to the retailer, of which Gordon Brothers holds £22.5m.

But the recent emergence of Premier, a Dubai-based wholesaler, and Zachert, a German-based investor, has turned the bidding process into a four-horse race, City AM understands.

“There are multiple routes here to see this business to a new acquirer. It’s just a matter of time,” one person with knowledge of the discussions told City AM. 

Premier’s bid for Poundland is not reliant on third-party funding, unlike some other offers being considered by Gordon Brothers, City AM understands.

Zachert, a German-based group founded by former Bloomberg journalist Olaf Zachert, has “funding and credibility” on its side and is “moving at a quick pace,” a source with knowledge of the discussions said. 

Xyra Group has presented Gordon Brothers with a detailed plan to boost Poundland’s performance, which would include an overhaul of its product range. This has been received well by Gordon Brothers but would require additional funding, it is understood.

Martin Property Group has already had several offers rejected by Gordon Brothers so has completed much of the work towards due diligence and proof of funds that these other bidders are racing to complete. 

Meanwhile, administrators AlixPartners are putting together contingency plans in case Poundland falls into administration on Thursday. 

This would occur because a notice of intention to appoint administrators – filed and later extended by Poundland’s management – comes into force on Thursday, following a moratorium preventing creditors from calling in their debts.

At this point, AlixPartners would become responsible for finding the best value for the retailer’s creditors. The administrator would replace Alvarez & Marsal, the City advisory firm which has been overseeing Poundland’s solvent sale.

The administrator would run a process to sell off the retailer’s stock and stores, likely to multiple buyers. A number of retailers – including B&M, Tesco, Lidl, Iceland and The Range – have expressed an interest in picking up some of Poundland’s assets.

Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds held talks with Gordon Brothers on Monday in a bid to ensure that the investment firm protects the retailer’s near-12,000 jobs.

A collapse of Poundland would be the most significant failure in Britain’s retail sector in years and would strike a blow to Andy Burnham’s pledge to revive the high street. The Prime Minister has previously urged Gordon Brothers to find a deal that preserves jobs.

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said last week: “Funds necessary to support Poundland’s ongoing trading continue to be released.  

“We are assessing multiple bids for the sale of the whole company and we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation.”

articles.title: Farage: It was easier when it was just me
articles.summary:
Nigel Farage has blamed Reform UK’s recent woes on his peers but argued the party has “weathered” a recent political storm.

Speaking at the Confederation of British Industry’s conference on Monday, Farage appeared to strike a despondent tone on Reform’s electoral chances even as he said the party remained electorally in a “great position”.

Farage’s reflections in front of business chiefs focused on rows around financial donations, ethnicity questions and online disputes between senior party figures.

Asked on how he looked back on a difficult last six months, Farage said: “It would be an awful lot easier if it was just me really.

“I could stand and fall on what I said and did.”

Farage may ‘thank Burnham’ for reopening Brexit

The Reform leader argued that undercover investigations on the party’s handling of donations and racism allegations had not been “seen before in British politics”, arguing that some reporting was “criminalising”.

Farage said some councillors had said “stupid things”. He then argued that Suella Braverman’s move to say she was not English but rather British-Asian was an “academic debate”, adding “it’s not one I want to have or I wish hadn’t been had”.

He added that he did not know when a parliamentary standards investigation into him would conclude but vowed to stand again and win a “bigger majority” in a by-election in Clacton if he is booted out of Parliament. Farage is under investigation for allegedly failing to register a £5m donation from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the 2024 election.

Farage also noted that the party had survived recent turmoil.

“We’ve weathered it,” Farage said. “What I can tell you [about] is what’s been happening beneath the bonnet, in the engine, over the last six months, puts us in a great position.”

But in a final taunt aimed at his critics, Farage teased: “If you hack my bank accounts, heaven knows what will come out.”

The leader’s remarks point to struggles to maintain popular support throughout a difficult period for Reform where senior figures appear to have come to blows online and undercover sting operations have put the party’s integrity under intense scrutiny.

Various polls suggested that the Conservatives have pulled ahead of Reform by a narrow margin.

At one point during an on-stage interview chat, Farage suggested that he may “end up thanking the Prime Minister” for reviving debates about Brexit. However, he acknowledged that Andy Burnham has “always got the backup of a coalition deal with the Liberal Democrats” even if Labour shed public support.

Polanski also faces business chiefs

Earlier in the day, Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is also facing some leadership tensions, defended a proposal to call Zionism racist.

He also said he wanted to “slam on the brakes” on the construction of AI data centres and called for full nationalisation of water companies, followed by the national grid.

articles.title: Estée Lauder lawsuit against Jo Malone moves ahead
articles.summary:
Beauty giant Estée Lauder’s legal dispute against British perfumer Jo Willcox (nee Malone) over her fragrance collaboration with Zara is moving through pre-trial preparations in the High Court.

The US cosmetics firm bought Malone’s self-named perfume brand, Jo Malone London, in 1999, including the trademark rights to her name. She stayed on as creative director until 2006, when she left her eponymous perfume brand.

After a five-year legal ban on creating any new cosmetics products was lifted, she launched a new fragrance label, ‘Jo Loves’, in 2011. Via her new brand, she agreed to a partnership with Zara to launch a perfume collection which retails between £35 and £50.

Estée Lauder Companies filed the passing off and trademark legal claim in March against Malone, Jo Loves, and ITX UK, Zara’s retail distributor, over the use of Malone’s name on the fragrance packaging, which read “a creation by Jo Malone CBE, founder of Jo Loves.”

The collaboration between Jo Loves and Zara began in 2019. Under the terms of the agreement with Estée Lauder, Malone agreed to avoid using the “Jo Malone” name in relation to commercial purposes, which includes marketing perfumes.

In a case management hearing on Monday, various issues were discussed prior to the trial which is currently scheduled for 2028, mainly in relation to documents which are to be disclosed to support the arguments.

What’s in a name?

ITX UK, in its claim, said the use of “Jo Malone CBE” on the perfume packaging was merely “a creator message” used so shoppers could identify who created the fragrance.

However, roughly 3 per cent of the perfumes from this range did have the same message on their packaging, instead just “Jo Loves” or Malone’s signature “Jo x”, which ITX UK claims to be a mislabelling error.

“These allegedly mislabelled products are significant because they undermine the primary case that they put ‘Jo Malone’ on the packaging merely to describe the products,” Estée Lauder’s legal team said, adding that using the ‘Jo Malone’ name on the packaging “exacerbated confusion beyond what would have occurred if they had just used ‘Jo Loves’ and ‘Jo x’.”

Among the issues discussed were whether Zara must share a redacted quota of fragrances the firm was contracted to design under their 2018 agreement with Jo Loves.

As well as this, it was discussed whether historical product price lists must be provided in order to assess the attention of the average consumer and whether Zara’s pricing may affect the connotations of the Jo Malone brand.

Estée Lauder’s legal team told the court the “luxurious connotations of Jo Malone are undermined” by the pricing.

ITX UK’s legal team compared the pricing to how supermarkets price items, arguing it “would be absurd to share disclosure of prices” as “inevitably, prices fluctuate based on market conditions.” Instead, they offered to share average price brackets in the claim.

Estée Lauder, Jo Loves, and Zara were contacted for comment.

Estée Lauder ‘will protect the brand’

Commenting on the legal proceedings when they were filed, a spokesperson for Estée Lauder Companies said:  “When Ms. Jo Malone sold the brand to The Estée Lauder Companies in 1999, she agreed to clear contractual terms that included refraining from using the Jo Malone name in certain commercial contexts, including the marketing of fragrances.”

“She was compensated as part of this agreement, and for many years, she abided by its terms.”

“We respect Ms. Malone’s right to pursue new opportunities. But legally binding contractual obligations cannot be disregarded, and when those terms are breached, we will protect the brand that we have invested in and built over decades,” they added.

articles.title: Afcon final: Senegal to learn fate of CAS appeal over stripped title
articles.summary:
Senegal will learn tomorrow whether they have been successful with a legal challenge to the decision to strip them of this year’s Africa Cup of Nations title.

The Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport after African football chiefs ruled their team had forfeited the final with Morocco by walking off in protest at a decision – only to return and win 1-0 in extra time.

CAS has said it will render its decision on Tuesday afternoon, having heard arguments from the FSF, African football confederation CAF and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF).

It could uphold CAF’s view that Senegal forfeited the final, overturn that verdict or send it back to CAF for reconsideration. The decision will be binding, with the only recourse for challenge being the Swiss Federal Tribunal on procedural grounds.

Senegal’s victory in the final in Rabat was an upset for hosts Morocco and capped a hugely controversial end to the tournament.

Their players staged a walk-off when Morocco were awarded a penalty late in the game. Play only resumed 14 minutes later, when Brahim Diaz missed the spot-kick. The match went to extra time and Pape Gueye scored the only goal in the 94th minute.

How Senegal win was overturned and Afcon title handed to Morocco

CAF initially fined and suspended individual players and officials from both sides but upheld the result, yet a further appeal from the FRMF led to CAF overturning that decision and awarding Morocco a 3-0 win – and the trophy.

The dispute comes down to whether the Laws of the Game or the Afcon rulebook take precedence. While Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon regulations state that walking off the pitch without authorisation should trigger a forfeiture, Fifa’s laws say that the referee’s decision is final.

CAS said in a statement on Monday: “This is a procedural update regarding the decision for the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF).

“Today, the Parties have been notified that the CAS decision will be rendered Tuesday 24 November 2026 in the course of the afternoon.

“Only information provided through CAS channels is considered official and any announcement concerning this case will be published on the CAS website. CAS is pausing all communications to media concerning this decision until formally announced.”

articles.title: Women’s World Cup to be held in UK in 2035 after Fifa approves bid
articles.summary:
A football World Cup finals will be played in England for the first time since 1966 after Fifa confirmed that the UK will host the women’s tournament in 2035.

The joint bid from England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland faced no rival proposals and was rubber-stamped today at a special congress at governing body Fifa’s Zurich headquarters.

It comes after England’s successful hosting of the Women’s European Championship in 2022 and ahead of the UK and Ireland staging the next Men’s Euros in 2028.

“Today is a day of celebration of women’s football with a day of congress dedicated to that,” said Fifa president Gianni Infantino. “Our objective is making women’s football truly global and to build the future together with all member associations and stakeholders.”

The UK’s 2035 bid was awarded by acclamation, in the absence of any challenges.

FA chair Debbie Hewitt said: “Dear delegates, on behalf of the FAs of England, Northern Ireland, Wales and Scotland, thank you for your trust and confidence in awarding us the Fifa Women’s World Cup in 2035.

“We’re deeply honoured by your support and grateful for the opportunity to host the pinnacle of women’s football on behalf of the global football family.

“We look forward to welcoming you to the United Kingdom in 2035 and working closely with you all in the years ahead to deliver an exceptional Fifa Women’s World Cup that the entire football community can be proud of. Thank you, we can’t wait to begin this journey together.”

Women’s World Cup 2035 format and venues

The 2035 Women’s World Cup will feature 48 nations following the tournament’s expansion for the 2031 edition, which is to be held in the US, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica.

The UK’s bid features up to 22 venues in 16 cities, with the majority of the 39-day, 104-match schedule set to be played in England.

The English venues include Wembley Stadium, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Arsenal’s Emirates Stadium, Old Trafford and Manchester City’s Etihad Stadium.

Others in the bid are Villa Park, Brighton’s American Express Stadium, Ashton Gate in Bristol, Elland Road in Leeds, Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, St James’ Park in Newcastle, the City Ground in Nottingham, Sunderland’s Stadium of Light and Crystal Palace home Selhurst Park.

The non-English venues are Hampden Park in Glasgow, Easter Road in Edinburgh, the Principality Stadium and neighbouring Cardiff City Stadium, and Belfast’s Windsor Park.

Three more stadiums could yet be added, subject to planned development: Birmingham’s Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham’s Racecourse Ground and a mooted Chelsea venue.

articles.title: FCA bans jump by a third as regulator cracks down on bad actors
articles.summary:
The City watchdog has handed out more career-ending bans this year as it steps up its crack down on bad actors, City AM can reveal.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) barred 24 individuals from working in financial services between January and 9 November 2026, up from 18 across the entirety of last year, according to figures obtained through a Freedom of Information request.

The data also reveals a wider clearout across the sector. Nearly 4,200 City workers saw their regulated roles wiped off the Financial Services Register during the same period, after the watchdog shut down or stripped permissions from the firms employing them.
