Over the course of last year, 6,541 individuals ultimately lost their roles after their firms were struck off. 

Wider shakeup

The Financial Services Register is the FCA’s official database of every individual and firm permitted to carry out regulated financial work in the UK.

Consumers and employers are able to check the register to confirm if a firm or adviser has legal authority to carry out services. The database also permanently flags disciplinary actions, revoked permissions and individuals barred from the industry. 

The surge reflects a deliberate shift in strategy by the regulator, which has pledged to deliver “timely and visible” enforcement, leaning more heavily on banning bad actors and removing authorisations from dormant or rule-breaking firms rather than letting investigations drag on for extended periods.

The watchdog also tightened its accountability rules to prevent rogue financiers from jumping to rival employers before internal misconduct probes have been completed, forcing firms to flag suspected wrongdoing in references. 

String of strike-offs

The jump in bans comes amid a wave of high-profile enforcement cases spanning the Square Mile so far this year, ranging from personal misconduct to ignoring compliance rules.

In September, the regulator saw its ban and a £1.5m fine against high-profile hedge fund founder Crispin Odey upheld by the Upper Tribunal. Odey was banned for his “lack of integrity” and breaching of governance rules.

This included twice using his majority ownership powers of Odey Asset Management (OAM) to remove its executive committee when it was to hold a disciplinary hearing into allegations that he breached a warning for misconduct towards female employees.

Elsewhere, financial adviser Frank Breuer was banned and fined £755,000 after stripping cash out of his firm to dodge paying compensation to pension clients, while trading boss Kasim Garipoglu was barred after treating compliance rules as an “inconvenience”.

The watchdog has also gone after misconduct that occurs outside of the workplace. In October, the FCA banned a former HSBC worker for dodging nearly £6,000 in train fares, ruling that his dishonesty made him unfit to work in the industry.

An FCA spokesperson said: “We’ve increased the pace and focus of our enforcement work to protect consumers and markets.

“We will take action against firms and individuals where they fail to meet our standards, using the full range of powers available to us to tackle misconduct and keep our markets clean.”

articles.title: Tech stocks surge as Jensen Huang is reinstated as Nvidia chief executive
articles.summary:
Tech stocks across Wall Street surged after the opening bell on Monday, as Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive sent investors rushing back into AI-linked companies.

Nvidia’s shares surged 33 per cent after markets opened in new York, a sharp reversal from its 21 per cent loss last week. Until Monday, the stock had lost $2.5 trillion in value since its October peak.

The share moves follow Nvidia’s announcement that it would resinstate its co-founder to his role as chief executive, after he initially resigned following news of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

In a statement, Nvidia said its board had voted unanimously to reinstate Huang “following a series of discussions and meetings…after which the board was satisfied with respect to Huang’s candour and ability to lead Nvidia”.

The board said it had received input from “senior levels” of the US government and that the investigation into Huang was still ongoing.

The chipmaker’s surge into the green also revived major US indices.

The Nasdaq 100 increased 7.1 per cent in early trading, while the S&P 500 increased 4.8 per cent. The Nasdaq 100 briefly saw futures trading halted due to volatility before markets opened, as investors rushed back following the announcement of Huang.

“Nvidia is once again at the centre of the market, with Jensen Huang returning as chief executive helping fuel a spectacular rebound in the shares and a broader revival in risk appetite,” said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG.

“The scale of today’s move shows just how important Huang has become to the Nvidia story…whether investors will ultimately change their minds remains another question, but for now Huang’s return is proving to be exactly the shot in the arm that the battered AI trade needed.”

Anthropic fails to follow

Anthropic shares failed to follow the resurgence following its blockbuster listing last week. What was initially billed as a defining moment for the AI boom, granting investors a chance to gain exposure in a company at the technology’s frontier while avoiding worries elsewhere in the trade, soured when its shares plunged in the day after its IPO.

The Claude-maker’s shares fell 20.2 per cent from its initial opening price of $111.5 on Thursday and shares slumped 1.8 per cent to $87.2 after market open, extending its steep 8.5 per cent Friday loss.

Other tech stocks and chipmakers recorded gains alongside Nvidia, including Intel which increased 14.1 per cent.

Broadcom and Micron also rose 5.1 per cent and 14.8 per cent respectively.

Asia losses deepen

Prior to Huang’s reinstatement, the tech-sell off deepened in Asia, led by major chipmakers.

South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.3 per cent to 4,708.5 points, bringing its monthly losses to 15.1 per cent.

The decline was led by index heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, two key suppliers of memory chips needed for AI application, which shed 3.1 per cent and 2.8 per cent respectively.

Taiwan’s Taiex managed to recover from last week’s fall into the red, gaining 2.1 per cent, after Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) avoided losses and reported an uptick in share price.

articles.title: London’s skills shortage is really an opportunity shortage
articles.summary:
When Alan Milburn talks about the barriers holding young people back, those of us working in local communities recognise the story immediately.

Where a young person grows up continues to shape the opportunities available to them. Talent may be evenly distributed, but opportunity is not. That should matter to anyone concerned about London’s future prosperity.

Businesses across the capital say they cannot find the talent they need. Yet thousands of young Londoners struggle to access the jobs, networks and experience needed to start their careers. This is not a skills shortage. It is an opportunity shortage.

For those of us working with young people every day, that conclusion feels obvious. We meet talented, ambitious young people every week.

They have ideas, energy and determination in abundance. What they often lack is access: to employers, professional networks, work experience, mentors and opportunities many professionals take for granted.

In Tottenham, we see the consequences every day. In Haringey, 38 per cent of children grow up in poverty after housing costs. In neighbouring Enfield, the figure rises to 40 per cent. Many employers talking about skills shortages are just a few miles from young people they have never attempted to recruit.

How Together Tottenham is helping

The talent is there. The ambition is there. What is often missing is a connection. Take Levi Ngimbi. Last year, Levi joined one of our entrepreneurship programmes. Today, at 24, he runs his own creative agency, Preacher, has secured his first paying clients and sits on Spurs in the Community’s youth advisory board.

He says the programme gave him a platform he could not have built alone. His story is inspiring. It should also be entirely unremarkable.

That is why Tottenham Hotspur and Spurs in the Community have launched Together Tottenham: a commitment to create 150,000 opportunities for young people to learn, earn and lead by 2030.

Bringing together work across education, employability, skills, health and community development, our ambition is to create clear pathways from a young person’s first experiences at school through to employment and leadership.

We want their postcode to have less influence over their prospects than their ability and determination.

But no single institution can solve this challenge alone. Football clubs have a role. Schools have a role. Local authorities have a role. The missing piece is business.

Opening up access means widening the talent pool, finding people with different experiences and capabilities, and building a workforce that better reflects the city in which businesses operate. Employers overlooking young people on their doorstep may also be overlooking their future workforce.

What businesses can do

And the contribution businesses can make is often simpler than they think. A week of work experience. A paid internship. An apprenticeship. A mentoring session. A careers talk. An introduction. For a young person with limited professional networks, any one of these can change what feels possible.

That thinking sits behind Call Up, the first major initiative under Together Tottenham. Run by Spurs in the Community with Maikai, it connects young people across North London with jobs, apprenticeships, mentoring, training and work experience.

Tottenham Hotspur has also committed to using its apprenticeship levy to create more skilled, paid pathways into the club. Now we want other employers and organisations to join us.

London’s future prosperity depends on how effectively we develop and use the talent already here. We cannot keep talking about economic growth while leaving so much potential untapped.

The next generation of talent is already here. The question is whether we are prepared to invest in it. Together Tottenham is our commitment to playing a part in that effort. But one football club cannot employ a borough.

If we are serious about economic growth, social mobility and building a more competitive city, we need to stop treating opportunity as something that happens by chance. Talent is everywhere. Opportunity should be, too.

Marc Leckie is chief executive of Spurs in the Community.

articles.title: Badenoch tells business chiefs she won’t back Burnham’s ‘terrible’ EU deal
articles.summary:
Kemi Badenoch has told business leaders Andy Burnham’s deal to sign up to EU rules on food standards and carbon emission markets will leave the UK without a “seat at the table”.

The Tory leader said the deal was “more than just sacrificing sovereignty” as it meant the country would have to follow the EU’s rule changes for the foreseeable future. Her deputy has said previously that the party would scrap the deal if it was elected into government.

Speaking to business leaders at the Confederation of British Industry’s annual conference, Badenoch suggested the UK should resist being a “rule taker from the EU” and said Burnham had agreed a “terrible deal” even if alignment in some areas of the economy could add 0.4 per cent to GDP, per initial Treasury estimates.

Burnham hails ‘reset’ deal

Burnham’s EU deal has been one of the chief ways that he has sought to win over the private sector and boost the government’s growth credentials. The split between the two mainstream parties and disagreements within either could set Britain up for a heated debate on relations with Europe once again.

Badenoch argued that the Tories back greater “access to markets” and understood why some businesses wanted an “easier trading relationship with the EU”.

She added that the UK could benefit from agreements that New Zealand has by recognising each other’s standards on areas of goods and services, in an early indication of the Conservatives’ own approach on dealmaking with the EU.

But when asked whether she accepted that closer ties represented trade-offs on sovereignty and rule-making, Badenoch told City AM the argument had been made years ago and that the UK should not take rules that it had “no control over”.

“We are not just protecting the rules the EU has today, we are accepting any future rules they may decide to put in, and they’re not going to be thinking about us when they make those rules or what works for us,” Badenoch said.

“We’re not going to have a seat at the table.”

She also argued that Europe was “not the market of the future” given lower growth rates while saying that the issues facing Britain related to energy costs, borrowing and a struggle in retaining talent and high-growth companies.

Burnham attacks zombies entering EU debate

In a broadcast interview on Monday, Burnham said he would ignore advice from several former prime ministers, including the likes of Theresa May and David Cameron, who urged the Prime Minister against rejoining the bloc.

“”I’m not sure they’re the people I’ll be listening to”, he said.

“They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did.”

“If we can do something to boost growth, why wouldn’t we do it?”

He added: “That would be my question to those former prime ministers.”

The government is set to introduce legislation this week on the trade deals. The deal at a summit last week featured agreements on food standards, energy markets and allowing 100,000 EU migrants under the age of 32 to study and work in the UK every year after 2030.

articles.title: Back with a Huang: Jensen reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia after Trump call
articles.summary:
The board of Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive just days after his resignation, following revelations of multiple affairs with subordinates and a suspected Chinese spy.

In a statement the company said: “The board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia. 

“In the process of reaching its decision, the board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Huang, who co-founded the chipmaker and had been at the helm for decades, abruptly resigned earlier this month after a string of revelations over extramarital affairs with clients and colleagues, one of whom was reportedly a Chinese spy. 

The company began an internal investigation, while the US FBI also began its own probe.

But Huang has since sought to rejoin the board as boss, attracting the support of Silicon Valley tech founders such as Elon Musk, as well as US president Donald Trump.

“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang said in a statement posted to X.

“I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes entirely.

“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Nvidia shares tumbled as much as 40 per cent over the past month, wiping more than $1 trillion in value from one of the world’s most valuable listed technology companies.

But the stock rapidly rebounded on Monday following Huang’s surprise reinstatement, adding back the lost $1 trillion to the firm’s market cap.

US President Donald Trump said it was “the correct and proper decision” for the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang, adding that the US government did not possess evidence that the tech executive had engaged in any unlawful conduct.

“On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” he said.

But Trump cautioned that Nvidia “should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security.”

articles.title: The story of The Ned’s spectacular Christmas tree
articles.summary:
Exclusive: The Ned’s tree is on display from today in the former banking hall

With hoteliers across the capital entering a luxury arms race to present the most fabulous Christmas tree, how has the Square Mile got ahead?

How about spending eight days crafting each handmade floral decoration, with every leaf or flower made from organic silk? “It’s quite tricky to make a large petal that has to defy gravity!” says Juliet Carr, founder of the Paper Poms company that made the pieces for this year’s Christmas tree at The Ned. There are 2,000 decorations and 6,000 lights on the tree, which was sourced by the hotel’s in-house florist, who spent weeks scouring Christmas tree farms to find the right specimen. 

The Ned’s triple height ceilings and wide halls demand a particularly tall and full tree, although, reminds managing director Gareth Banner, it still needs to fit in the door. “It arrives on a flatbed lorry and takes at least 15 people to carry it in,” says Banner. “It’s quite an operation.”

‘More is more’ at The Ned

Indeed, The Ned’s plushness – those majestic emerald green columns, original stone flooring and latticework – requires a tree with character to compete with the former banking hall. “More is more,” says Banner.

At The Ned last night, it was operation as usual. A wintery Sunday, hundreds were gathered in the centre of the building, listening to the live music at The Nickel Bar, or sitting at the famous ‘posh’ buffet, as they do every Sunday. But when the final guests emptied their glasses at midnight, 20 workers arrived to quietly begin the careful installation of the 22 foot tall tree felled from Kent. They worked through the night, placing the final petals at 6am this morning, ahead of a media launch (with champagne, naturally) while guests slept soundly upstairs.

More than 60 handmade flowers, some 80 centimetres wide, will cascade down the tree, inspired by the flowers on Perrier-Jouët’s Belle Époque bottle, created by the French artist and designer Emile Gallé for Perrier-Jouët in 1902. The champagne house has partnered with the hotel for the second time and are delighted with the evergreen, which they say “brings the Maison’s signature white anemones to life in a spectacular winter setting.”

Baubles in Champagne pink

Indeed, the fine French bubbles are referenced on the tree itself, whose baubles will be in gold and pink to reference the drink’s effervescent quality. Champagne will be sunk on the deep sofas near the three, as a live band thumbs instruments atop the podium at the heartcentre of the lobby, around which The Ned’s 12 bars and 10 restaurants mean you can truly have anything: there is tableclothed silver service, if you should so wish, or milkshakes at a US themed bar.

As for those magnificent petals, which reference the Japanese anemone motif, a French supplier dyed the fabrics in two distinct shades of maroon, adding tonal depth, and gold tips have been added to the tips to welcome in a little fantasy. Lightweight but strong fabric is used so the petals are robust while also able to glow, with amber and peach tonation to bring warmth. As well as adding rich textures and layers of decorations, “embracing nature and the natural shape” is the secret to a perfect tree, says Mary Wood, director of Grandirosa, the venue’s in-house florist. 

It’s a great opportunity to staycation in the Square Mile. Why would you bother leaving the capital when you could book a room at The Ned for access to their private in-house spa facilities, and spend the weekend gawping at this fabulous tree?

But what about the competition? Claridge’s? Or more locally in the Square Mile, Pan Pacific’s tree, which is the tallest in London? “No competition,” she laughs. “Just great company.”

articles.title: Next says data stolen in cyber attack on supplier
articles.summary:
Fashion giant Next has warned that hackers have accessed some of its customers’ data in a cyber attack on one of its suppliers. 

The firm said on Monday morning that a third-party supplier had been hit by a “cyber incident that resulted in unauthorised access to certain benign data relating to Next”.

The incident comes amid rising fears of firms’ vulnerability to rampant hackers, whose recent targets include fintech Revolut, fast-fashion seller Asos and cryptocurrency exchange Binance. 

Next said it is “working closely with the supplier, law enforcement and relevant regulatory authorities” in the wake of the attack, which it stressed has not affected customers’ data.

The group told shareholders: “We took immediate steps to investigate the nature and scope of the incident with the supplier. 

“Our investigations are ongoing; however, current evidence indicates that no customer personal data has been compromised.  

“The information affected is limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next.”

The FTSE 100 firm insisted that the cyber attack only affected its supplier, which was not named. The group said: “For clarity, we are confident that NEXT’s own systems have not been compromised and that this remains an incident affecting the supplier’s environment.”

Shares in Next gained about 0.6 per cent on Monday, to 15,980p. The stock has gained 18 per cent in the year to date.

M&S, Asos and Co-op among targets

Next has become the latest high-profile retailer to be affected by a cyber incident, but it is far from the first. In October, hackers sent a push notification to users of Asos’ app, warning the online retailer that it would leak customer information.

The incident, which cost the group between £4m and £8m in lost sales, came after a hacker duped an Asos employee into sharing information needed to log in to its systems. 

Retailers in Europe have been rocked by a series of cyber attacks on fridges and freezers, in which hackers put up the temperature of the devices, costing millions of euros in spoiled food.

Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre have carried out a behind-the-scenes operation to secure thousands of fridges and freezers at UK supermarkets from a potential attack, the BBC has reported.

Last year also saw a spate of cyber attacks, in which retailers including Marks & Spencer, Co-op and Harrods were affected. M&S said their attack cost it more than £100m, while Co-op lost out on £206m in sales.

articles.title: Arm boss Haas reaffirms commitment to chip designer after Nvidia approach
articles.summary:
The boss of Arm has reaffirmed his commitment to the chip designer after speculation he may be tapped as a replacement to the ousted founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang.

Rene Haas, who leads the $162bn Nasdaq-listed company, said he is “wholly committed” to its future as he inked a new deal that will extend his leadership until 2033.

“I’ve never been more confident about Arm’s future,” Haas said in a statement. “I believe deeply in our people, our strategy and the opportunity ahead. I’m incredibly proud of what we’re building and wholly committed to realizing Arm’s full potential for many years to come.”

As part of the agreement, Haas will also take on the the role of Vice Chairman of SoftBank Group, Arm’s biggest shareholder, from next week.

The move locks in the boss of the Cambridge-based firm after he was reportedly approached by headhunters to gauge his interest in replacing Huang at Nvidia.

Nvidia has been in crisis after Huang, who founded the company 33 years ago, was ousted following revelations of relationships with multiple subordinates and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based customer Megaspeed who is suspected of Chinese intelligence links.

Haas previously worked at Nvidia for seven years, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business. He was immediately tipped as a potential successor following Huang’s resignation, alongside candidates including interim Nvidia chief Collette Kress and Lisa Su, boss of rival AMD.

The American executive led Arm through its IPO in 2023 and overseen an explosive period of growth that has cemented the company at the heart of the AI boom.

In its statement today, Arm said it had an opportunity to “extend its leadership and become an even more integral part of the world’s computing infrastructure, creating long-term value for shareholders”.

While Huang has said publicly he would be willing to return to Nvidia should it call on him to do so, its board has ruled out a return.

articles.title: Haigh sets Natural England up for axe and hints at control of water companies
articles.summary:
Louise Haigh, the Prime Minister’s chief enforcer, has paved the way for the abolition of quangos across Whitehall, including the environmental regulator Natural England, yet suggested that water companies could be nationalised in the coming years.

In a speech to business leaders at the Confederation of British Industry conference, the chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster – and de facto deputy prime minister – said the government was reviewing the role of “unelected regulatory bodies and independent agencies”. 

Haigh mentioned that Natural England, the Environment Agency, the Drinking Water Inspectorate and Ofwat were under review for potential changes, with the government looking to bring more powers under ministerial briefs as part of Andy Burnham’s public control agenda. She said some public bodies could be “dissolved” or passed on to local leaders. 

Burnham’s ten-year plan

She argued that the PM’s 10-year plan would not usher in “full fat nationalisation” although public ownership of water companies should “absolutely be an option”.  She pointed to public ownership of utilities such as power and water in the US, which was “hardly a hotbed of state socialism”.

“We’ve spent forty years attempting, and failing, to simulate market conditions where consumers lack other options,” Haigh told an audience of business owners and investors. 

“Public control is simply about achieving the desired results. It’s not driven by ideology – ownership itself isn’t a prerequisite.”

She also directly addressed public servants, saying that the government would “accept a higher level of risk” and take greater accountability for failings. 

The first secretary of state also repeated that “time is a tax” throughout her speech and hinted at a further clampdown on judicial reviews, which she described as a “chill factor” for major infrastructure projects. 

“When challenge is unavoidable for the most critical projects, we will offer indemnities so that developers do not down tools.

“That is what public control offers: an opportunity for stability and certainty, for national renewal through public and private investment.”

Further proposals on the planning system and the cost of housebuilding are set to be laid out by the government, she said.

Haigh opens door to tariffs on China

Haigh also fielded questions on the government’s bid to pursue closer ties with the EU.

When asked about whether the UK would be prepared to increase tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles to bring the country in line with the economic bloc’s ‘Made in Europe’ policy, she said there was a “process in order to protect our critical industries, including the automotive industry and steel, from the Made in Europe agenda”. 

She added that Burnham “share[s]the concern” held by the EU that Chinese products were “flooding” onto European markets. 

Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, said: “For far too long, Natural England has been allowed to hold the country to ransom, blocking desperately needed homes and vital infrastructure.

“That’s why the Conservatives have pledged to abolish it. Now, it seems Labour are lifting that plan wholesale.”

articles.title: Rapport London: 128 years of family craft comes to London Watch Week
articles.summary:
When The Royal Exchange hosts London Watch Week – The City Edition this November, Rapport London will be among the names celebrating the City’s longstanding connection with watchmaking. Founded in 1898, the fourth-generation family business brings 128 years of horological heritage to an event rooted in the Square Mile’s own history.

For centuries, the City has moved to the rhythm of time. From pocket watches and elegant dress watches to contemporary mechanical timepieces, watches have accompanied generations of Londoners through their working days.

One can almost picture a City gent in pinstripe trousers and bowler hat, umbrella under his arm, consulting a pocket watch as its gold chain catches the light.

Four generations of family clockmaking

In watchmaking, expertise takes time to develop. Genuine heritage cannot be acquired overnight, and the roots of lasting traditions run deep.

Its story began with twenty-year-old clockmaker Maurice A. Rapport, whose first timepieces laid the foundations for a family business that has since evolved from traditional clockmaking into luxury accessories for watch collectors.

Still a family business today, Rapport has been guided by four generations. From Maurice A. Rapport’s earliest timepieces, the family built a reputation for British horology, with clocks finding their way into homes in Britain and beyond.

Over the decades, Rapport established a reputation for finely made clocks and timepieces, including elegant carriage clocks, with careful attention to design and detail.

There is a particular charm in the quiet presence of a fine clock on a mantelpiece: a reminder that timekeeping can be both practical and beautiful.

That clockmaking heritage laid the foundations for the craftsmanship, innovation and meticulous attention to detail that continue to define the company.

Now in its fourth generation of family ownership, Rapport remains faithful to the principles established by its founder: quality, service and thoughtful innovation.

Rapport London today: Watch winders and collector boxes

Today, Rapport London combines its British heritage with contemporary design and modern technology, creating watch winders, collector boxes and luxury accessories for collectors around the world.

The result is a brand that respects traditional materials and craftsmanship while responding to the changing needs of modern watch enthusiasts.

Across its collection of watch winders, watch boxes, trunks and travel accessories, Rapport brings together considered design and practical functionality, offering fitting companions to treasured watches and jewellery.

A Rapport London leather watch pouch for travel

Why automatic watches need a watch winder

A fine watch deserves a fine home. For owners of automatic watches, a carefully configured winder can help maintain the movement’s power reserve between wears, particularly when resetting a complicated watch takes time.

A Rapport London double watch winder

From carefully selected woods and Italian leathers to beautifully finished lacquered surfaces, the collection offers a variety of ways to store and display a treasured timepiece.

The Evolution, Paramount and Heritage collections

This combination of heritage and innovation is evident in the Evolution Single Watch Winder, available in an elegant Macassar finish, where practical winding technology meets refined design.

The company’s contemporary collections also embrace features such as biometric fingerprint access, touchscreen controls and adjustable winding settings, offering collectors security and flexibility for a wide range of automatic watches.

For larger collections, the Paramount range of multi-watch winders provides an impressive display. Equally, the Heritage Ten Watch Box in Burr Walnut offers a beautifully traditional way to store and enjoy a collection.

A Rapport London nine-watch box

Yet, as with a fine watch, these pieces are best appreciated in person: the richness of the finishes, the craftsmanship of the details and the reflections across a carefully polished surface.

See Rapport London at London Watch Week

London Watch Week offers an opportunity to explore the collection firsthand, whether seeking a thoughtful Christmas gift or a lasting addition to a personal collection.

On Wednesday 18 November 2026, visitors to The Royal Exchange can discover Rapport London’s collection and the attention to design and detail that has shaped the family business for four generations. True heritage, like true craftsmanship, is measured in time.

articles.title: Isa providers face £20m bill as HMRC tightens scrutiny of allowance breaches
articles.summary:
Isa providers are set to be hit with a £20m bill as HMRC looks to tighten its monitoring of accounts and savers in a bid to crack down on allowance breaches and wider errors.

Under regulations published following the Autumn Budget, the tax authority is overhauling its oversight of the tax-free savings accounts by scrapping the current system of annual reporting in favour of a monthly digital feed.

From April 2028, roughly 500 Isa managers will be required to report ‘subscription events’, which are any actions that alter an investor’s position, to HMRC each month. This includes deposits, allowance adjustments and provider transfers.

Savers will also be legally forced to hand over their national insurance number, or formally confirm they are ineligible for one, before opening or paying into an Isa.

The tax authority added providers will have to chase down national insurance numbers from existing customers who did not previously supply one.

While the government anticipates the overhaul to carry no operational costs to HMRC, it expects the changes to hit financial services firms with £20m in one-off bills and £1.7m in ongoing annual administrative costs.

Tightening the framework

HMRC said the tighter framework is designed to “enable subscription breaches to be identified” and resolved “closer to the point at which they occur”, rather than relying on slow interventions once the tax year ends.

The authority added the monthly reporting will also allow it to identify subscriptions exceeding the £20,000 annual Isa limit “more quickly”, meaning affected investors will face strict deadlines to fix excess contributions once flagged.

The changes will affect both cash and stocks and shares Isas.

According to the latest government statistics, between April 2023 and 2026, there were just 357 Isa compliance audits of 16.8m accounts. Tim Stovold, head of tax at Moore Kingston Smith, said the figure represented “a fraction of a percent of the population”.

“HMRC has finally acknowledged that individual compliance checks into people with accounts is not an effective way to police the Isa system,” Stovold said.

“Now, HMRC will gather data each month from providers, linked to a person’s national insurance number, so they can check how many people are using multiple Isas to avoid the £20,000 cap on contributions.”

Cash Isa u-turn

The overhaul follows Chancellor John Healey’s decision to reverse cuts to the cash Isa ceiling made by his predecessor.

Healey decided to end plans to lower the annual cash Isa limit from £20,000 to £12,000 from April 2027 in his maiden Autumn Budget.

Cutting the allowance had been designed by former chancellor Rachel Reeves to funnel cash into UK companies and get more amateur investors placing capital in the stock market. Healey argued this was the wrong approach to persuade people to invest more in stocks and shares.

An HMRC spokesperson said: “These changes will help us spot and correct ISA mistakes sooner. This will reduce time and hassle for savers when errors are made and help ensure everyone is playing by the same rules.

“We’ve given ISA managers more time to prepare for these changes, including the new digital reporting requirements.”

articles.title: The Office for Investment is a true success story for the City
articles.summary:
A year on from its launch, Chris Hayward says the Office for Investment has been a true triumph for financial services

It’s nearly five years since I was elected policy chairman of the City of London Corporation. In that time, I have travelled around the world meeting government leaders and international investors, promoting the wealth of opportunity that can be found in our great nations and regions.

But for too long, international investors have found it difficult to navigate our regulatory and legal landscape, understand who to speak with, and determine where to establish and expand their businesses.

That simply isn’t good enough, not least when our closest competitor in financial and professional services, the United States, has long recognised the importance of providing dedicated support via programmes such as SelectUSA, which has helped attract more than $500bn worth of investment to America, including in banking, insurance and fintech. 

So, in July 2025, following earlier calls from the UK regulators for a concierge service, I urged then Chancellor Rachel Reeves to create the Office for Investment: Financial Services (OfI:FS), a one-stop shop to support international investors looking to establish or expand in the UK. To her credit, she responded quickly, launching the office in October that year. The Financial Conduct Authority and Prudential Regulation Authority were advocates of the concierge service, which was established as a true partnership across government, regulators and industry.

Around a year on from that defining moment, and as chair of the OfI:FS Advisory Committee, I am proud to see the office delivering.

A one stop shop for financial services

OFI:FS has delivered or is currently delivering tailored supportive actions for more than 100 individual firms, encouraging international firms to grow and scale in the UK. This support takes the form of regulatory guidance and business setup to immigration assistance and making connections with government.

This matters because it demonstrates a fundamental shift in how we approach investment. Rather than leaving firms to navigate a complex web of institutions independently, OfI:FS brings together expertise from across government, including HM Treasury, the Home Office, the Financial Conduct Authority, the Prudential Regulation Authority and the City of London Corporation to provide coordinated, practical support. We’re also proud to have KPMG, BDO and Eversheds Sutherland collaborating with OfI:FS, offering tailored support to companies looking to invest in the UK.

Ultimately, OfI:FS is a one stop shop geared towards improving access, helping investors understand the right processes, find the right people and make informed decisions more quickly.

The companies being helped by the Office for Investment

Take the experience of international fintech firm Ramp. Unfamiliar with the UK’s regulatory architecture, the company needed to understand which permissions it might require to operate here. OfI:FS helped clarify the possible routes, allowing the firm to identify an appropriate pathway.

Or consider Rogo, the AI partner for top financial institutions that’s been establishing a London presence. When its founder encountered questions around the appropriate immigration route, OfI:FS connected the company with the relevant government team. Rogo has since built an initial London team of 20, with ambitions to grow to around 50 by the end of 2026.

These examples illustrate why joined-up government working with business is so powerful. Investment decisions are rarely made on the strength of one factor alone. Firms need confidence in regulation, access to talent, suitable locations and the ability to engage with the right institutions.

The prize extends far beyond the Square Mile. OfI:FS is designed to connect international investors with opportunities across all four nations and every region of the UK. This ambition is complemented by initiatives such as Invest Connect, the City Corporation’s new AI investor-led platform connecting UK and global institutional capital with infrastructure and real-asset investment opportunities across the country, helping turn regional investment potential into tangible growth and jobs. Early progress shows what can happen when government, regulators and industry work together towards a shared objective.

Chris Hayward is policy chairman at the City of London Corporation

articles.title: Crestfallen: Under-pressure housebuilder slumps as cash woes persist
articles.summary:
Shares in Crest Nicholson took a pounding after the beleaguered housebuilder said it will suffer from “challenging” conditions “well into next year”. 

The London-listed builder told shareholders it will meet only the bottom end of its housebuilding targets and deliver a bigger loss than previously expected, as emergency talks with its lenders drag on.

Shares in Crest Nicholson fell by more than 25 per cent to 46.5p in early trading, meaning the stock has lost 67 per cent of its value in the year to date.

UK housebuilders like Vistry and Taylor Wimpey have cut homes targets and slashed jobs in recent months, as higher mortgage rates slow the market, but Crest Nicholson has been among the worst affected. 

The housebuilder said it has built 1,353 homes, at the bottom end of its 1,350-1,400 target. The firm now expects an EBITDA loss of between £30m and £40m, well below its previous £10m guidance. 

Crest Nicholson had previously warned of “subdued” market conditions but said on Monday that these have “deteriorated further” in recent months. Its sales rate slipped to 0.34 in the last two months, significantly below the year average of 0.43.

The group said it “expects the current challenging trading conditions to persist well into next year” and warned of a “prolonged period of weak sales volumes, weak pricing and persistent build cost inflationary pressures”.

The firm said it will review its land bank and downgrade the value of a number of its assets in response to this “deteriorating market environment”. 

Lending talks drag on

Since April, Crest Nicholson has been locked in crunch talks with its lenders in a bid to secure softer borrowing terms. The group delayed its half-year results in July in the hopes of completing these talks but said on Monday that it has still not found a resolution.

The firm said: “The Group remains in constructive discussions with its lenders to amend its covenants and ensure that it has an appropriate level of funding and liquidity going forwards. The Group is also thoroughly exploring alternative sources of debt financing.”

Analysts at RBC Capital Markets said this latest delay suggests “current discussions are not as supportive or constructive as we would have hoped, although the Group is leaving no stone unturned to find the best deal for the business and shareholders”. 

The analysts said they expected Crest Nicholson’s shares to suffer on Monday, though they added that its better debt position, with £240m available, will “mitigate some of the impact”. 

The housebuilder said it welcomed the government’s revival of George Osborne’s Help to Buy scheme, which offered equity loans to help buyers afford the deposit on their first house.

But the government has been criticised for the timing of its Your First Home scheme, which will not take effect until April next year. Analysts suggested that Crest Nicholson would not see an uplift from the programme until the second half of next year.

articles.title: Zurich warns firms face ‘hidden’ AI risks despite using separate models
articles.summary:
Insurance giant Zurich has warned businesses which rely on multiple AI systems to protect against disruption remain exposed to risks caused by underlying tech failures.

In new research from the Swiss insurance firm and the University of St. Gallen based on interviews with 50 industry and risk experts, Zurich warned that while firms may believe they have hedged their AI risk by using multiple suppliers, those tools often share the same foundational models and digital infrastructure beneath the surface.

Zurich said this means the systems may “behave or fail in similar ways because they draw on similar data, assumptions, architecture or decision logic.”

Recent events, including a wave of cyber attacks which hit high-street retail firms and European supermarket refrigerators, have “demonstrated how digital disruptions can quickly spread across organisations and sectors, highlighting the risks created by shared dependencies,” Zurich said.

The insurance firm warned that correlated AI failures may emerge through otherwise separate industries through waves of complaints, claims, regulatory action or litigation.

AI failures, Zurich said, may “spread across companies and sectors through hidden connections between systems.”

“AI will transform business. The opportunity is enormous, but we also need to understand the risks. Companies need to know where they depend on AI, what can happen when it fails, and be prepared to respond and recover quickly,” Mario Greco, group chief executive officer, Zurich Insurance Group, said.

Professor Dr Karolin Frankenberger, university of St. Gallen, said the challenge posed by AI now “is not simply to innovate faster, but to build systems we understand, can trust and can recover when they fail.”

“That resilience will be critical to economies and societies,” Frankenberger added.

While risks tied to AI are easier to insure against when they can be identified and measured, Zurich said insurance “cannot replace risk reduction or absorb every systemic loss.”

‘Hidden risks’ of autonomous AI and IP

The firm also warned that businesses using autonomous AI systems to negotiate contracts or execute payments without human intervention are creating hidden risks where legal liability is hard to trace when the tech fails.

Another hard-to-measure risk, Zurich said in its report, may hit firms using generative AI without knowing what data the models have been trained on, leaving them potentially exposed to intellectual property issues.

articles.title: Another blow to London as FTSE 100 catering giant departs for New York
articles.summary:
One of the biggest companies in Britain is set to switch its main listing from London to New York, dealing another heavy blow to the UK’s public markets. 

FTSE 100 catering firm Compass, which operates canteens in schools, offices and sports venues, could announce an end to its decades-long primary London listing as soon as Tuesday, according to sources familiar with the matter. 

The Surrey-headquartered firm is poised to launch a consultation on the move which could see the switch take effect in 2028 if approved by shareholders, the Financial Times first reported.

Compass has been listed on the London Stock Exchange since 1988. The group operates in 30 countries but generated about two thirds of last year’s $46bn revenue in North America. The group’s switch to a US main listing would be part of its efforts to capitalise on its opportunities in this market, sources said.

In April, the firm switched the trading currency of its shares from sterling to US dollars in a bid to attract international investors. 

Compass gets a significant portion of its business from the tech sector, where Google, Amazon and Microsoft are among its clients. The group also provides catering for the defence industry, airline lounges and data centres.

In July, the firm said a glut of new outsourcing clients had helped it secure $4.3bn in new business across the previous 12 months, marking a 16 per cent year-on-year uplift.

There would be no impact on the company’s operations in the UK, where it employs about 55,000 people, if the switch was approved by shareholders, it is understood. The firm would retain a secondary listing in London if the move went ahead.

London becoming ‘hostile environment’

Compass is one of the FTSE 100’s 20 biggest companies, with a market value of £43bn. Its shares closed trading on Friday at 33.5p and have gained nearly nine per cent in the year to date.

The firm’s potential main-listing switch to New York would deal another blow to the London Stock Exchange, which has suffered a flurry of high-profile departures in recent years. 

UK-founded fintech Wise, Paddy Power owner Flutter and equipment rental firm Ashstead are among those who have recently ditched primary listings in London in favour of New York. 

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Compass’s move to quit London shows the UK “is becoming a hostile environment for the welath creators who create jobs and pay for our public services.”

He added: “Too many companies are leaving or never listing in the UK thanks to the red and green tape being imposed upon them.

“We have a ‘listings crisis’, yet far from de-regulate to allow London to compete, ministers plan to force companies to come up with ethnic pay reporting, and have allowed the FCA to go ahead with new environmental reporting that even their own Listing Advice Panel told them not to do.”

London’s recent departures have exacerbated a years-long drought of new listings. The city sits behind Turkey and Malaysia in 12th place globally for the value of new floats this year. 

The government’s attempts to slash red tape to encourage IPOs are yet to rejuvenate London’s public markets. Earlier this month, a Nigerian cement empire owned by Africa’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, scrapped plans for a UK listing.

Compass Group declined to comment.
