articles.title: Ukraine deals major blow to Putin’s Crimea lifeline, European intel assessment claims
articles.summary:
Ukraine's repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prized infrastructure projects, have dealt a potentially significant blow to Moscow's military supply routes into occupied Crimea, raising questions about Russia's ability to sustain operations as both sides prepare for a difficult winter.

A European intelligence assessment dated Nov. 18 and obtained by Fox News Digital describes Ukraine's latest assault as likely its most successful attack on the heavily defended crossing, following a coordinated campaign targeting Russian air defenses, radar and electronic warfare systems.

Ret. Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital the consequences could extend far beyond the destruction of a symbolic Russian landmark. "The Russians are extremely limited in how they get supplies to Crimea and cutting the Kerch bridge will severely, severely damage their ability to resupply Crimea," Breedlove said.

UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

On Nov. 17, Ukrainian missiles and drones struck the 12-mile bridge linking Russia's Krasnodar region to Crimea, collapsing a major section of the roadway into the Kerch Strait and damaging the adjacent railway.

The crossing, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, has served as both a critical transportation link and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

According to the European intelligence assessment, the attack followed a multiweek Ukrainian operation against Russian defensive systems, intended to weaken the bridge's protection before the main strike.

Ukraine subsequently struck the railway again on Nov.19, temporarily halting train traffic and bringing the number of attacks to three in four days.

The damage has disrupted one of Russia's most direct supply connections to Crimea, which Moscow uses to support military operations in southern Ukraine.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

Russia has developed an alternative land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, but the European intelligence assessment warns that shifting additional military supplies onto those roads could create significant vulnerabilities.

The assessment identifies slower transportation routes, exposure to Ukrainian drone attacks and pressure on other logistical infrastructure as potential consequences.

Breedlove said Ukraine's campaign should be viewed as an attempt to weaken Russia's hold on the peninsula, rather than simply destroy a bridge. He argued that Russia's options are further constrained by Ukraine's success in challenging Russian naval power in the northern Black Sea.

He pointed out that Ukraine has used maritime and aerial drones to push back Russia's Black Sea Fleet despite lacking large conventional warships.

The European assessment also warns that repairing the bridge could take months. Although limited road traffic might resume within weeks, replacing the collapsed section could take considerably longer, particularly if Ukrainian attacks continue.

Damage above the Kerch–Yenikale Canal could also disrupt shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

Despite Ukraine's success in striking the bridge, a European intelligence source familiar with Russian strategic assessments offered a pessimistic view of the broader conflict.

"It has more symbolic meaning, but also logistics is paralyzed right now," the source told Fox News Digital, describing the immediate impact of the attacks.

However, the source warned that Moscow is preparing to intensify its winter offensive while using negotiations with Washington to increase political pressure on Kyiv.

"The general trend is not good for Ukraine," the source said.

According to the source, Russia believes it can sustain military pressure long enough to force Ukraine into territorial concessions, particularly in the east.

"They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source said, describing Moscow's expectations.

Breedlove strongly disputed the assessment that Russia was gaining the upper hand militarily.

"Militarily, the tide is turning against Russia," Breedlove told Fox News Digital, arguing that Russian forces have suffered staggering casualties while making limited battlefield gains.

He said Russian losses in recent months had been extraordinarily high and argued that Moscow's military was failing to achieve significant territorial advances.

Breedlove did, however, acknowledge a distinction between military momentum and the political pressure facing Ukraine.

He suggested that changes in Washington's approach to negotiations could strengthen Putin's position even if Russian forces were struggling on the battlefield.

The competing assessments highlight a central question facing Ukraine: whether its military successes can translate into greater diplomatic leverage before Russia's winter offensive intensifies.

UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA

Putin has threatened retaliation over the bridge attacks, and on Friday Russia launched a massive missile and drone assault against Ukrainian cities, killing at least eight people, according to Ukrainian authorities.

The strikes came hours after Putin appeared alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a summit in China, as Washington continued efforts to advance peace negotiations.

The European intelligence assessment warns that further Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge during repairs are highly likely, potentially prolonging disruptions to Russian supplies.

For Moscow, restoring the crossing is now both a logistical challenge and a political priority. For Kyiv, keeping it vulnerable offers a way to increase the cost of Russia's occupation while demonstrating that even Putin's most heavily defended infrastructure remains within reach.

articles.title: New drug combo shrinks tumors in most patients facing aggressive cancer type
articles.summary:
Pairing an experimental pill with standard chemotherapy shrank tumors or halted growth in most patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, according to early clinical trial results presented Friday at a major international cancer conference.

The findings, shared at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium in Barcelona, come from a phase ½ trial testing a daily oral medication called daraxonrasib, along with two standard intravenous chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel.

The trial focused on 61 patients whose pancreatic cancer had already spread to other organs and who had not yet received treatment for their advanced disease.

PANCREATIC CANCER PATIENT BEN SASSE SEES 'MASSIVE' TUMOR REDUCTION WITH EXPERIMENTAL NEW DRUG

Pancreatic cancer is notoriously difficult to treat because more than half of patients are diagnosed after the disease has already spread, research shows.

In major clinical trials for metastatic pancreatic cancer, chemotherapy alone shrinks tumors in about 23% to 42% of patients, but the disease typically begins growing again after five to six months, and most patients survive between 8 and 11 months.

According to National Cancer Institute data, only about 3% of patients with distant-stage disease live five years past diagnosis.

In the new study, which tracked patients for a median follow-up of 18 months, tumors shrank in 60.7% of cases, including 8.2% where they disappeared entirely on scans. Overall, the combination stopped tumor growth in 90.2% of participants.

FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

Patients went a median of 12.8 months before their cancer worsened, almost double the timeframe typically seen with standard chemotherapy, and 76.6% were still alive at the one-year mark, the study found.

"We are now seeing not only substantial tumor shrinkages, including complete responses, but also durable disease control, with median progression-free survival exceeding one year," study lead Dr. Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, said in a press release.

More than 90% of pancreatic cancers are driven by a faulty gene called RAS, which allows tumors to keep growing. Daraxonrasib is designed to turn off that growth signal, something scientists long thought was impossible to fix with medication.

Dr. Elena Garralda, chair of the symposium and co-director of the clinical research program at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology in Spain, who was not involved in the research, said the results show that RAS-targeted drugs can be combined with existing treatments at the start of treatment to potentially achieve longer-lasting benefits.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Side effects included rash, diarrhea, fatigue and low blood cell counts linked to chemotherapy, most of which were manageable with standard care.

Only 5% of patients stopped treatment because of side effects tied to daraxonrasib.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers emphasized that the findings carry some limitations.

Because this was an early-phase, single-group study involving 61 people, all participants received the experimental combination. Without a direct comparison group of patients receiving standard chemotherapy alone, doctors cannot yet confirm how much better the new regimen performs or whether it definitively extends overall survival.

The findings also apply strictly to metastatic pancreatic cancer, even though RAS mutations drive several other cancers, including certain lung, colorectal and gynecological cancers. Separate studies would be needed to test whether the combination works in those diseases.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The trial was funded by Revolution Medicines, the California-based developer of daraxonrasib.

To determine whether these early findings translate into a durable survival benefit, researchers have launched a larger, randomized Phase 3 trial, called RASolute-303, which directly compares daraxonrasib — both on its own and combined with chemotherapy — against standard chemotherapy alone.

articles.title: Uber Parking could save you from circling the block
articles.summary:
You finally make it downtown for dinner, but now comes the real challenge. Finding somewhere to park. You circle the block once, then again. Before you know it, you're late and getting frustrated. Sound familiar? Well, Uber thinks it has a solution. The company just launched Uber Parking, a new feature that lets you reserve a parking spot directly through the Uber app before you even leave home. Yes, the same company that built its business around getting you into someone else's car now wants to help when you drive your own. And there's another interesting twist. Uber has plans for those parking garages that involve robotaxis.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

UBER LETS PARENTS WATCH TEEN RIDES LIVE

On Nov. 9, Uber announced the launch of Uber Parking, bringing parking reservations directly into its app. The feature follows Uber's acquisition of SpotHero, a popular parking reservation service. Through that deal, Uber gained access to a network of more than 13,000 parking garages, lots and valet locations across more than 400 cities in the United States and Canada.

So, instead of driving around looking for parking, you can search for an available spot near your destination. You can also see the price upfront, making it easier to decide whether driving makes financial sense. For someone heading into the city for dinner or trying to get to an important appointment, that could save some aggravation. And if you've ever paid a small fortune to park somewhere, you'll probably appreciate being able to compare prices before arriving.

Uber has made the process pretty simple. You can book parking using the same app you already use to request a ride.

Here's how it works:

Once you've booked, your digital parking pass appears inside the Uber app. Depending on the location, you'll either scan a QR code or enter through a system that recognizes your license plate. Uber also says you can extend reservations through the app if you need more time. Cancellation policies vary by parking facility. Some reservations qualify for a full refund if canceled before the scheduled start time. Always check the booking terms before paying.

One thing worth mentioning: Uber generally won't physically park your car for you. Unless you choose a valet location, you'll still be the one behind the wheel.

FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

Uber Parking launched in 15 U.S. cities on Nov. 9.

Those cities are:

Uber plans to expand the service into additional markets. However, there's an important detail here. Although SpotHero operates across more than 400 cities, Uber Parking has not yet expanded throughout that entire network. Also, the new feature is still rolling out. So, even if you're in one of the launch cities, you may not see the Parking icon immediately. First, make sure you're using the latest version of the Uber app. You can also visit SpotHero's website to search for parking in areas where the Uber feature is unavailable.

Here's a little bonus if you already pay for Uber One. Uber says eligible members can earn 10% back in Uber One credits on qualifying parking reservations once their parking session is complete. You can use those credits toward future eligible Uber rides or Uber Eats orders. For example, if you spend $30 on a qualifying parking reservation, you could earn $3 in Uber One credits.

That may not sound like a fortune. However, if you're regularly parking downtown, those credits could add up. Just keep in mind that the 10% reward only applies to eligible reservations. You also need an active Uber One membership to qualify and redeem the credits. And remember, these are Uber credits rather than cash back to your bank account. Before booking, compare the total parking price with other nearby options. A cheaper garage could still save you more money than the rewards you'd earn.

Uber also sees parking garages as part of its future robotaxi business. Think about it. When a driverless taxi drops someone off, what happens next? If another passenger needs a ride nearby, that's easy enough. But what happens when nobody needs the car? Does it keep driving around until another request comes in? That could mean more empty vehicles on already crowded streets. Uber is reportedly exploring ways to use parking facilities as waiting areas for autonomous vehicles. Instead of driving around without passengers, robotaxis could pull into nearby garages and wait for their next assignment.

Then, when someone requests a ride, the vehicle could head out to pick them up. Uber believes that approach could reduce unnecessary driving and help lower operating costs. There's another potential benefit. Keeping autonomous vehicles in nearby facilities could make it easier to have them ready when demand increases. However, this remains a developing plan. Uber has not announced that every SpotHero garage will accommodate robotaxis, and the company has not provided a timeline for a broad rollout of these facilities. For now, the immediate focus remains helping people find parking for their own cars.

There's something else worth paying attention to here. For years, Uber built its business around giving people an alternative to driving. Now, the company wants you opening its app even when you plan to take your own car. Let's say you're going downtown for dinner. You could check the price of an Uber ride. Then, you could compare that with the cost of driving and parking.

If driving looks cheaper, you can reserve a space through Uber. If taking a ride makes more sense, you can book that instead. Either way, Uber stays part of your plans. And as autonomous vehicles become more common, the company could eventually use that same parking network to support its robotaxi partners. It's an interesting strategy, especially as Uber looks for more ways to keep people using its app.

The biggest benefit is pretty straightforward. You may be able to reserve parking before leaving home and spend less time driving around looking for an available spot. That could be especially useful when you're heading somewhere unfamiliar or trying to make a flight. However, there are a few things I'd recommend checking before you book.

Don't assume Uber offers the lowest rate. Check the final price against other parking options before paying. Also, make sure your reservation covers the time you'll actually need.

Some parking garages have height limits. If you drive a larger SUV or truck, check those restrictions before booking. Also, confirm the exact entrance address, which may differ from the garage's street address.

Some parking reservations can be canceled for free before they begin, but the rules vary by location. Review the specific garage's cancellation terms before booking. Once your reservation starts, Uber says it can no longer be canceled or refunded.

Some garages use QR codes for entry. That's convenient, but criminals have also placed fake QR codes on parking meters to trick drivers into visiting fraudulent payment websites. Use the parking pass provided directly through your Uber app rather than scanning an unfamiliar sticker. We've previously reported on how criminals use fake parking QR codes to steal money.

Even with a reservation, finding your car afterward can still be a headache. Fortunately, Google Maps and Apple Maps have tools that can help you remember where you parked. Our guide to finding your parked car with Maps explains how to set them up.

I think Uber is onto something here. Who hasn't wasted time driving around looking for parking, especially when you're already running late? Being able to reserve a spot before leaving home sounds pretty convenient. Of course, I'd want to make sure I'm getting a good price. But what really caught my attention is Uber's plan to use parking garages for robotaxis. Having driverless cars park between rides makes sense, especially if it means fewer empty vehicles clogging up our streets. Still, I wonder what happens when those garages start filling up with robotaxis. Will there be enough room for the rest of us? That's something I'll be watching as this technology takes off.

Would you trust Uber to handle your parking reservations, or do you worry that parking garages could eventually become crowded with robotaxis, leaving fewer spaces for the rest of us? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse launches in UK
articles.summary:
LONDON — Meta rolled out its personal AI agent Muse to the U.K. adults on Tuesday, promising users a tool they can trust to lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping.  

It is the first AI agent product to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., and regulators will be watching closely. 

The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF), comprising the Competition and Markets Authority, Financial Conduct Authority, Ofcom, and the Information Commission, published a statement last month warning that AI agent products “may amplify and accelerate risks” to consumers.

Reuters reported last week that Meta staffers had raised concerns internally about “undesired actions” carried out by the agent since its debut in the U.S., from accessing encrypted messages to supplying bogus information about purchases (a Meta spokesperson said these were “isolated incidents.”)  

In a blog post published Tuesday morning, Meta sought to reassure would-be users that although the agent is built to carry out tasks on their behalf, Muse is “private, safe and secure by design.” For example, users can choose whether their interactions with the agent are used to develop and improve Meta’s AI — though will need to actively switch this setting off.

“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta said in its blog post.

articles.title: Budget de l’UE : c’est Noël avant l’heure pour Emmanuel Macron
articles.summary:
BRUXELLES — Emmanuel Macron se rendra jeudi à un sommet européen des chefs d’Etat et de gouvernement en position de force, après les concessions cruciales qu’il a obtenues sur le budget de l’UE pour 2028-2034. En privé, d’autres Etats membres se sont montrés optimistes quant à la conclusion d’un accord en décembre.

Le président français, dont le mandat se terminera au printemps 2027, est apparu comme le grand gagnant de la dernière proposition dévoilée samedi par le président du Conseil européen, António Costa. C’est d’ailleurs sur ce texte que vont batailler les dirigeants européens lors de leur réunion à Bruxelles.

Même s’il a suscité des critiques de toutes parts — y compris venant de Paris —, un projet budgétaire qui penche du côté des positions françaises est le signe qu’un compromis est possible, sachant que la France est à mi-chemin entre les deux principaux camps qui s’opposent dans ces négociations.

Le plus beau cadeau de Costa à Macron est d’avoir inclus, parmi ses propositions de nouvelles recettes fiscales européennes, l’instauration d’une taxe sur les géants du numérique — une ville idée française, écartée en 2018 par crainte de représailles américaines. Parmi les autres concessions faites à Paris, António Costa a préservé les aides aux agriculteurs de toute coupe, proposé de nouvelles taxes pour plafonner les contributions nationales au budget de l’UE, et reporté le remboursement de 10 milliards d’euros de l’emprunt commun post-Covid.

Preuve de la complexité du débat : la députée européenne Renaissance Fabienne Keller a, d’un côté, qualifié de “bonne nouvelle” la proposition de taxation des géants du numérique et, de l’autre, fustigé des coupes budgétaires qui “sapent les ambitions de l’Europe” et “lui coupent les ailes”.

Avec une enveloppe globale de 1 780 milliards d’euros sur sept ans, la dernière proposition budgétaire d’António Costa est inférieure de 44 milliards à la version présentée le mois dernier par l’Irlande, qui assure actuellement la présidence tournante du Conseil de l’UE. Les Etats membres se divisent entre ceux qui veulent un budget plus modeste, axé sur les priorités actuelles, telles que la défense et la compétitivité ; et ceux qui veulent que l’UE dépense davantage et se concentre sur les domaines habituels, comme l’agriculture et le soutien aux régions les plus défavorisées.

Malgré des divergences importantes, António Costa et la plupart des gouvernements nationaux sont déterminés à parvenir à un accord d’ici la fin de l’année.

“On dirait que le père Noël est passé plus tôt cette année pour les Français”, ironise un diplomate européen qui, comme d’autres personnes citées dans cet article, a souhaité garder l’anonymat afin de pouvoir s’exprimer librement sur ces négociations sensibles.

“Profondément décevant”

Le pas de Costa vers Macron représente une victoire rare en cette fin de mandat compliquée pour le président français. La perspective d’un second tour en 2027 entre une Marine Le Pen eurosceptique et un Jean-Luc Mélenchon qui veut “désobéir aux traités” — tous deux étant actuellement en tête des intentions de vote — est l’une des principales raisons qui motivent l’UE à parvenir à un accord sur le budget cette année.

Selon plusieurs diplomates, Costa et Macron entretiennent une relation de travail étroite et partagent des ambitions similaires en matière de dépenses européennes. Ils “ont la même stratégie qui consiste à considérer les nouvelles ressources propres [les taxes] et le report de NextGenEU [le remboursement de la dette post-Covid] comme des questions à résoudre avant la fin de la partie”, observe un deuxième diplomate.

Les Etats membres se préparent néanmoins à des négociations difficiles. Scène typique du théâtre politique : le président français a qualifié la proposition d’António Costa de “très décevante”, ajoutant qu’elle “ne constitue pas une base pour un accord”.

Ce pourrait aussi être une tactique, les Français étant réputés pour leur fermeté dans les négociations et, comme le fait remarquer un autre diplomate européen, pour vouloir remporter chaque match 10 à 0 plutôt que de se contenter d’une victoire plus modeste. “Je ne comprends pas vraiment les critiques de l’Elysée”, souffle l’un des diplomates. “En gros, ils ont obtenu ce qu’ils voulaient.”

Manifestation d’agriculteurs

Aux yeux de Paris, la proposition d’António Costa prévoit des coupes budgétaires excessives, et des garanties insuffisantes pour les agriculteurs — une profession puissante aux enjeux importants dans le budget de l’UE.

Une critique reprise par le puissant lobby agricole Copa Cogeca, qui a annoncé une manifestation à Bruxelles le jour du sommet européen.

Des policiers sont aperçus à côté de tracteurs lors d’une manifestation d’agriculteurs à Bruxelles, le 18 décembre 2025. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

Cependant, d’autres Etats membres n’ont pas tardé à démasquer le bluff de Paris. Ils ont noté qu’António Costa a maintenu 297 milliards d’euros d’aides directes aux agriculteurs, et qu’il a transformé un objectif vague de dépenses “rurales” en de nouveaux fonds destinés au secteur.

“Chaque nouvelle [proposition budgétaire] s’accompagne d’un nouveau cadeau à l’agriculture et d’une nouvelle réduction des fonds alloués à la modernisation”, résume un troisième diplomate européen originaire d’un pays dont les contributions au budget dépassent les montants que le pays perçoit.

Malgré les plaintes, les diplomates interrogés par POLITICO se sont montrés plus optimistes quant à la capacité d’António Costa à mener les Vingt-Sept vers un accord définitif d’ici la fin de l’année — avant les élections en France, en Italie et en Pologne, qui menacent de faire dérailler les négociations. Les Etats membres doivent d’abord parvenir à un accord entre eux avant de chercher à s’entendre avec le Parlement européen.

Dans une déclaration samedi, le chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz a souligné la nécessité de conclure les négociations “avant la fin de l’année 2026”.

Le risque Le Pen “pas pris au sérieux”

Malgré ces coupes budgétaires — qui touchent la quasi-totalité des dépenses, à l’exception des subventions accordées aux agriculteurs —, le projet de budget reste, en termes réels, supérieur d’environ 25% au cadre financier pluriannuel 2021-2027, même si une grande partie de cette augmentation est due au remboursement de la dette post-Covid.

Tout au long des négociations, Emmanuel Macron a plaidé en faveur de nouvelles taxes européennes, appelées “ressources propres”, afin de générer des recettes supplémentaires et de limiter la contribution de la France au budget de l’UE, qui est la deuxième plus importante après celle de l’Allemagne.

António Costa a fait une concession à Paris en maintenant largement le niveau de recettes visé avec ces nouvelles taxes — environ 60 milliards d’euros, comme l’avait proposé la Commission européenne l’année dernière.

Le Portugais a également mis au point une solution pour reporter certains paiements — et économiser des milliards d’euros lors du prochain cycle budgétaire —, en prolongeant d’un an le délai dont disposent les Etats membres pour dépenser leur part des fonds régionaux.

Selon le président du Conseil européen, cela permettra de limiter la hausse des contributions nationales, qui passeraient de 0,80% à 0,82% du revenu national brut des pays — une priorité majeure aussi pour d’autres contributeurs nets, surnommés les “frugaux”, parmi lesquels figurent l’Allemagne et les Pays-Bas.

Il se pourrait toutefois que ces concessions ne suffisent pas pour faire accepter un accord d’ici la fin de l’année aux pays frugaux les plus radicaux.

“Il y a toujours le sentiment qu’il vaut mieux ne pas conclure d’accord plutôt que de conclure un mauvais accord”, soulève le premier diplomate européen. “Les discours alarmistes concernant Le Pen ne sont pas pris au sérieux dans le camp des frugaux.”

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

articles.title: Türkei sieht Europas Wohlstand in Gefahr – wegen des IAA
articles.summary:
Wenn ein türkischer Handelsminister nach Deutschland reist, gibt es meist etwas zu feiern. Der Handel hat sich in 30 Jahren verdreifacht, in diesem Jahr jährt sich das Gastarbeiterabkommen zum 65. Mal, das seit 1996 bestehende Zollabkommen zwischen Ankara und Brüssel gilt für beide Seiten als Erfolg.

Doch der Besuch von Ömer Bolat vergangene Woche lief anders: Es war eine Abrechnung mit der EU-Politik. Und eine Warnung an Deutschland, dass ein Wohlstandsverlust drohe. Der Grund liegt in einem ganz bestimmten Brüsseler Gesetzesvorhaben.

Bolat kam am Donnerstag nach Berlin, um auf dem Deutsch-Türkischen Automobilgipfel zu sprechen. Im Anschluss traf er Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche unter vier Augen.

Er nutzte seinen Auftritt vor der Autobranche für Kritik an einer EU-Verordnung, die, so sagte er es im Interview mit POLITICO, Deutschland und der Türkei schaden könnte. „Die deutsche Wirtschaft hat sich als drittgrößte Volkswirtschaft der Welt dank internationaler Investitionen, des Außenhandels und einer offenen Außenwirtschaft erfolgreich entwickelt“, sagte Bolat. „Würde man sich dem internationalen Wettbewerb verschließen, würde der Wohlstand sofort sinken und die Preise für die Verbraucher steigen.“

Es geht ihm um den sogenannten Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). Dessen Ziel ist es, die europäische Industrie zu stärken und Arbeitsplätze zu sichern – vor allem gegen den unfairen Wettbewerb aus China. Als Mittel sollen bei allen Förderungen innerhalb der Europäischen Union und in der öffentlichen Vergabe sogenannte „Made in EU“-Quoten eingeführt werden. Sie sollen dafür sorgen, dass ein bestimmter Anteil der Wertschöpfung in der EU erbracht werden muss.

Die Verhandlungen darüber laufen noch in Brüssel. Ein Abschluss wird Anfang kommenden Jahres erwartet. Die große Streitfrage ist: Zählt für die Erfüllung der Quote wirklich nur Produktion innerhalb der 27 EU-Staaten? Was ist mit Produktion in Partnerländern wie der Schweiz, Großbritannien und der Türkei? Und was mit den rund 80 Freihandelspartnern Brüssels?

Nach aktuellem Verhandlungsstand zwischen EU-Parlament und Rat wäre die Türkei raus. Das hätte massive Auswirkungen auf die europäische Autoindustrie, warnt Bolat.

250.000 Jobs in Europa seien in Gefahr, die Kosten für Autos könnten sich um bis zu neun Prozent verteuern, besagen Zahlen des türkischen Handelsministeriums. Da in Deutschland mehr als ein Drittel der europäischen Auto-Arbeitsplätze liegen, stünden 90.000 der noch 887.000 Jobs in der Autoindustrie infrage.

Auch für die Türkei könnte der IAA gefährlich werden. Um 68 Prozent könnten die Autoexporte in die EU bis 2035 einbrechen, so Bolats Zahlen. 330.000 türkische Jobs wären weg.

Die Ursache liegt in den engen Verkettungen zwischen der türkischen und europäischen Autoindustrie. Da die Montage am Bosporus wesentlich günstiger ist, verlagerten spätestens nach der Einführung der Zollunion 1996 viele Autobauer den letzten Schritt, darunter Stellantis (unter anderem Opel, Fiat und Citroën), Renault und Ford. Nur wenn sie an dieser Stelle Geld sparen, ließe sich der Rest der Industriearbeitsplätze in Europa erhalten, so lautet das Argument der meisten Unternehmen.

„Ford ist seit fast 100 Jahren in der Türkei vertreten, und diese Präsenz hat sich im Laufe der Zeit erheblich weiterentwickelt“, sagte Nicola Walker, Chefin des Politik-Teams bei Ford Europa, zu POLITICO. Dort baut Ford seine Nutzfahrzeuge, vor allem den erfolgreichen Van Transit. „Etwa zwei Drittel der Transporter, die wir in der Türkei produzieren, werden im EU-Binnenmarkt verkauft.“

Die elektrische Version des Fahrzeugs bestehe zu 56 Prozent aus Komponenten, die aus der EU stammen. „Sämtliche Batterien beispielsweise werden in der EU hergestellt“, sagte Walker. Weil die Endmontage aber außerhalb der EU stattfindet, könnte so ein E-Transit nach dem IAA nicht mehr gefördert oder vom Staat gekauft werden. Da E-Fahrzeuge hierzulande von der Kfz-Steuer befreit sind, sind 100 Prozent der E-Autos subventioniert. Das Geschäftsmodell von Ford in Europa wäre gefährdet.  

In Gefahr sind damit aber nicht türkische Standorte. Denn während das Geschäft mit den Nutzfahrzeugen ordentlich Geld in die Kasse spült, und Ford in der Nische zum Marktführer macht, schwächelt das Pkw-Business. Am Kölner Standort wurden seit 2025 mehr als 4000 Arbeitsplätze abgebaut.

Das Werk in Köln machte 2024 das erste Mal wieder Gewinn – nach jahrelangen Verlusten. Die Zahlen für 2025 stehen noch aus. Der Anteil an Neuzulassungen an Ford-Wagen in Deutschland schrumpft aber kontinuierlich.

Ob durch den IAA am Ende auch das Werk in Köln in Gefahr ist, wollte Walker nicht beantworten. Nur so viel: „Die politischen Entscheidungsträger, die über den IAA beraten, sollten all die Arbeitsplätze und Investitionen in der EU berücksichtigen, die unmittelbar durch die Montage in der Türkei gesichert werden.“

Deutschland hat sich in der Vergangenheit immer für Freihandel ausgesprochen. Katherina Reiche spricht deshalb lieber von „Made with Europe“. Ihrer Meinung nach sollten sämtliche Freihandelspartner integriert werden. Damit würden bestehende Lieferketten weitestgehend erhalten bleiben. Doch innerhalb der Bundesregierung konnte sie sich mit dem Ansatz nicht durchsetzen.

Kanzler Friedrich Merz und Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron haben über den Sommer einen Deal abgeschlossen. Sie verbanden damit verschiedene europäische Themen, bei denen Berlin und Paris unterschiedliche Ansichten haben. Viel Einfluss auf die Verabredung soll Reiche dem Vernehmen nach nicht gehabt haben.

Am Ende stand ein Kompromiss: Macron kommt Merz bei der Auto-Regulierung entgegen. Im Gegenzug gab Paris beim IAA klein bei, sodass auch Berlin seitdem offiziell dafür ist, dass „Made in EU“ für Autos gilt. Nur Großbritannien und die Schweiz sollen für die Quote zusätzlich berücksichtigt werden, nicht aber die Türkei.

Für Katherina Reiche ist das heikel. Denn sie verhandelt den IAA in Brüssel, obwohl sie selbst weiter für „Made with Europe“ ist. Auch den Termin mit Bolat hat ihr Haus erst auf Nachfrage von POLITICO bestätigt und machte ihn nicht im Nachgang – wie sonst üblich – öffentlich.

Der Deal zwischen Kanzleramt und Élysée betreffe nur die Autoindustrie, heißt es aus dem Wirtschaftsministerium auf Anfrage. Der Auto-Deal „verändert nicht die Position der Bundesregierung zum Industrial Accelerator Act im Weiteren“, heißt es weiter. „Die Bundesregierung setzt sich beim Industrial Accelerator Act für die anderen Sektoren und Technologien weiterhin für einen ‚Made with Europe‘-Ansatz“ ein.

Die Regierung fährt also zweigleisig: Während für alle Technologien außer Autos alle Partner integriert werden sollen, würde das für Deutschlands wichtigste Industrie bedeuten: Nur Autos, die auch in der EU zusammengeschraubt werden, gelten als europäisch. Davon profitieren dürften die Autobauer Volkswagen, Mercedes und Audi, die große Werke in der EU haben.

Doch die Türkei würde zum Kollateralschaden für eine härtere Abschottungspolitik Europas gegen China.

articles.title: Back to 1936? Civil war ghosts haunt Spanish election campaign
articles.summary:
Back to 1936? Civil war ghosts haunt Spanish election campaign

With the far right poised to enter government, politicians are reopening the wounds of a war that began 90 years ago.

By AITOR HERNÁNDEZ-MORALES
in Belchite, Spain

Picture taken in 1936 of Spanish soldiers loyal to the young republic as they arrive in Madrid from Vicálvaro to fight against nationalist troops of Gen. Francisco Franco. | AFP via Getty Images

Ninety years after the outbreak of the civil war, Spain’s campaign for the Nov. 29 election has unmistakable echoes of 1936, with politicians resurrecting the rhetoric of a conflict that still runs deep in the polarized national psyche.

At a meeting of Socialist Party supporters in Puerto de la Cruz, Tenerife, on Saturday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the crowd in chants of “¡No pasarán!” (“They shall not pass!”), the slogan immortalized by the left-wing forces that resisted fascist leader General Francisco Franco’s three-year siege of Madrid.

Meanwhile, both far-right leader Santiago Abascal of the Vox party and Madrid’s regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso, of the center-right People’s Party, are referring to their left-wing opponents as the “Popular Front,” the name used by the coalition of communist, socialist and republican forces that governed Spain on the eve of the outbreak of the civil war.

“The Popular Front that Pedro Sánchez has assembled will not relinquish power democratically,” Ayuso warned during an interview on the Cuatro television network last month, accusing the prime minister of leading Spain toward “revolution.”

Tensions over those historic fault lines of 1936-39 have only been heightened by the prospect of the far right entering national government for the first time since the restoration of democracy in the 1970s. Vox is expected to become the PP’s junior coalition partner, meaning old antifascist songs and slogans have become commonplace at left-wing rallies.

The resurgent guerracivilismo — rhetoric evoking the divisions and existential stakes of the civil war — underscores Spain’s increasingly divided society today.

A September survey tracking social cohesion and political polarization by More in Common found that 70% of Spaniards view their country as divided — the highest proportion since the polling organization began tracking the sentiment in 2021.

Pedro Riera, head of the social sciences department at Madrid’s Carlos III University, said he was not surprised to see politicians invoking the conflict. For Spanish society, he said, the war remains the most emblematic example of the country’s divisions and has become less taboo.

“Our transition to democracy was built on a pact of silence, but as time has passed, people — and political parties — have become less afraid of addressing the war, and politicians now invoke it to mobilize their supporters,” he said.

Riera stressed the civil war was hardly top of mind for most Spaniards, who are far more concerned with “issues like housing or the overall cost of living.”

But the conflict still weighs on the national conscience. “The fact that political parties are resorting to this issue indicates that it is a divide that is still not fully resolved for a relatively important segment of the population,” he continued.

The battle over the dead

That fracture is particularly visible in Belchite, a municipality in the northeastern region of Aragón where the battle over the legacy of the civil war foreshadows the politics a PP-Vox government could bring to the rest of Spain.

Fierce fighting devastated Belchite during the war, changing hands between Republican and Francoist forces within a year. Although the town could have been rebuilt, Franco ordered its residents to be relocated to a newly built settlement and decreed Belchite be left as a ruinous monument to the destruction wrought by left-wing forces loyal to the Republic.

Today, the shattered streets and bullet-scarred buildings routinely serve as a film set. But the ruins are also a physical reminder that the civil war remains unfinished business — not least for the families still searching for the bodies of those who went missing during the conflict.

The ruins of the old village of Belchite, Aragón seen on Nov. 12, 2015. | Gerard Julien/AFP via Getty Images

Around 114,000 people disappeared during the war and Franco’s dictatorship. Some 12,000 of the missing victims’ remains are believed to still be recoverable from mass graves and other burial sites across Spain, with more than 200 possibly lying in and around Belchite.

José Vidal, president of the Mariano Castillo Association for the Recovery of Democratic Memory, said his group had excavated 11 mass graves and recovered 105 sets of remains. Yet some of the largest burial sites remain inaccessible, buried beneath cemetery niches built in the late 1940s and 1950s. “And there are many more bodies elsewhere,” he said, including on roadsides.

The association’s work has become more difficult since the PP and Vox formed a regional coalition government in Aragón in 2023. Within a year of taking office, the new administration repealed the region’s democratic memory law, which recognized victims of the civil war and Francoist repression and established a framework for exhumations. Aragón’s official inventory of mass graves and its dedicated research center were also scrapped.

The PP and Vox defended the repeal — which is currently under review by Spain’s Constitutional Court — as a way to end what they called a “partisan interpretation of history,” arguing that victims on both sides deserved recognition.

But regional democratic memory groups say this framing obscures the far greater scale of Francoist repression and overlooks how the dictatorship prioritized the recovery and commemoration of its own dead. While those killed on the Nationalist side were given Christian burials and public memorials, many of Franco’s victims were left in unmarked graves, their whereabouts unknown to their families.

Since the law’s repeal, relations with the regional administration have iced over and previously discussed projects to commemorate victims have also been postponed indefinitely, according to Vidal. “We think their intention is to cancel them altogether,” he said.

An archaeologist is seen working in a mass grave in Belchite on Nov. 15, 2021. | Marcos del Mazo/Getty Images

Carlos Villanova Mutilva, spokesperson for Aragón’s PP-Vox coalition government, said that rather than undercutting the associations’ efforts, the region had increased funding for exhumations by 10% in 2024 and 2025, with annual budgets amounting to €110,000. He argued relations had soured due to “pure sectarianism” because “they do not accept replacing the democratic memory law.”

In Belchite, Vidal fears resistance to his group’s work will intensify if the PP and Vox take power nationally in the upcoming election. For him, the issue is deeply personal: He is still searching for his grandfather, a trade-unionist farm laborer last seen in 1936, when Francoist forces escorted him away from his field.

“This isn’t just about recovering bones: It’s about recovering the dignity of the person and their families,” he said. “Who doesn’t want to know where their relatives’ remains are?”

A timeless war

The civil war’s relevance in Spanish politics is not simply a question of laws, funding or graves. It is also a cultural phenomenon — a collective fascination with a conflict that refuses to be confined to history books.

Since hitting Spanish cinemas last month, “La Bola Negra,” a historical drama that follows a love story between two gay soldiers on opposite sides of the conflict, has drawn over five million viewers. The movie, which has become a cultural sensation and is Spain’s pitch for next year’s Oscars, carries a pointed message about the dangers of exclusionary politics.

But that message has not been universally embraced. As theaters screened the movie across Madrid on Nov. 20, more than 200 people gathered outside the capital’s Santa Bárbara church to mark the anniversary of Franco’s death, singing the far-right anthem “Cara al Sol” and raising their arms in fascist salutes.

Spain has seen greater tolerance for authoritarian ideas in recent years, particularly among younger generations: Almost 20% of 18- to 24-year-olds consider the Franco dictatorship to have been “good” or “very good,” a 2025 survey from the CIS center for sociological research found.

Such attitudes are increasingly visible on the streets. After Spain’s National Day parade on Oct. 12, dozens of teenagers converged on a housing-protest encampment in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol, chanting slogans such as “Rojo muerto, abono para mi huerto” (“Dead reds are compost for my garden”), referring to leftist parties.

Members of Spanish neo-Nazi group Núcleo Nacional perform the Nazi salute during a demonstration in Madrid on Oct. 3, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

Gutmaro Gómez Bravo, who directs the civil war and Francoism research group at Madrid’s Complutense University, said Spain has made significant progress in confronting its past: A unanimous parliamentary resolution was passed in 2002, condemning Franco’s July 1936 coup and recognizing the victims of the civil war and subsequent dictatorship.

But progress, he says, now appears to have stalled.

“Confrontation over the past yields electoral gains for Vox and other parties,” he said. “But what’s interesting is that they are capitalizing on a view of Franco’s regime that is positive but notably not nostalgic.”

Gómez Bravo argued that efforts to roll back democratic memory laws, challenge the historical consensus surrounding Franco’s overthrow of the Republic and play down the repressive nature of his regime create a climate in which such views could gain ground.

The dispute over how Spain remembers its past could soon move to the national level.

In their election manifestos, both the PP and Vox propose rolling back the national democratic memory law. The PP pledges to repeal it and replace it with legislation that would follow the model of the one in Aragón, while Vox calls for the “overcoming” of what it describes as divisive ideological laws that seek to impose an “official truth.”

The PP says it remains committed to recovering the war’s victims, but on “humanitarian grounds.”

Yet the record of Spain’s last conservative prime minister offers a cautionary precedent: Within a year of taking office in 2011, Mariano Rajoy’s government scrapped funding for historical-memory projects and the office coordinating exhumations, effectively ending state-funded efforts to recover the remains of Franco’s victims.

Gómez Bravo warned that reversing these policies would go beyond politics, compounding the injustice suffered by those who endured repression during and after the war.

“What’s at stake is the recognition of the victims themselves, their status,” he said. “They will become invisible again.”

articles.title: Estonian foreign minister: Why we’re closing our border with Russia
articles.summary:
Margus Tsahkna is Estonia’s minister of foreign affairs.

TALLINN — In response to Moscow’s long-standing escalation of hostile activities against Europe, Estonia has decided to close its land border with Russia. This is about more than border security. We are making Europe safer, closing opportunities for Russia to exploit our openness and increasing pressure on Moscow to end its aggression against Ukraine.

Across Europe, we have witnessed a growing number of acts of sabotage and intimidation. In Poland, Russian intelligence services were behind the arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s Marywilska shopping center. Polish authorities have also attributed two acts of railway sabotage to individuals cooperating with Russian intelligence. In Germany, an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in an incident that the German government has attributed to Russia. And just last week, Denmark attributed an attempted assassination targeting an American-Ukrainian citizen to Russian intelligence services.

These incidents form part of a broader Russian campaign targeting the whole of Europe, including countries far beyond its borders. The aim is to undermine the European security order, intimidate its neighbors and dictate the choices of sovereign nations. Civilian infrastructure, businesses and facilities connected to support for Ukraine have increasingly become targets.

Russian intelligence services exploit cross-border movement to gather intelligence, establish contacts and recruit individuals to carry out hostile activities. These operations are often deliberately designed to create fear, sow distrust, divide our societies and undermine confidence in our institutions from within.

Closing our border will not eliminate these threats, but it will limit opportunities for hostile intelligence activities. It will also help close channels for sanctions evasion, a crucial part of depriving Russia of the resources it uses to finance its war economy and sustain its aggression.

The same logic should guide Europe’s wider approach to forcing Russia to abandon the imperialist ambitions that continue to drive its actions. Let us recall the months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when Moscow issued ultimatums to NATO and the United States, demanding a fundamental revision of Europe’s security arrangements. Russia wanted NATO to roll back its military presence to the levels of 1997, effectively challenging the sovereignty and security choices of countries across Europe, including Estonia, Finland and Sweden.

Five years of war, death and destruction have done nothing to change the Kremlin’s ambitions. Following the talks in Abu Dhabi, Russian representatives have once again referred to the 2021 ultimatums and even suggested going further, adding new demands based on their experience during the war.

This should leave no room for illusions. Russia is not genuinely moving toward ending its war against Ukraine. Instead, it is trying to use negotiations to achieve what it has failed to accomplish on the battlefield, forcing sovereign nations to surrender their security choices and restoring Russian spheres of influence in Europe. Moscow made these demands five years ago and continues to make them today. Its latest invitation for European leaders to visit Moscow to hear Russia’s position changes nothing.

All this makes one thing clear: The way forward is to continue increasing pressure on Russia and strengthening Ukraine. We still have considerable instruments at our disposal, including tightening sanctions, closing loopholes, making use of frozen Russian assets and restricting the travel of Russian tourists and former combatants.

Only through sustained pressure can we make Russia accept a ceasefire, which must be the very first step toward peace, as recently stressed at the Berlin meeting of the Coalition of the Willing. Only then can meaningful negotiations on a lasting peace in Ukraine take place. Discussions about wider European security must not become a precondition for ending Russia’s aggression — nor must they give Moscow an opportunity to dictate the security arrangements of sovereign states.

Allowing Russia such a victory would send a dangerous message to the world. It would suggest that force pays off, borders can be redrawn and the sovereignty of smaller nations can be bargained away. The consequences would reach far beyond Ukraine, threatening Europe’s security and emboldening other authoritarian powers to pursue their ambitions through force.

Estonia’s decision to close its road border crossings with Russia, following Finland’s decision to close its entire eastern land border in 2023, is one part of this broader effort to increase pressure on Moscow and strengthen European security. Whatever inconveniences the closure may cause, responsibility lies squarely with the Kremlin. Russia’s hostile actions and aggression are the reason these measures are necessary.

Europe has the means to make Russia change course. What we need now is the political will to use them. Russia must emerge from this war facing a stronger Ukraine, a more united Europe and a clear understanding that any future attempt to threaten our security will come at an even greater cost.

articles.title: EU’s Socialists to hold formal discussion on Frederiksen’s migration stance
articles.summary:
STRASBOURG — The Socialists and Democrats group in the European Parliament will hold an internal discussion on Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s migration stance after lawmakers from several member countries raised concerns at a meeting in Strasbourg on Monday.

MEPs objected to remarks Frederiksen made on Nov. 17 that critics said echoed the “great replacement” theory, which falsely asserts that elites are plotting to dilute the white population, chiefly through nonwhite immigration. The MEPs also took issue with Frederiksen’s support for an agreement involving Denmark and four other EU countries to establish a so-called “return hub” in Rwanda for deported migrants.

“I am not a supporter of a great replacement of the population,” Frederiksen told the Borgerlig Tabloid podcast, Le Monde reported. “We are a Danish society, and we form an ethnically Danish indigenous tribe. Of course, this evolves when new people arrive here. But it is also necessary that, in the future, Denmark still has a strong majority culture.”

Portuguese and German lawmakers objected to those comments at Monday’s meeting, then more members sought the floor. Group Chair Iratxe García proposed scheduling a formal discussion at a future meeting, according to four people who were in the room or were briefed on the exchange. They were granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations.

The discussion will put a renewed spotlight on divisions within the center-left group over how far the Socialists can support tougher migration policies. Frederiksen’s approach has drawn criticism from fellow party leaders before, including after she joined Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in condemning uncontrolled migration.

Following the Ceuta migration crisis, Frederiksen also co-signed a letter urging European Council President António Costa to take action to protect the EU’s borders. Frederiksen’s position does not represent that of the Socialist political family, Garcia told Spanish media at the time.

Christel Schaldemose, who leads the Danish delegation in the group, was caught off guard by the criticism, two of the people said. “I welcome the opportunity to discuss migration policy with my colleagues in the S&D Group,” she told POLITICO.

One Socialist staffer in the room said “this topic generates tensions in the group, and [Garcia] clearly stopped it from happening right there so things wouldn’t escalate.”

“There was a lot of clapping to the objections raised … clearly the debate needs to happen,” they added.

A spokesperson for García declined to comment on the group discussions. A spokesperson for Frederiksen did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

articles.title: Peace in Ukraine won’t end Russian sabotage in Europe, Poland warns
articles.summary:
A peace deal in Ukraine wouldn’t end Russia’s sabotage campaign against Europe, the minister overseeing Poland’s intelligence services has warned.

Russian covert operations have intensified in recent months, Tomasz Siemoniak said in an interview Monday, describing how operatives have expanded beyond setting fires at warehouses and shopping centers to targeting railways, communications equipment and defense facilities.

Some of the attacks aim to disrupt supplies to Ukraine, he said, but Moscow also wants to intimidate European governments and weaken NATO — objectives that would remain even if the war between Ukraine and Russia ends.

“It is hard to imagine that a peace agreement would change the Russian leadership’s stance or stop it from carrying out these operations,” Siemoniak said.

The Russian Foreign Ministry and Russia’s mission to the EU didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment, but Moscow has previously denied responsibility for numerous attacks, plots and instances of vandalism attributed to it by Western intelligence services.

He linked the recent intensification to a broader Russian strategy of squeezing Ukraine’s economy and disrupting the routes through which European countries supply Kyiv. Poland, a major transit hub for Western aid, has been particularly exposed, he said.

Last year, saboteurs acting on Russian orders blew up a section of railway near Warsaw on one of the main routes used to transport supplies to Ukraine. Earlier this month, security guards in Estonia thwarted an attempt to set fire to a drone factory, which authorities blamed on Russian military intelligence.

Siemoniak said the changing nature of the attacks makes it difficult to measure their intensity by counting incidents alone. While arson remains relatively common, a single attack on a railway could cause a catastrophe with mass casualties. EU governments have already begun preparing for such a scenario, as POLITICO reported in October.

The aim is not simply to destroy infrastructure. Russia also wants to “weaken the will to support Ukraine,” Siemoniak said, by spreading fear, sowing tensions and undermining confidence in European governments.

Both favorable and unfavorable developments for Russia in Ukraine “could encourage it to expand hybrid aggression,” Siemoniak said, arguing that Moscow could try to draw more countries into confrontation or deter their populations from supporting Ukraine or taking anti-Russian stances.

He also said the probability that Friday’s Russian incursion into Polish airspace was accidental was “close to zero,” describing such incidents as attempts to test Poland’s response and that of its NATO allies.

“It’s about linking peace in Ukraine to a so-called new security architecture in Europe,” Siemoniak said.

Russia has renewed demands for NATO to roll back its military presence to where it was in 1997, before Poland and the Baltic states joined the alliance. That would mean withdrawing allied forces stationed in those countries to help defend them. No such concessions have been agreed.

Siemoniak said Moscow refuses to accept that Poland and other NATO members can decide for themselves how many allied troops and military installations they host.

As POLITICO reported Sunday, some European officials fear Moscow could demand restrictions on NATO deployments in Eastern Europe in return for accepting security guarantees for Ukraine.

Ultimately, Siemoniak argued, Moscow wants to reverse the changes that followed the Cold War, when former Soviet-bloc countries joined NATO and the European Union.

“Russia is trying to bring back the Cold War idea of spheres of influence,” he said.

articles.title: 5 ways Europe could revamp its security architecture to please Putin and Trump
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS — The U.S. and Russia are pressing Europe to overhaul the continent’s security architecture in a bid to end the war in Ukraine — and that could mean anything from giving Moscow a bigger say to no change at all.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has long insisted on a rethink of European defense, demanding that NATO pull back its forces and that Russia be given a key voice in the continent’s security — calls that predate the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

But Donald Trump — keen to get a deal to end the war — is now aligning with some of that thinking.

“Security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalized in isolation from post-war European security architecture. The two must be considered together,” Trump’s peace envoy Jared Kushner wrote Sunday.

POLITICO spoke to 12 former and current European officials, experts and NATO diplomats, many of whom were granted anonymity to speak candidly. They laid out clear red lines: no talks without Europe, no unilateral decisions about Ukraine’s NATO accession and no new deal until the war ends.

“We have a security order in Europe, we don’t have any need of changing that,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said in an interview. 

Here are five possible scenarios — and POLITICO’s assessment of how likely they are to happen. Not all are mutually exclusive.

1. A beefed-up OSCE

The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, headquartered in Vienna, is one of the few European security bodies Russia still belongs to.

Its Vienna Document lays out risk-reduction measures like asking countries to announce military activities involving 9,000 or more troops at least 42 days in advance.

If there is a peace deal, the OSCE could be a ready-made venue for ceasefire monitoring, finalizing more granular aspects of peace talks and confidence-building measures like new military activity notifications, said Ulrich Kühn, head of the research department for arms control at the IFSH think tank.

That comes as over 40 countries in Dublin this month backed “discussions on further risk management and reduction mechanisms that contribute to stability in Europe” in the event of a peace deal.

The downside is the 57-member organization’s “cumbersome” size and consensus-oriented decision-making, said Sven Biscop, director of the Europe program at the Egmont Institute.

The institution is open to a broader role.

“We need to make full use of this unique platform to preserve dialogue, rebuild transparency, reduce risks and manage tensions,” OSCE Secretary-General Feridun Sinirlioğlu told POLITICO. “The OSCE remains a key forum for rebuilding a more stable and predictable security architecture in Europe.”

Likelihood: 3/5

2. A revived NATO-Russia Council

Reviving the moribund NATO-Russia Council is an idea backed by Kushner.

Established in 2002, it was a forum for consultation, risk reduction and joint decision-making — leading to limited agreements like a mutual submarine crew rescue deal and joint counterterrorism plans. The council could make decisions by consensus on its own work, but gave Russia no veto over NATO’s decisions or allied defense policies.

It last met a month before Moscow’s full-scale invasion. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has since declared the format is “dead.”

The military alliance still maintains a communication line to Russia’s top general, Valery Gerasimov. But that link is largely unused, primarily because Russia refuses to engage, according to one NATO diplomat and one NATO official.

When contact does happen, “the content of exchanges is more of parallel monologues,” said the diplomat.

Reviving the council after a peace deal could help manage escalation, said two other alliance diplomats. But they cautioned that it should be done carefully, as it could lend Russia legitimacy.

Likelihood: 2/5

3. A new security treaty

A sweeping new Europe-wide agreement that builds on today’s institutions — or replaces them wholesale — is another possibility; but it’s also likely to meet the most resistance from Ukraine’s allies.

A new pact would have advantages, said Egmont’s Biscop. It could bring into play new realities like Finland’s and Sweden’s membership in NATO and Ukraine’s EU aspirations, as well as new military risks like AI.

“The geopolitics have changed … so you can’t just restart where you left off — you will have to renegotiate,” he said.

Any new treaty also risks fueling European fears over giving Russia too much say over the continent’s security architecture. 

“There is absolutely no basis for questioning existing alliances. We will not discuss such matters,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said last week. 

Even less palatable for Europe is Russia’s proposal to strike deals with individual NATO nations. “These could be bilateral agreements that … meet the criteria of mutual non-aggression pacts,” Russian foreign ministry policy planning chief Alexey Drobinin said earlier this month.

For NATO, that’s a “complete no-go,” said one alliance diplomat, arguing it would allow Moscow to drive wedges between allies.

A narrower option is the U.S. suggestion that Ukraine be granted NATO-like security guarantees.

But Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov on Friday called it “an option that is unacceptable to us.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also has questions.

“When we talk about ‘Article 5-like’ guarantees, we need answers to some very clear questions. Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again? What exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all this cost? And will it really work?” Zelenskyy told the NATO Parliamentary Assembly on Monday.

Likelihood: 1/5

4. A fresh EU-Russia format 

The EU, too, once had a formal cooperation channel with Russia under the 1997 Partnership and Cooperation Agreement. 

The Permanent Partnership Council convened ministerial meetings on external security, justice, research and economic issues and led to agreements on visa facilitation and border cooperation. It was frozen after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014. 

The EU’s mandate in issues like trade, sanctions, visas and border management gives it flexibility and leverage with Moscow in establishing post-war relations, said one EU diplomat, while stressing that the bloc has a limited mandate on security issues.

“As long as such a format is perceived as an alteration of the current security architecture in Europe, it will not fly,” the diplomat said. “It will need to be framed as an annex to the current architecture.”

Any bid to normalize economic and energy ties with Russia carries risks, added Kühn.

“You don’t want to go full speed and let the Russian gas flow again because you make yourself very vulnerable,” he said. “This will take some time … confidence [and] security-building measures come first.”

And it won’t just be Brussels alone talking to Moscow.

“Any meaningful discussions about Europe’s security framework can only be undertaken once a ceasefire in Ukraine has been achieved … in particular with NATO allies and EU members,” said a European Commission spokesperson.

Likelihood: 2/5

5. Everything stays the same

Officials say this is the likeliest option — even as Moscow makes clear this is unacceptable.

In part, that’s because Europe’s most important military and economic alliances have never included Russia, said Biscop.

“There’s just one EU and one NATO of which Russia cannot be a member, so this means geopolitically, Russia is now a neighbor of Europe,” he said. “We’re never going to devise a sort of security architecture that allows us to co-decide.”

“It’s not a good scenario … it will be very unstable,” said Biscop, but “given the unrealistic Russian demands, it’s quite likely that this is where we end up.”

The same NATO diplomat cited above put it more bluntly. “Russia has completely disregarded any peace agreements agreed upon in the past 30 years,” they said. “If you want to rebuild a conversation, you need to have both people agreeing on its terms, you can’t have just one — that’s talking to yourself.”

Likelihood: 4/5

articles.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
articles.summary:
A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November

AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy

A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Read more

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.

Advertisement

But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.

Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.

Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”

Free newsletter

Sign up to The Earth Edition

Sign up to newsletter

The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.

Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.

Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.

Read more

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”

Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.

But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?

The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.

With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.

Read more

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.

The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.

There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
articles.summary:
The Riemann hypothesis describes a pattern within the prime numbers

ROBERT BROOK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Alamy

A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.

The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Read more

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI.

Advertisement

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof.

Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.

Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt.

However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.”

A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out

Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans

Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems!” says James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London. “I suppose most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. What is both unsettling and tremendously exciting, is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results. It is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.”

Alpöge has been involved in a number of recent discoveries involving AI. In July, he announced that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof.

He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution.

Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after. “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier,” he writes, saying that he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that “there was a constraint to respect” before the announcement could be made.
