articles.title: Collision between bus, truck kills 11 in UAE
articles.summary:
Eleven people were killed when a bus and a truck collided in Ras Al Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), authorities in the Gulf nation said on Tuesday.

“Investigations into the circumstances and causes of the accident are ongoing,” the Ministry of Interior stated on its X account.

According to the ministry, emergency teams were dispatched to the accident site immediately after receiving the report. They launched rescue and emergency response operations in coordination with ambulance services, Civil Defence and other relevant authorities.

The response also included securing the scene and managing traffic, it added.

The ministry said the findings of the investigation would be announced once it had been completed.

It also expressed condolences to the families of the deceased, praying for mercy and forgiveness for the victims and patience and strength for their loved ones.

The ministry urged the public to exercise caution, rely on official sources for information and refrain from circulating rumours or unverified reports about the accident.

It is the second major road accident to occur in the UAE this month.

On November 12, a multi-vehicle pile-up in Fujairah killed 14 people and left 30 others injured after a truck driver lost control of his vehicle and struck several other vehicles.

articles.title: 'Carrying hopes of 250m people': Zeeshan Ali to be 'first' Pakistani astronaut in space aboard China’s Shenzhou-24
articles.summary:
Zeeshan Ali was named a crew member of China’s Shenzhou-24 space mission on Tuesday, which is scheduled to launch on November 25, with Ali set to become the first Pakistani to undertake an orbital space mission.

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, who is in China, referred to Ali on X as “Pakistan’s first astronaut”.

Ali will also be the first foreign national to board Beijing’s Tiangong space station, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) announced.

“Pakistani astronaut Mohammad Zeeshan Ali is the first foreign national to visit Tiangong,” CMSA Spokesperson Zhang Jingbo said during a press conference.

According to the CMSA, the Pakistani astronaut will serve as a payload specialist during the mission and return aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked with the Tiangong space station in May.

China’s astronaut Tang Hongbo will command the mission, with Wu Yi serving as the mission pilot and Ali taking on the role of payload specialist, according to the CMSA.

The crewed spaceship is scheduled to be launched at 8:18am (Beijing Time and 5:18am Pakistan Time) on Wednesday from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.

Ali is expected to spend around a week in space, conducting various experiments alongside the Chinese crew. CMSA said that during the mission, the crew will conduct around 90 experiments.

The Chinese space agency said the mission’s objectives included conducting an orbital rotation with the crew of the earlier Shenzhou-23 mission, carrying out routine operations and maintenance of the Chinese space station, and continuing space science research, including experiments involving space payloads.

The crew currently aboard the Tiangong space station is headed by 40-year-old Zhu Yangzhu, Lai Ka-ying and Zhang Zhiyuan, also 40.

Lai is Hong Kong’s first astronaut and the only woman currently aboard the space station.

After the new crew reaches the space station, Ali will return to Earth alongside Lai and Zhang.

Zhu will remain on board to complete China’s first full-year stay in space — a key test of endurance critical for future lunar and potentially deep-space ambitions.

Zhu will be accompanied for the next six-month Tiangong rotation by 51-year-old space veteran Hongbo and Yi, in his late thirties and making his first voyage to space.

‘We have already made history’

Speaking at a press briefing in Jiayuguan, Ali said he was “deeply grateful” to the Chinese government for helping “us realise our dream of going into space”.

He said he arrived at the Astronaut Centre of China a few months ago, carrying with him the hopes of 250 million Pakistani people.

Detailing his experience in China, he said what he gained had far exceeded his initial expectations. “First, I have acquired space flight skills. The management, staff and instructors at the Astronaut Centre of China have provided me with comprehensive training […] Day after day, I take another step upward.”

Pakistani astronaut Mohammad Zeeshan Ali. — Screengrab

Moreover, he continued, “I have learned the Chinese language and developed a friendship with my Chinese colleagues. Now, I can communicate with my Chinese crewmates in Chinese.”

“We trained side by side, and our friendship embodies the friendship between China and Pakistan: higher than the mountains, deeper than the oceans, sweeter than honey and as vast as outer space.”

He said he had come to deeply appreciate the meaning of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s words: “Exploring the vast universe, developing the space industry and building China into a space power is our unremitting pursuit of the space dream.”

“Now, this dream belongs to me and also belongs to Pakistan,” he said, adding that it would become a reality through the Shenzhou-24 space mission.

He said he believed that “what comes after this flight matters more than the flight itself”.

“This mission is not a finish line; it is a launch pad. And I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut, one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, Mars and beyond.”

Ali noted that 2026 marked the 75th anniversary of China-Pakistan space cooperation, as well as the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries.

“Together with my Chinese crewmates, I will show that this friendship is real — not only on paper, but also in orbit.”

Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali gesture as they attend a press conference before the Shenzhou-24 spaceflight mission to China’s Tiangong space station, at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, near Jiuquan, Gansu province, China on November 24, 2026. —Reuters

Addressing Pakistanis, he said: “I now feel the true weight of the words of our Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, when he told me that we were about to write a new chapter in Pakistan’s history. I want to assure you that I am not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.

“To every child who is watching while I am in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams.”

In his message to his family, he said: “I want to say that I will travel farther from home than ever before. But I promise you one thing: whenever I look back at the Earth for the first time, I will always search for the light of our home before I look at anything else. No matter how far I fly, we will still share the same Moon, and I will still be looking back at the same Earth.”

He then thanked his teammates, those who supported him, his instructors, scientists, engineers, Pakistan’s space agency Suparco and CMSA.

“You are the reason that I am here today, and no matter who flies, we have already made history together,” he said.

Ali said the “two great nations of China and Pakistan have turned a pilot into an astronaut in a remarkably short span of time. Now it is time to show this great achievement, innovation and send the world a message that we work hand in hand for the peaceful utilisation of space”.

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal congratulated Ali and said the joint mission marked “the trust and iron brotherhood between Pakistan and China”.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar posted on X that a Pakistani astronaut going into space was a source of joy and pride for the entire nation.

Earlier in April, astronauts Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud were chosen to start training in China.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met the two in April, and congratulated them on their selection. He said the space mission was a “matter of pride for the entire nation” and further commended their “round-the-clock efforts” in achieving the milestone.

PM Shehbaz hoped that the space mission would “add new dimensions to the brotherly relationship between Pakistan and China”.

Beijing has invested heavily in its space programme in recent years — catching up with its main rival the United States — and aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030.

Pakistan is a natural partner, given the country’s decades-long, “all-weather” friendship. China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a major foreign investor.

In February 2025, Suparco and CMSA signed a cooperation agreement. Under the pact, two Pakistanis were to train in China, with one joining a mission on the Tiangong space station operated by Beijing.

China has been barred from participating in the International Space Station since 2011, when the US prohibited Nasa from collaborating with Chinese space agencies. Since then, Beijing has sought to build partnerships with other countries — including Pakistan — in its expanding space programme.

articles.title: Liberté, égalité, fatigué—the young are tired of everyone
articles.summary:
The writing was on the wall. Calls for mobilisation on 17 October had been followed by viral videos, parodying Japanese anime and Marvel productions to rally the troops. The streets had caught on: with each new day of mobilisation, walls became covered in angry, audacious graffiti, ranging from ‘F@ck the 17 (the generic number for the French police), bring on the 17th’ to ‘17 October, better than October 17 (the second of two revolutions in Russia in 1917)’.

When the day finally arrived, a perfect storm swept across France, from its largest metropolitan areas to its mid-sized towns. High school and university students, who had been mobilising for weeks, took to the streets in large numbers. They were joined by demonstrators protesting the rising cost of living, including some associating themselves with the Yellow Vest movement, as well as by French and foreign far-left activists. All in all, between 550,000 and 800,000 persons went into the streets on that day. In the violence that ensued, some turned on police forces and official buildings, while others targeted small businesses and department stores. Mass looting and damage to public buildings, including the town halls of Limoges and Marseille, led the government to impose curfews in several cities over the next few days.

In each city, even in each neighbourhood, this day of mobilisation took on a different character, depending on the composition of the crowds and their interactions with the police. In some parts of Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Nantes, Rennes or Bordeaux, the attacks against police forces and government buildings took a quasi-insurrectional character. Elsewhere, the riots were more reminiscent of the ordered disorder of carnival. As law enforcement remained at a distance, the streets were left to jubilant protesters, often dressed up in costumes. In this space wrested from the ordinary constraints of everyday life, the Republican motto of ‘liberté, égalité, fraternité’ (liberty, equality, fraternity) suddenly took a new meaning as protesters of different ages, classes and racial backgrounds revelled in the furious spectacle of their momentary unity. This subversion of the protest order — it was no longer the demonstration that overflowed, but the overflow that demonstrated — nevertheless remained contained within certain bounds. In the parts of Paris that I walked through, at least, vehicles and shops were not set on fire and the forces of disorder remained somewhat contained, at least until the looting began.

Protesters in Paris on 17 October 2026. Photo L. Gayer

This day of wrath and jubilation will probably not be repeated soon. The stars that aligned on that day have since then changed their orbit. Suburban youths, many of them first-time protesters, have not been durably integrated into street protests, while the intensity of repression deterred more privileged youths from repeating the experience of the 17th. In the following weeks, the mobilisation thus took a less belligerent turn and returned to a more conventional social movement led by student and labour unions. In many lycées, however, blockades persist and tensions are rising between mobilised students and parents worrying about the impact of a prolonged closure of the schools.

A clap of thunder in a troubled sky

Calls for a mobilisation against ‘la vie chère’ (high cost of living) started circulating on social media in September 2026, autonomously from the labour unions that traditionally organise demonstrations in France. In September 2025, a similar attempt to ‘block everything’ across the country was a failure and French intelligence agencies did not take the hype around 17 October seriously. They miscalculated the amplifying effect of the student movement, without which this call to action would probably have fizzled out.

In September 2026, a nationwide movement of high school and university students started calling for better teaching conditions, including increased teaching staff and renovated school buildings. The mobilisation was also fuelled by a deep crisis within the French higher education system. In 1980, only 40 per cent of a whole age group obtained the baccalaureate. Today, 80 per cent obtain this prestigious school-leaving certificate, leading to severe pressure on higher education institutions. Rather than the increase of baccalaureate-holders per se, stagnant state funding of universities and limited vocational education options have severely constrained the access to higher education. While asking for 200,000 new positions in universities, high school students have also been asking for the suppression of Parcoursup, the pre-enrolment platform for first-year higher education programmes, which they see as opaque, discriminatory and stressful.

By protesting underfunding of high schools and universities, mobilised students also defended an idea of public education as a public good. As Leila, a 12th grade student in the 9th arrondissement of Paris, told me while sitting on a dustbin during the blockade of her high school on 5 November, “We are calling for pay rises for our supervisors, our cleaners and our teachers. We cannot expect teachers to work themselves to the bone if their salaries do not reflect the effort they put in. Our teachers are the backbone of education and teaching. And education is a weapon against disinformation and the dumbing down of society.”

The movement initially started in late August in Mayotte, an overseas department and region located in the Indian Ocean, before expanding to impoverished suburbs of the Greater Paris region, such as Créteil and Saint-Denis. With a significant number of them of North African or Sub-Saharan African descent, local students denounced the unkept promises of the French meritocratic system of education. By draping themselves in the national flag or singing the national anthem in protests, they reiterated their attachment to egalitarian ideals, while pointing out the systemic discrimination undermining the professed ideal of equal opportunity for descendants of postcolonial immigrants. By early October, the protests expanded to more privileged sections of the youths, including the so-called ‘jeunesse dorée’ (golden youth) attending the most prestigious public schools. Expressing solidarity with suburban youths, students from city centres shared their concern with the clogging of higher education, their anxieties towards the possibilities of the far-right Rassemblement National coming to power in 2027, as well as more diffuse fears towards a future compromised by the compounding threats of climate change, armed conflict and artificial intelligence.

A wildcat demonstration of high school and university students in Saint-Denis, 1 October 2026. Photo L. Gayer

Even if it does not yet translate into joint structures of mobilisation transcending deep social, racial and residential divides, the sense of unity among this anxious youth is palpable. Besides shared concerns specific to this age group, it is rooted in demographic transformations. In 2026, the number of people aged 65 and over became nearly equal to the number of those under 20, and this trend toward a demographic reversal will only intensify in the next decades. By 2070, 32 per cent of the population will be 65 or older — twice the proportion of those under 20. In this ageing society, which it holds responsible for the current state of world affairs, the youth feel belittled and silenced.

The brutal repression of the movement only added fuel to the fire. During the first weeks of October, protests spread to numerous high schools and universities, many of which were subsequently blockaded across the country. In the meantime, increasing price of petrol at the pumps and rising costs of living more generally stoked concerns about purchasing power. This led young influencers and activists to call for a resumption of the Yellow Vest movement, which was prompted by similar concerns in 2018. As 17 October approached, clashes with the police multiplied around high schools and during street demonstrations. In many cities, the atmosphere was electric.

Clashes between protesters and the police during a demonstration in Paris on 6 October. Photo L. Gayer

Joyful anger

In its early phase and even more so on 17 October, this social movement disrupted the rules of political contention in France. Like the Yellow Vests before them, students initially evaded the control of labour unions that, historically, have been leading protests, articulating claims and negotiating with governmental authorities. Instead, high school and university students were mobilised by content on social media and they organised horizontally, through messaging applications like Snapchat. Their privileged forms of action were blockades and, to a lesser extent, wildcat demonstrations. Every morning, students would collect dustbins and building materials to block the entrance of their school, sometimes before going on an unauthorised demonstration across the area. On 1 October, I attended one such event in Saint-Denis, in the northern periphery of Paris. After assembling near Lycée Paul Éluard, about 200 high school and university students walked — and occasionally ran — across the town, visiting one high school after the other to mobilise other students. The mood was joyful but resolute: while provoking the police chasing them, students laughed, sang and delivered fiery speeches. Among the protesting students was a young boy dressed as Spider-Man and wearing a motorcycle helmet. Sitting on a dustbin pushed by jubilant teenagers, he was the focus of attention and added a dash of colour among young men and women often dressed in black and wearing surgical masks to protect themselves against tear gas.

High school students at a wildcat demonstration in Saint-Denis, 1 October 2026. Photo L. Gayer

As the movement expanded, student and labour unions started joining the fray and organising massive demonstrations across the country. These protests were more conventional in nature, and easier to manage for law enforcement. The large participation of high school and university students, however, endowed them with an energy and a creativity evading the usual mobilisations of labour unions. Expanding on a protest repertoire that emerged during the movement against the reform of pension laws in 2023, young participants brought placards with ironic, witty slogans drawing from various sources of influence: the Revolution of 1789, the protest movement of May 1968, as well as social media and popular culture. The reclaiming of revolutionary symbols — the caps of the sans-culottes, the guillotine, Liberty leading the people — coexisted with references to video games such as Mario Bros, Legend of Zelda or GTA, to popular film series such as Star Wars and the Hunger Games, as well as to more contemporary Internet memes and ‘brain rot’. Some of the slogans were franchised: after circulating on social media, they were picked up by young protesters, who in the process reaffirmed their belonging to a protest community united by shared cultural references.

Protesters dressed up as the Pink Panther, Santa Claus, Inosuke Hashibira (from the manga Demon Slayer), Batman and Captain America, during a demonstration in Paris on 7 November 2026. Photo L. Gayer

As Céline, a student at EPSA, the Paris school of graphic design and visual communication, explained during a demonstration on 5 November, “popular culture allows you to convey political messages more easily, because everyone has the reference”. On that day, she was herself dressed up as Luigi, the secondary protagonist of the video game franchise Mario Bros, and she carried a placard showing this popular character removing President Emmanuel Macron and the far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen with a vacuum cleaner.

Indeed, beyond making claims for better working conditions in lycées and universities, these youthful protests have also been directed against the far right and the imminent threat of its access to power after the presidential elections of May 2027. Besides a general sense of dread towards an uncertain future, this threat has been a major unifier among the youth, across social and racial divides. Drawn from a song by the 1980s punk band Bérurier Noir, ‘La jeunesse emmerde le Front National’ (The youth tells the Front National [the original name of the Rassemblement National] to f@ck off) remains one of the popular anthems among the protesters, although a new one emerged in early November, ‘J’ai deux passions, la fanfare, la révolution’ (I have two passions: the brass band and the revolution!).

A brass band performing at a demonstration in Paris on 7 November 2026. Photo L. Gayer

‘Everyone hates the police’, but the police have many friends

Both joyful and belligerent, this social movement has met with unprecedented levels of repression, which has fuelled hostility, even hatred towards the police. As of 17 November, at least 155 protesters or passers-by had suffered serious injuries by the explosive weapons used by law enforcement — including 11 eye losses, seven amputations and 18 fractured skulls. The number of arrests has also reached unprecedented levels: between mid-September and mid-November 2026, more than 12,000 protesters were sent to custody, most of them minors. By comparison, 6,730 protesters met the same fate during the 2018–2019 movement of the Yellow Vests, 890 during the protests against the reform of labour laws in 2016, 150 during the student movement against the Loi Devaquet in 1986 and only 95 during the uprising of May 1968.

Police officers using tear gas spray against students during a protest near Sciences Po in Paris on 7 October 2026. Photo L. Gayer

Far from restraining law enforcement officers, the Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has encouraged them to show “no restraint” when dealing with the protesters, whatever their age. Meanwhile, the Minister for Justice, Gérald Darmanin, has asked judges to be “merciless” with looters and rioters, especially after the events of 17 October. By and large, the judges have obliged and the judicial repression of the movement has been extremely severe, with large numbers of protesters being sent to jail for petty offences. During the days that followed 17 October, drastic measures were also taken to contain the protests.

October 24 protests in France, measures taken. Sylvie Husson, Valentina Breschi. AFP

Incidents of police violence have been widely publicised among the youths, through social media in particular. This has fuelled detestation of the police, exemplified by popular slogans heard at every demonstration: ‘ACAB’ (All Cops Are Bastards) or ‘Tout le monde déteste la police’ (Everyone hates the police).

Everyone does not hate the police in France, though. As a recent opinion poll by the Centre for Political Research at Sciences Po (CEVIPOF) shows, the level of confidence in the police remains high, at 73 per cent. Moreover, as violence escalated during protests and blockades dragged on, a growing number of individuals started volunteering to lend a strong hand to the police. Following the mass lootings that took place on 17 and 18 October, some influencers launched platforms to gather volunteers in support of shopkeepers. While the individuals behind these initiatives claimed to be politically neutral and to act in accordance with the law, the reality on the ground was rather different. On 24 October, as new protests were organised across the country, far-right militants assaulted demonstrators in a dozen cities under the pretext of protecting shopkeepers. Not only did the police refrain from interfering, in several cities, they actively collaborated with far-right groups, who delivered protesters to the men in blue after roughing them up. In Montpellier, a couple of days later, a judge sentenced one of these protesters to a suspended prison term after acknowledging that he had been arrested “by a militia“. After these collusions were exposed, several investigations were launched and far-right extremists became less visible in the following weeks, but the threat lingers on.

As high school blockades dragged on in many large cities, some parents also started acting as auxiliaries of law enforcement, if not as vigilantes taking the law in their own hands. Especially after the government of Sébastien Lecornu granted a few concessions to protesting students on 28 October — including a reform of Parcoursup and the creation of 15,000 additional seats in higher education — some parents started claiming that their children had been taken hostage by a minority of unyielding extremists. Some of these parents were also concerned about the challenge to authority — that of the state, as well as their own — posed by the student revolt. In Paris, Bordeaux, Marseille, Rennes or Montpellier, these infuriated parents organised on WhatsApp groups and started waking up at dawn to help the police contain the blockers. Forming human chains to protect students willing to go to class, they also tussled over the control of dustbins used by protesting students to block their lycées. In the ensuing scuffle, some students were hit and verbally abused by parents.

Parents trying to circumvent the blockade of Lycée Carnot, in Paris, by giving access to students. Photo L. Gayer

At Lycée Carnot, a prestigious public school in the 17th arrondissement of Paris, students told me that one of their schoolmates was the target of racist insults, while another received intimidating messages on his phone. For Adrien, a Senior Year student at Carnot, “These parents try to take the law into their own hands and, by doing so, they escalate violence because they make everyone furious.” School authorities are aware of this threat and the principal of another lycée in the 8th arrondissement, who asked to remain anonymous, said that he feared the opening of a “third front”, after those of students and cops, due to the counter-mobilisation of these parents.

Besides the risks of violent escalation, these initiatives seem to have mixed results. However menacing they try to be, parents are often outsmarted by the kids, who may give up blocking their school from outside only to foment trouble from within, leading school authorities to suspend activities anyway. As a result, hundreds of high schools (out of a total of 3,700) continue to be disturbed in the country — a figure which is difficult to verify since the Ministry of Education systematically scales down its statistics to convince public opinion that order has been restored. Whatever the exact figure, the return to normalcy remains elusive in many public schools and universities. While the kind of violence and looting witnessed on 17 October has not returned, tens of thousands of protesters continue to take to the streets every Saturday in major cities, with occasional skirmishes between them and the riot police.

Another Gen Z protest?

This ongoing student mobilisation shares characteristics with recent movements led by the Gen Z (composed of those born between 1997 and 2012) in Indonesia, Bangladesh, Nepal, Madagascar, Morocco or Peru. In France, even if labour unions started co-organising the protests from October 2026 onwards, the mobilisation has primarily involved youths between the ages of 15 and 25 years. This has infused it with a youthful energy and an irreverence characteristic of similar protests in the Global South and, more recently, across Europe (in Albania, Belgium, Italy and Germany). Especially in its early phase, the movement shared its horizontality with other youth revolts organised through Internet forums and communication apps such as LIHKG during the 2019 anti-ELAB movement in Hong Kong or Discord during more recent protests in Nepal and Morocco.

French students also draw on global cultural references that have provided young protesters worldwide with powerful role models. As Issa, a twenty-something protester who likes to dress up as Luffy, the main protagonist of One Piece, explained to me, “Luffy is the character who embodies freedom the best. He is devoted to living a free life. At the same time, he always cares for others. Whether in the manga or the anime, he always puts the interests of others ahead of his own, and those of the have nots ahead of those of the haves.” Coming from a Japanese manga and popularised by young Indonesians as a symbol of youthful rebellion, Luffy and his ragtag pirate crew are exemplary of the globalisation of popular culture and protest repertoires, which are no longer shaped exclusively by the West. Even the ubiquity of the three-finger salute drawn from the Hunger Games cannot be reduced to the success of Suzanne Collins’ books and their adaptation for the big screen. The gesture became a symbol of democracy and anti-authoritarian struggles in response to the Thai coup d’état of 2014, before being adopted by Hong Kong protesters the same year and by opponents to the military junta of Myanmar in 2021.

Protesters in Paris on 17 October waving the pirate flag popularised by the manga One Piece. Photo L. Gayer

The analogy between the ongoing French student movement and other youthful protests of the past few years should not be overblown, however. In France, unlike in Nepal or Madagascar, the critique of elites has not been focusing on their nepotism but, rather, on their compromising with the capitalist class and the far right. A newly emerged theme, until then reserved to conspiracy theorists leaning to the far right, is that of ‘paedophile elites’ — a theme which seems to have been nurtured by the global scandal of the Epstein files but which has a special resonance among French youths due to the fact that President Emmanuel Macron was only 15 when he met his future wife Brigitte Trogneux, who at the time was 39 years old.

A protester on 17 October in Paris carrying a placard that reads ‘Why are paedophiles being protected? Ask Brigitte Macron’. Photo L. Gayer

The deeply unpopular president has been a target of much criticism by young protesters. But even though some of them have been asking for his resignation, the movement has not put this demand at the forefront. Protesters do not really have the will — nor the means — to take down the government, the way their counterparts in Bangladesh, Nepal or Madagascar did. And while the government of Sébastien Lecornu was seriously rattled by the scenes of chaos of 17 October, it stood its ground and survived the storm. So far, it has only made minimal concessions to the protesters and does not seem ready to move further due to budgetary constraints. As a result, if some young activists strive to keep the movement afloat, most eyes are now set on the presidential election of April/May 2027, which could bring its own share of civil strife, possibly on an even grander scale.

All photos by author

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina seeks to return to Bangladesh on December 16 on state carrier
articles.summary:
Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return home from more than two years of exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson told Reuters on Tuesday, though the government said she can only return through extradition.

It is the first time Hasina, 79, has set a specific date for her return, potentially raising political and legal tensions in a country where her party is banned and where violence has risen since she sought a new passport and other documents earlier this month.

In addition to seeking the paperwork, cancelled months after she fled to Delhi following the uprising against her, Hasina has urged the Bangladeshi government to arrange her return on flag carrier Biman Bangladesh Airlines.

“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” the spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said in a statement.

“Having exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th.” The government, however, reiterated that she can only be extradited by India, having been sentenced to death by a Bangladeshi court last year in her absence for ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising. Hasina has denied the charges from exile.

“She can only return home by extradition treaty; in handcuffs, and under strict surveillance,” Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh’s minister of state for foreign affairs, told Reuters.

India’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, the ministry said it was examining Bangladesh’s extradition request and wanted to “engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties”.

On the request to arrange a flight, Kobir said: “Bangladesh will not entertain any such delusional request”.

Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal, which sentenced Hasina to death, said it was unreasonable for a convicted fugitive to expect the government to arrange her return.

A Bangladeshi minister told Reuters on Sunday that Hasina would be arrested and jailed on return and that there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring her back.

The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced her out of power.

articles.title: Digital gateway launched in Sindh for youth to access banking, education and jobs
articles.summary:
• Under Sindh Youth Card, govt, financial organisations and private sector will provide support system to young people, says Murad
• Registration begins across all 30 districts to select 100,000 young people in first phase; initiative to be expanded to one million

KARACHI: Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah has described the Sindh Youth Card as a landmark youth empowerment initiative designed to connect young people with education, employment, financial inclusion, skills development and entrepreneurship opportunities through a single digital platform.

The initiative was formally launched by Pakistan Peoples Party Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari at a ceremony held here at Chief Minister House on Monday.

According to a press statement issued by the CM House, registration for the programme began on Monday across the 30 districts of the province. It will initially benefit 100,000 young people aged 15 to 29, with a plan to expand coverage to one million beneficiaries.

The card offers an integrated package of facilities, including digital bank accounts and Visa debit cards, scholarships, vocational and digital skills training, discounts at more than 180 partner businesses, transport concessions, job placements, paid internships and entrepreneurship support, including proposed interest-subsidised loans of up to Rs500,000.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, the chief minister termed it a practical commitment to placing young people at the centre of the province’s development agenda.

“The future of Sindh and Pakistan depends on the opportunities we create for our young people today. They are not merely the leaders of tomorrow; they are an important force for progress, innovation and transformation today,” he said.

“The Sindh Youth Card is a practical expression of our commitment. It is much more than a card; it is a platform of opportunity, inclusion and empowerment,” he said.

Paying tribute to PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, Mr Shah said his emphasis on youth development, social justice and equal opportunities had provided the vision and direction for the initiative.

He said the programme would bring together government departments, educational institutions, financial organisations and private sector to establish a comprehensive support system for young people.

He urged all provincial departments, public institutions and private organisations to become active partners, stressing that youth empowerment required collective efforts in education, skills development, technology, healthcare, sports and employment.

He emphasised that young women, minority communities and persons with disabilities must have equal access to the programme’s benefits.

“From Karachi to Tharparkar and from Hyderabad to Larkana, every young person must have an equal opportunity to benefit. Geography and financial circumstances should never limit their ambitions,” he said.

“The success of the Sindh Youth Card will ultimately be measured not by the number of cards issued, but by the opportunities created, lives improved and aspirations fulfilled,” he said.

Launched through the Sports and Youth Affairs Department in collaboration with Sapphire Consulting Services and JS Bank’s Zindigi platform, the Sindh Youth Card has offered eligible beneficiaries access to a bank account, digital wallet, mobile banking application and Visa debit card; special discounts through more than 180 partner businesses in food, retail, fashion, healthcare, education, entertainment, travel and technology.

The card will also facilitate recipients in getting merit- and need-based scholarships, university financial assistance, exchange programmes, digital training, vocational courses and professional certifications.

The youth card holder will also get transport discounts, interest-subsidised microloans ranging from Rs10,000 to Rs500,000 and interest-subsidised instalment facilities for laptops, tablets, smartphones, motorcycles, electric bikes and work equipment.

Speaking on the occasion, Sports and Youth Affairs Minister Sardar Muhammad Bux Khan Mahar described the launch as a historic day for Sindh’s youth, saying the initiative was not merely about issuing a card but opening a new gateway to opportunity, empowerment and prosperity.

“Our message is clear: One Card, One Youth, One Sindh,” he said, adding that the objective was to create an integrated support system where education met opportunity, talent met resources and ambition received the support it deserved.

In his welcome address, Sports and Youth Affairs Secretary Munawar Ali Mahesar highlighted the department’s efforts to establish partnerships with financial institutions, businesses, educational organisations and other stakeholders to make access to opportunities easier and more organised.

The ceremony was attended by provincial ministers, elected representatives, Chief Secretary Asif Hyder Shah, provincial secretaries, representatives of financial institutions, civil society members and other distinguished guests.

articles.title: The missing link
articles.summary:
RULERS who don’t bring power closer to people via strong local bodies want us to believe that they will now bring power closer to people via more provinces. So, the false idea of making many provinces as a cure for our many ills is back with a bang.

Months after it first emerged, the bang is still more noise than a clarion call of reason. I have seen three key reports against it, but none in its favour.

Support — strong on rhetoric but weak on evidence — comes mainly from ministers and friendly analysts. One minister cites Afghanistan’s 34 units. That’s odd as Afghanistan helps us avoid the blushes of being last in South Asia on key governance metrics. It’s a unitary state whose units lack legislative powers and elected bodies. We have 150-plus stronger units (districts) which have elected bodies, at least as per the law.

Some cite unitary France’s 18 units. They too lack legislative powers. Counting them is easier than proving they cause its progress. It has democracy and civilian sway, unlike us. These key parts of the causal chain are not cited in our French politics lessons.

Rulers also ignore the proven merits of local bodies. These offer no instant cure. But with higher democracy and civilian sway present, they bring power closer to people globally. And when the two aren’t in place, nothing usually does that. But they remain our missing link between power and the powerless.

Most of us don’t have elected local bodies, they being absent in Gilgit-Baltistan, Quetta, Punjab and Islamabad and now KP due to emergency rule. Even when and where they exist, they are too weak to fix problems.

Provinces often delay their elections for long but dissolve them early. Elections are often held on non-party basis; local officials often lack a public mandate, as in Punjab, and seats for weak groups are often hogged by elites. Citizens have little say in what they do, little recourse when they fail and little voice in how they spend money. Uneven council sizes and missing tiers weaken them further. Local tasks are split among local bodies and many higher-level agencies. Local heads often lack effective control as vague supervisory powers allow interference from above. Weak coordination and capacity gaps further hamper them. Such split and bureaucratic control is high in Islamabad, Sindh and Punjab.

The setups closest to the people have the least powers.

Provinces first make voters wait for local bodies. They later make local bodies wait for cash. They only spend about five per cent of our total state funds, much lower than in many similar states. They depend heavily on provincial funds and can’t legally and practically collect much cash locally. For example, over 95pc of their funds come from such transfers in Sindh. It is often hard to see how provinces divide money across districts, but easy to see that favoured districts get more cash per head.

So, the setups closest to the people have the least powers. Would rulers who have kept local bodies so weak for so long empower new provinces? Their new capitals may be closer, but still out of reach of the masses.

The aim behind dividing provinces may be to make them powerless like local bodies and actually move power away from the people. What provinces have done to local bodies, the centre may now do to the provinces. So, the masses will have one more government level between them and real power.

Deep divisions within a setup held together tightly by its strong fear of PTI and its weak mandate make the division of provinces dicey. Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s diatribes exposing its electoral misdeeds and warning against forcing matters via a referendum emitted shockwaves. Our new troi­­ka — the president, prime minister and interior minister — representing all key parts of the hybrid regime, soon agreed on talks. Perhaps those fond of force have shelved it, for now.

The PPP was largely mum when judges, the opposition and activists faced abuses. It has reacted strongly, now that it’s at the receiving end of the stick. Even though it opposes the idea for the wrong reason — the fear of losing the golden goose of Karachi — the right reasons do exist.

PML-N supports this latest demand of powerful quarters via ministers, but the Sharifs stay mum. Perhaps it wants strong promises of extended patronage before giving top-level support. But it, too, may be forced to speak up when it eventually faces problems.

While our hybrid rulers continue to play self-serving games, a nuclear-armed state of nearly 250 million inches closer to multifaceted crises given their misrule. Uninterrupted democracy and civilian sway are the only way to avoid doom.

The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

articles.title: Delaying the inevitable
articles.summary:
THE PPP is worried, very worried. Since the talk of the new provinces began, it has been the only party (in government) to take the ‘rumours’ seriously, in public as well as otherwise; the Noonies would rather ignore the matter. It struck back with vehement rejections and heated speeches in Sindh.

And then last week, Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari took the proverbial bull by the horns. At a speech at the Karachi Press Club, not only did he push back against the idea of new provinces, he also created shock and awe by what he said on other issues. He questioned the award of the reserved seats of PTI to other parties; he expressed concern over the state of the judiciary and even alleged the 27th Amendment had been passed by force. He then also called Imran Khan a political prisoner and said both the PTI head and Maulana Fazlur Rehman needed to be wooed rather than pushed away.

The speech did not go down well, it seems. Within minutes, Atta Tarar, the information minister of the federal government that is yet to own the new provinces officially was on television, to criticise BBZ. Others followed suit, though neither the prime minister nor anyone from the Sharif family spoke up. And no one was willing to spare BBZ.

The next day came a number of interviews in which it seemed at times that the PPP chairman was walking back on his earlier harshness. For instance, when asked to explain his comments on the 27th Amendment, BBZ argued that he meant it was passed by brute majority of the government. Then he called Mohsin Naqvi ‘bhai’ after having described him as the minister of everything a day before.

Some feel the PPP, since the meeting with the president, has accepted the inevitable.

But the explanations didn’t prove enough; soon came the news that the prime minister and interior minister met Asif Ali Zardari, the president, and the press release after their interaction said that any future amendments would be passed with consensus as had happened in the past. Released by the presidency, this press release provided a stamp of legitimacy to the 26th and 27th Amendments, and a contradiction of what BBZ had said.

This is not the first time it has appeared to outsiders that BBZ has been put in his place by his father, but the frequency with which this happens is now more a case of the father and son playing good cop/bad cop as have the Sharif brothers for decades. That it ends up making the son seem mercurial doesn’t seem to bother the party.

Since then, the war of words between the government and the PPP has dialled down a wee bit on television, but on social media, it continues unabated. And the culprits are not just the anonymous accounts. A senior cabinet member such as Khawaja Asif has posted provocatively on X, leading to angry reactions from senior PPP leaders.

However, the ceasefire hasn’t put an end to the larger ‘debate’ on new provinces. And neither has it really clarified the position of the parties in power on the matter.

For instance, some feel the PPP, since the meeting with the president, has now, like the N, accepted the inevitable. After all, no one thinks the N in Lahore is too happy with the idea but it realises the futility of pushing back. This is lent credence by the statements of Rana Sanaullah, who continues to insist the proposal has not been discussed by the government. But it is perhaps too simple to assume an easy capitulation despite what the country continues to be ‘told’.

Journalists with sources and contacts in the highest echelons of power continue to inform us that new provinces are as real as climate change. With their access to the hallowed halls of power, they are privy to some information on how the provinces may go forward, despite the resistance from the PPP.

The first step is a referendum. That Atta Tarar defended this idea in his video talk that followed BBZ’s press conference means there is some truth to the matter; since then Rana Sana has also agreed that a referendum might be the way forward.

In addition, a story in The News has also explained the referendum votes will not be counted nationally but provincially. The Constitution also allows parliament to lay down the procedure “for the holding of a referendum and the compiling and the consolidation of the result of a referendum” in Article 48.

Obviously, some Doubting Thomases continue to point out that a referendum cannot override the need for the provincial assemblies to pass a resolution in favour of new provinces with a two-thirds majority. And while it continues to be a hurdle, some experts, such as Malik Ahmed Khan, the Punjab Assembly speaker, are of the view that once the people have spoken, it should be given more weight than the voice of the representatives of the people. Perhaps he knows how this will translate legally and constitutionally, but it does seem to suggest that the hurdles have been or are being worked out.

But this is what one side is telling us at a time when hybridity afflicts us. And the parties’ disquiet is not entirely hidden. The PPP is more vocal but the N remains coy. And till they are on board the hybrid train, they will have a say. In parliament, in creating a consensus and so on.

It seems that at the moment, their instinct might be to stretch the process out by debating the finer points of the question and how it will be conducted. Consider that in a recent speech BBZ emphasised the need to focus on the economy instead of creating new problems. Beyond that, can this issue strike another blow to the hybrid system? Most probably.

The writer is a journalist.

articles.title: LHC rejects US-Indian origin citizen’s plea for Pakistan Origin Card
articles.summary:
LAHORE: Dismissing a petition by an American citizen of Indian origin, the Lahore High Court (LHC) has ruled that marriage to a Pakistani citizen does not create an automatic right to seek a Pakistan Origin Card (POC).

The petition says Dr Talha Muadh Ghulam Jilani, formerly Dr Jaysinha Shamrao Shinde, embraced Islam in 1990 and renounced Indian nationality before taking American citizenship in 2007.

He approached the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) for a POC in May 2021 and was told in 2022 that his case had gone for ground verification.

After earlier petitions in the LHC, Nadra rejected his representation in January 2023.

Says marriage to a Pakistani doesn’t create an automatic right to seek Pakistan Origin Card

A request for relaxation was declined by the authority, which he challenged before the court.

A counsel for Jilani and his wife argued that Rule 4(5) of the Nadra (Pakistan Origin Card) Rules, 2002 covers a foreign spouse of a Pakistani. He said Indian origin is not a bar and that a 2013 Interior Ministry policy cannot add conditions to the statutory provisions.

He also cited Article 35 of the Constitution, which requires the State to protect marriage and family.

However, a law officer for the government supported the impugned decision, saying the provision of relaxation was discretionary.

He said the 2013 policy provided a uniform mechanism for enhanced scrutiny of applicants belonging to List-B countries, including India and Afghanistan, in view of legitimate national-security considerations.

In his judgement, Justice Muhammad Ajmal Zahid held that a POC is not citizenship but a facilitation document.

He noted that marriage under Rule 4(5) establishes threshold eligibility but not an entitlement as final issuance remains contingent upon mandatory verification and subject to Nadra’s statutory authority to refuse a card on grounds of national security or public interest.

The judge drew a distinction between Indian origin and Indian nationality.

He said statutory eligibility must be determined on the basis of the legal status prescribed by the rules and not merely by reference to ethnic origin, ancestry or an unverified assertion regarding nationality.

The judge observed that the petitioner’s renunciation certificate had not been independently verified.

The judge held that the 2013 policy was an executive instruction that cannot override the rules or create a disqualification, though it may serve as a mechanism for enhanced security checks.

The judge found the policy rationally linked to national security.

He said an adverse security input is not an automatic disqualification and the competent authority must form its own opinion.

Justice Zahid declared that the petitioners failed to demonstrate that the competent authority acted without jurisdiction or reached its conclusion through mala fide exercise of power.

Addressing the petitioners’ argument of relaxation, the judge stated that the law lets the federal government relax the bar in “special and extraordinary circumstances”.

He maintained that the discretion vested in the government is subject to judicial review on recognised grounds of illegality, arbitrariness and mala fides, but relaxation cannot be claimed as a matter of right.

The judge said the petitioners identified no special circumstance beyond the marriage.

Finding no jurisdictional defect or mala fide in the impugned decisions, Justice Zahid dismissed the petition.

articles.title: Used phone import surge hits industry
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: Imports of used smartphones surged from 1,434 units in July to 98,383 in October, as the duty gap between locally manufactured phones and imports narrowed.

The country recorded 150,133 arrivals, including 51,750 new smartphones valued at $71.7 million in October, compared with 18,431 smartphones valued at $17.8m in July.

The Pakistan Mobile Phone Manufacturers Associ­ation (PMPMA), in a letter, has raised concerns with the Ministry of Industries and Production and the FBR about the development, noting that the most alarming issue is the sharp increase in used smartphone imports. A delegation from the association is scheduled to meet with authorities in the capital in the coming days to discuss the matter.

The association stresses that this is having a clearly negative impact on local smartphone assembly as production fell from 906,711 units in July to 752,870 units in October.

PMPMA Chairman Abdul Rehman told Dawn on Monday that the surge in CBU imports is driven by two factors: narrowed import tariff gaps, which have fuelled the ‘khepia’ business, and a downward revision in FBR taxes on imported phone sets.

He explained that the tariff gap between completely built-up smartphones and CKD kits for locally assembled smartphones has narrowed sharply, to around 11pc for a $100 phone and 14pc for a $200 phone.

“The $100-$200 category is the largest-selling phone segment, and the 11pc and 14pc gap has nearly disappeared as bulk importers use methods such as under-invoicing, leaving little room for the country’s regulated manufacturers,” he said.

Mr Rehman added that another factor driving the influx of used phones was a downward revision in FBR valuations under the Device Identification, Registration and Blocking System (DIRBS), allowing cheap imported smartphones to be registered with the PTA. Imported completely built-up units (CBUs) have captured 41.8pc of the country’s smartphone market in just a few months.

The association has said that the mobile manufacturing industry has complained about reverse cascading for the past three years, making it impossible to localise parts such as chargers, batteries, cables, and motherboard assemblies.

A charger can currently be imported duty-free as part of a CKD kit, but the cumulative duty on importing its raw materials and subcomponents is nearly 20pc.

articles.title: Civilisational dialogue
articles.summary:
WHENEVER representatives of Pakistan and India meet, even in multilateral settings, there is hope for a rekindling of ties. This is so because bilateral engagement is currently close to zero, mainly because of New Delhi’s rigidity. But considering last year’s armed conflict between both states, and the ensuing toxic atmosphere in South Asia, it is a welcome development that Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik travelled to New Delhi recently for the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum.

This was a multilateral meeting and there were no great expectations of a bilateral breakthrough attached to the visit. But the fact that it took place at all despite the state of ties is significant. Sometimes at such events, behind closed doors, representatives of both states can discuss small steps to improve relations.

Mr Malik brought up the issue of climate change threatening the whole region, while highlighting the common civilisational bonds that tie South Asia and Eurasia together — bonds which have unfortunately become hostage to the rigidity of some, particularly in the subcontinent. The minister also deserves praise for deftly handling pointed questions from the Indian media about ‘terrorism’ — apparently New Delhi’s favourite refrain when it comes to Pakistan — as well as the IWT. Mr Malik said that he was in India for an SCO event; when the Indians would call him to discuss terrorism and other irritants, he would address these specifically, as Pakistan also had concerns.

Though there are no signs of the deep freeze in bilateral relations thawing anytime soon, engagements such as these can help bring down the temperature, and lower confrontational rhetoric.

The fact is there is no viable alternative to peace in South Asia, and only through a structured dialogue can both states address their concerns satisfactorily, and work towards a more peaceful future for all.

Of course the Indian side must stop issuing threats to Pakistan, and using adversarial language. While Pakistan has defended itself against Indian aggression in the past, and will do so again if threatened, the subcontinent’s people deserve to live in peace, not eternal conflict.

When India is ready to engage Pakistan in a civil, frank and respectful dialogue, it will find this country ready to respond.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

articles.title: Petroleum dealers warn of another strike over unmet demands
articles.summary:
KARACHI: The Paki­stan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) on Monday warned that dealers would shut their petrol pumps unless the government fixes fuel prices for 30 days at a time, giving it 15 days to resolve the issue.

This is the latest of several strike calls by fuel retailers this year; on each previous occasion, the call was withdrawn after the government stepped in. This time too, dealers say, the issues they raised earlier remain unresolved.

At a joint press conference held at the Karachi Press Club, PPDA Chair­man Malik Khuda Bakhsh, Vice Chairmen Tariq Hassan and Anwar Kamal, Sindh Region President Ameer Khan, and Karachi Region President Saeed Khan said that daily changes to fuel prices were quickly draining pump owners’ working capital.

They said that if capital ran out, pumps would run dry, which could lead to a law and order situation.

They demanded that the dealers’ margin be raised immediately to 8pc of the retail price. They also claimed that refineries had cut supplies of petrol and diesel, and that one refinery had stopped supplying diesel altogether. According to the dealers, they collectively deposit Rs5.74 billion into the national exchequer every day.

Asked about earlier strike calls that were withdrawn after government intervention, Mr Bakhsh said this time was different. He said several issues raised with the government had stayed unresolved since the US-Iran war had changed market dynamics. With the war’s intensity now subsiding and prices falling, he said, the government should take notice of the association’s concerns.

The dealers’ first strike threat came in March this year, soon after the Mideast conflict broke out.

At the time, it wanted the dealers’ margin raised from 2.59pc to 8pc, after a Rs55 per litre increase in diesel and petrol prices. However, the association — then led by Abdul Sami Khan — had postponed their plans on the eve of the strike, citing the fragile situation caused by the Middle East war, which could disrupt oil supply chains.

The daily pricing system the dealers are opposing was introduced in July. At the time, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would be fixed daily because of volatility in international markets, with Ogra publishing prices on its website every day.

On July 22, the All Pakistan Petroleum Pump Owners Association — a separate body — deferred its nationwide strike call for two weeks after negotiations with the petroleum minister.

The association said they were told in writing that daily pricing would run for two weeks on a trial basis and could be reversed to monthly or fortnightly fixing if it caused significant difficulty.

However, the daily pricing regime has stayed in place since then.

In August too, the PPDA issued a 72-hour strike ultimatum, but backed down after the petroleum minister told a PPDA delegation that the government would continue the daily price-fixing mechanism, rejecting the dealers’ demand for monthly pricing. He said he could not commit to the 15-day timeline because the prime minister had the authority to make such decisions.

The next day, the Economic Coordination Committee of the federal cabinet approved a 15.5 per cent increase in dealers’ margins on petrol and high-speed diesel. The margin rose by Rs1.34 per litre, from Rs8.64 to Rs9.98, with effect from Sept 1. Resultantly, the PPDA then called off its strike.

But the ECC did not accept the dealers’ main demand. Official sources said that setting the margin at 8pc of the retail price would have meant about Rs26 per litre on petrol and Rs30 on diesel at prices at that time.

The latest pain point came in September, when the PM’s fuel subsidy scheme was rolled out, without much clarity on how pump owners would be compensated. However, that issue was settled through a mechanism managed by the State Bank of Pakistan.

In recent days, fuel prices have been falling. From Rs369.60 per litre on Nov 4, petrol is now down to Rs322, as of today. Mr Bakhsh said the daily price adjustments had become unbearable for dealers and warned that if the situation continued, they would face severe financial difficulties, forcing pumps to close and causing serious inconvenience to the public.

He urged the government to scrap the 24-hour pricing system and bring in a 30-day mechanism, along the same lines as refineries and oil marketing companies enjoyed.

While the authority to set petroleum prices should stay with the government, he insisted that dealers be taken into confidence before prices are deregulated, adding that no petroleum-related policy should be made without consulting them.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

articles.title: Plan to split gas firms lands on PM’s table
articles.summary:
• Framework proposes breaking up both companies into six to eight entities
• Separate transmission, distribution and sales businesses envisaged to create competitive gas market; IMF backs reforms
• Over Rs3tr in gas circular debt to be shifted to special purpose vehicle; domestic tariffs may rise

ISLAMABAD: The government has finalised a plan to unbundle the two Sui gas companies into six to eight smaller entities, separating their transmission, distribution, and sales businesses to transform gas monopolies into a “competitive gas market” with the ultimate obje­ctive of achieving “energy security, price rationality, and an efficient, investment-friendly economy”.

Top petroleum division sources told journalists during a background briefing that a summary containing the reform framework had been submitted to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif for in-principle clearance and guidance on whether formal endorsement should be sou­ght from the federal cabinet, the Council of Common Inte­rests (CCI) or parliament.

The plan has been finalised with technical support from the World Bank, KPMG and Wood Mackenzie.

It makes a departure from an earlier PML-N led botched attempt in 2016-17 to create four provincial distribution gas companies and a transmission company.

The prime minister’s “authorisation” is required to engage transaction advisers, who would help implement the plan and guide the government through the remaining constitutional, legal, regulatory and financial requirements within five to six months.

The sources said the Inte­rn­a­tional Monetary Fund (IMF) was on board, as its cle­a­rance was necessary un­­d­er the ongoing programme and the related gas circular debt management plan.

“We will be rolling out the transformation plan into the implementation stage by the fourth quarter of 2027,” a top official said.

More than Rs3 trillion in gas circular debt would be parked in a special purpose vehicle (SPV), following the model of the Power Holding Company Limited in the electricity sector. The SPV would be funded through a debt-servicing surcharge in consumer tariffs.

“The central structural reform is the legal and operational separation of the Sui companies’ transportation and distribution activities from their gas supply and marketing activities — the separation of molecules from pipes,” said the summary, a copy of which was seen by Dawn.

It said the separation would end the conflict of interest that allowed Sui Northern Gas Pipelines Limited (SNGPL) and Sui Southern Gas Company Limited (SSGCL) to act both as network operators obliged to give all users access and as gas suppliers with an interest in shutting out rivals.

The petroleum division has proposed at least four gas sales entities, with two competitive gas supply (CGS) companies for commercial and industrial consumers and two regulated gas supply (RGS) entities serving domestic consumers.

The Sui companies would be required to free up 20 per cent of their supply and consumer portfolios for the CGS companies in the first year, followed by 10pc in each of the next two years to allow private participants to compete in the market.

With 60pc chunk offloaded, the price regulation in the competitive regime would come to an end.

The financial projections, based on the companies’ FY2025 accounts, show that transportation and CGS businesses would be profitable from the outset, while the RGS segment serving residential consumers would incur losses. To address the issue, the government would gradually raise gas prices, reduce the number of domestic billing slabs from 12 to one and provide direct subsidies to vulnerable consumers in the protected category through the social safety net.

In SNGPL’s case, the transportation and CGS segments are projected to earn after-tax profits of Rs24bn and Rs36bn, respectively, while the RGS segment would post an after-tax loss of Rs158bn, with gas costs of Rs322bn far exceeding sales revenue of Rs224bn.

Domestic consumers currently pay an average of Rs1,268 per million cubic feet (MCF), against a break-even price of Rs2,152 per MCF — a “69.8pc increase required to reach break-even at the profit-before-tax level”. If prices are not raised, a subsidy of Rs150bn would be needed.

Commercial and industrial consumers, by contrast, pay an average of Rs2,893 per MCF against a break-even price of Rs2,737, leaving room for a 5.4pc price reduction.

For SSGCL, the projections allocate the cheapest gas from low-cost fields (Rs328 to Rs876 per MCF) to the RGS segment — the most favourable scenario for domestic supply. Even so, the segment would incur an after-tax loss of Rs59bn, and its average sale price of Rs732 per MCF would need an 82.7pc increase to reach the break-even price of Rs1,337.

SSGCL’s transportation and CGS segments would earn after-tax profits of Rs27.4bn and Rs19.6bn, respectively, with room for a 7.4pc cut in CGS prices.

The modelling concludes that the RGS segment remains structurally loss-making under any gas-cost allocation scenario because domestic tariffs are well below cost-recovery levels.

The plan seeks total capital expenditure of Rs736bn for SNGPL over six years, from FY2027 to FY2032, including a peak requirement of Rs165bn in 2030 for system augmentation and loss reduction. A similar requirement of Rs390bn has been estimated for SSGCL.

To meet these requirements, the plan proposes introducing a multi-year tariff based on the regulatory asset base methodology, following the model used by K-Electric.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

articles.title: Challan submitted in Hina Javed murder case
articles.summary:
RAWALPINDI: Police have submitted challan to the District Prosecution Branch in the murder case of Hina Javed after completing the investigation and incorporating forensic reports into the case record.

The district prosecutor has received the challan and initiated scrutiny.

Sources said it could not be submitted on Saturday due to unavailability of the district prosecutor.

According to sources privy to the development, the initial investigation found no incriminating evidence against the victim’s husband.

Consequently, his name has been placed in Column No II of the challan, leaving the matter to the discretion of the court.

Sources in the Prosecution Branch said if any legal deficiencies or shortcomings were identified during scrutiny, the challan could be returned to the police for rectification.

After completion of the scrutiny process, it will be presented before the court of the district and sessions judge.

Hina Javed, a 45-year-old married woman, was murdered at her residence on August 20.

The murder case has been registered with Civil Lines police station.

Meanwhile, the victim’s family has already expressed a lack of confidence in the police investigation, raising concerns about the manner in which the case has been investigated.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill UNRWA worker, two others in Gaza
articles.summary:
CAIRO/JERUSALEM: Israeli airstrikes killed at least three people in Gaza on Monday, including a man working for the UN Palestinian refugee agency UNRWA, the relief age­ncy and local health officials said.

The UNRWA worker, whom medics named as Adel Al-Helo, was working near a well in the Jabalia refugee camp in the enclave’s north, the agency and medics said. Three others were wounded in the strike, they said.

“The initial reports indicate that the strike hit a target on the street near the water well, which was manned by UNRWA staff and a guard. The staff were engaged in their regular duties associated with water well operations,” an UNRWA spokesperson said.

Helo’s body was wrapped in a white shroud, his blue vest bearing UNRWA’s logo stained with blood, as friends and relatives bade farewell outside the hospital’s morgue.

“(He) has been killed by an Israeli strike in Jabalia camp by the Israeli army, they don’t make any difference (between) the civilian people and other people, even the people of the United Nations,” said Helo’s brother Nizar, kneeling beside the body, speaking in English.

“He went to run the water well to supply the residents of Jabalia camp with water. He’s worked at the agency for 35 years,” he said.

Defence minister says police, not army, should handle settler violence

Later on Monday, another Israeli air strike targeted a vehicle in western Gaza City, killing two people and wounding others, medics said.

An October 2025 US-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory, but has not stopped Israeli attacks on Gaza or secured Hamas’s disarmament.

At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since then, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.

Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along Gaza’s coast. Israel’s more than two-year-long assault on Gaza has killed tens of thousands, caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza’s entire population and led to assessments of genocide from scholars and a United Nations inquiry.

Settler violence

The defence minister in Israel’s caretaker government on Monday said the police, not the military, should deal with violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, after Palestinian vehicles and properties were torched over the weekend.

It is not the first time Israel Katz, who serves in the right-wing caretaker government of Benjamin Netanyahu, has spoken about transferring civilian law enforcement over West Bank settlers to the police.

If implemented, the measure could constitute a step towards Israeli annexation of the Palestinian territory.

On Monday, Katz called the “ongoing violence by a handful of rioters extremely serious in every respect.” The military “should not and cannot deal with civilian law enforcement over the Jewish population in Judea and Samaria” he added, using the biblical name for the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967.

“Therefore, in accordance with my directive, the IDF has formulated a plan to transfer responsibility for civilian criminal enforcement in the territories to the Israel Police, which will be reinforced and prepared accordingly,” Katz said.

“Only in this way will it be possible to normalise reality in Judea and Samaria and enable the settlements to flourish and prosper,” he added.

Katz made a call to transfer law enf­orcement in August, during a siege of Palestinian homes in the nor­­­­t­­hern West Bank, saying the police would “prepare and establish an appropriate force to handle civil matters”.

His statement on Monday comes after Israeli authorities said they were investigating the torching of Palestinian vehicles and property in four West Bank villages over the weekend.

Social media posts showed vehicles in flames as well as slogans written on walls, including: “In blood and fire Judea has fallen, in blood and fire Judea will rise again”. At a conference, Israeli President Isaac Herzog said “violence by Jewish extremists against innocent people… is despicable and deserves strong condemnation,” insisting that law enforcement was working “to scour this terrible moral stain”.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

articles.title: Walkout over withdrawal of Fazl’s security
articles.summary:
QUETTA: Opposition members in the Balochistan Assembly staged a walkout on Monday to protest against the withdrawal of security guards provided to JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman. They later returned to the house after provincial ministers intervened and persuaded them to end their protest.

The assembly session was presided over by a member of the Panel of Chairmen Dr Ashok Kumar. Immediately after the session began, JUI-F MPA Zahid Reki rose on a point of order and drew the attention of the chair and members to the withdrawal of security provided to his party chief. He pointed out that the Maulana had already survived two assassination attempts.

Condemning the decision, Mr Reki warned that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif would be held responsible if any harm came to his leader. He then staged a walkout from the assembly.

National Party chief Dr Abdul Malik Baloch also expressed concern over the situation, saying that what was happening to the JUI-F was regrettable. He announced that National Party members would also walk out in protest.

JUI-F, NP members return to Balochistan Assembly after ministers intervene

Home Minister Ziaullah Langove said he was unaware of the details surrounding the withdrawal of the Maulana’s security. However, he described the JUI-F chief as a seasoned and astute politician.

He said the country was passing through a critical period and that security institutions continued to protect it while citizens slept at night. He added that it was inappropriate to make statements against institutions that were making sacrifices for national security.

Provincial Minister Noor Muhammad Dummar also highlighted the sacrifices of the country’s forces, saying that regardless of how influential a political leader might be, making statements against security institutions was inappropriate.

Following assurances and efforts by provincial ministers, the protesting opposition members returned to the assembly.

Two bills passed During the session, Provincial Minister Bakht Muhammad Kakar presented the Balochistan Fisheries and Aquaculture Bill, which had already been approved by the relevant standing committee. The house subsequently passed the bill.

Similarly, Parliamentary Secretary Wali Muhammad Noorzai presented the Balochistan Non-Formal Education Bill, which was also passed.

The Balochistan Assembly session was later adjourned until 3pm on Dec 8.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

articles.title: Punjab holds over 60pc of senior federal posts, Senate body told
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: Punjab holds 60.17 per cent of senior posts in the Federal Secretariat, a Senate subcommittee was told on Monday, prompting a sharp demand for immediate rectification and strict enforcement of the constitutional shares of all provinces in federal employment and natural resources.

The subcommittee of the Senate Standing Committee on Devolution, chaired by Senator Barrister Zamir Hussain Ghumro, said the over-representation was in violation of Article 38(g) of the Constitution, which requires shares of provinces to be maintained in federal services, corporations and bodies established under federal law.

Senators Jan Muhammad Buledi and Poonjo Bheel attended the meeting. The Establishment Division presented details of employees serving in the Federal Secretariat in Basic Pay Scales (BPS) 18-22, categorised by domicile for 2025-26.

Senator Ghumro observed that provincial shares must be strictly maintained in all ministries and departments. Expressing concern over the 60.17pc representation of Punjab in BPS 18-22, he stressed the need for equitable representation of the four provinces, particularly Sindh and Balochistan in the federal jobs.

Subcommittee demands strict enforcement of constitutional shares of four provinces in federal employment, natural resources

“This rectification must be made immediately,” he said. He said the rural-urban divide of Sindh was against Article 38(g), which envisages shares of provinces, and directed that the divide be done away with and only the share of the whole province, like other provinces, be maintained.

The convener expressed displeasure over the failure of the Establishment Division to submit a rectification plan for Sindh, as directed in earlier meetings.

The subcommittee reiterated its directions to submit a comprehensive rectification plan, including for posts in BPS 1-15, within two weeks and initiate the appointment process forthwith.

He also expressed concern over advertisements designed to favour specific individuals and stressed that the recruitment process must remain transparent, impartial and free from nepotism or individual bias, ensuring shares of provinces.
