articles.title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal.

When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties).

Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way.

Burnham is walking a fine line

Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself.

The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome.

Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him.

In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs.

These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls.

But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave.

At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time.

His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016.

He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield.

Martin Steven does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: People wade through floodwater because they underestimate danger – how to avoid risk
articles.summary:
A firefighter dealing with an emergency situation in Oxford after significant flooding. Alessia Pierdomenico/Shutterstock

A footpath home disappears beneath brown water. The other side is only a few metres away and someone has already crossed. Turning back means a long detour and you will be late. Would you wade through? This is the kind of everyday decision that flood safety advice must address.

People do not need to be thrill-seekers to enter dangerous water. They may just be trying to get home. But a familiar route can become an unfamiliar hazard within minutes.

Flooding is one of the leading causes of death during climate disasters worldwide. People can underestimate the speed or power of the water, or they might not spot underwater hazards that could mean they trip and fall.

A significant number of deaths are due to avoidable behaviour. There have been some recent UK fatalities during floods, including in 2023, when storm water rose suddenly.

In the US, the second highest cause of deaths during floods is people walking into or near water. The US National Weather Service warns just six inches (15cm) of fast-moving water can knock over an adult.

With the UK likely to see high levels of rainfall this winter, and flood risk increasing, it’s worth asking why people decide to wade through floodwater.

A review of research on behaviour around floodwater identified several reasons. One is just wanting to get to a destination, such as going to work or school. Other factors include people travelling to flooded areas to taking photos of the extremely high water levels. Protecting property or pets and helping others who are in trouble are other reasons. Underestimating danger and being influenced by other people were major themes.

Watching someone wade through flooded water could make you feel reassured, even though their height, strength and route may differ from yours. Previous success at walking through a flooded road can also encourage someone to have another attempt. Yet getting through safely last time tells you little about the current conditions.

Media images of floods sometimes depict people paddling through flooded streets. This can make the scene look recreational. This does not, of course, prove that such pictures cause risky behaviour. But it is a reason for news organisations to explain the hazards of entering flood water alongside them. What looks like harmless fun, of people getting on with life – being resilient despite the flood – in a photograph or clip may conceal a strong current or a missing drain cover. Government advice is not to walk through floodwater and also warns that floodwater could be contaminated.

Read more:
Floods and droughts are both signs of water insecurity – they show up in these four places

Why appearances can be deceptive

Even clear water can deceive us. Refraction, the bending of light as it passes from water into air, makes the bottom of a flood appear closer to the surface. This is why a swimming pool can look shallower than it really is.

In muddy floodwater, the more immediate problem is often that you cannot see the bottom at all. A submerged pavement may end at a kerb, ditch or uncovered drain. Knowing where the path normally goes does not establish that the ground beneath it remains intact. In a recent study of 185 drivers, participants often focused on depth even when asked how they would judge water speed. That study concerned driving, not walking, but it highlights why advice needs to explain both the depth and the flow conditions.

Depth is only part of the danger. Research shows how both water depth and speed of the water flow combine with body size to affect balance. Moving water pushes against the legs and body; as more of it is submerged, buoyancy also reduces our weight pressing feet against the ground, making it easier to slip and fall. For otherwise similar conditions, drag increases roughly with the square of water speed: doubling the speed can mean around four times the pushing force.

You can lose your footing well before the water reaches your thighs. The Environment Agency guidance warns that water around 15cm deep can knock someone over or conceal hazards. This is not a safe wading limit. Even shallower water is not automatically safe, and children or people with limited mobility will face different risks.

Heavy storms hit Monmouth in 2025.

What should make you turn back

Floodwater across your route is itself a reason to stop and find an alternative. You do not need to establish its depth or test its strength with your feet. The government advice is to avoid walking through floodwater altogether.

Rising levels, debris being carried along and water flowing forcefully across a path are additional warning signs. So are heavy rain and flood warnings. These signs call for moving away from danger, not getting closer to investigate. Flash flooding can develop before an official warning arrives.

Still water can also be dangerous. It can hide sharp objects, damaged surfaces and sewage. The advice is to stay away from flooded riverbanks as the ground can become unstable or may have already been eroded away below the water. Keep children away and dogs on leads, and never bypass a closure because another person has done so.

Read more:
A record-breaking El Niño is still developing – likely bringing a cold winter to the UK

How a game can help

People can explore what to do in an emergency through a game, the Flooding Mucky Dip, that I developed with Girlguiding, Global Link Education and the Environment Agency. At the moment, we are trialling it with schoolchildren in Leicestershire and Rutland, but it can be used by people of any age. It uses tubs of deliberately clouded water (with tea and coffee dissolved in it) containing cards representing flood risks. Participants retrieve cards from the “muddy water” and discuss actions.

Read more:
Did the hot summer make more people worry about climate change? Here’s what the latest indications show

Players can pause a story about a flooded school route and consider what a character should choose next and what to do. Children playing the game can then discuss why following a friend might feel reasonable, then identify another, safer, option. If floodwater blocks the way, choosing another route avoids having to discover what lies beneath it. Playing the game can help children, or adults, understand flooding dangers. Adults could use it to check whether their household plan works. It’s useful to help identify the dangers floodwater can bring.

Other work I am doing with colleagues also explores how stories and practical activities can help families discuss disrupted journeys, safer alternatives and who might need assistance.

With more heavy rains expected this winter, learning how best to respond to a flood could help people understand more clearly what dangers could lie ahead, and how to avoid them.

Katie Parsons receives funding from the Environment Agency and the UK Research and Innovation.

articles.title: UK’s nature healthcheck doesn’t stack up in wildlife’s favour – but volunteers are collecting plenty of crucial data
articles.summary:
encierro/Shutterstock

As nature declines over time, it becomes easier to normalise an increasingly impoverished environment.

One way to help counteract this so-called shifting baseline syndrome is the nation’s annual status report for nature, commissioned by the UK government. First published in 2007, this impressive environmental healthcheck explains how and why habitats and the wildlife within them are changing.

It brings together the best data on a diverse set of 28 biodiversity indicators. These cover measures such as air pollution and habitat condition. They show how birds and butterflies are faring and record how much time people spend volunteering in conservation. The report outlines struggles in the natural world as well as some reasons for hope.

Conservation volunteering highlights the best news. The number of hours worked by volunteer citizen scientists to support the natural environment has increased over both the short- and long-term. Between 2000-24, recorded volunteer time in UK increased by an amazing 70%. This shows the public’s keen appetite to engage with nature and do good. This nature data is being used increasingly by conservationists, planners and researchers to help protect and restore nature, to monitor change and to educate.

Read more:
Why grandparents should talk to children about the natural world of their youth

The latest UK biodiversity indicator report draws on a wide range of measures to give an unrivalled picture of how the environment is changing.

The indicators touch on direct and indirect drivers of biodiversity change, on conservation interventions, on data and expenditure, on awareness and nature connection. It allows researchers to track nature and begin to understand what drives the ups and downs and how to limit and counteract harmful change.

Using huge volumes of data generated by monitoring programmes and recording schemes, coordinated by many conservation and research organisations, many of the indicators go back several decades.

But disappointingly, only half of the 28 biodiversity indicators were updated this time, so the picture isn’t complete.

Looking at trends from all of the indicators that use data compiled over decades, 44% were assessed as improving, 44% deteriorating (12% little or no change). Over the last five years, 38% were assessed as improving, 29% deteriorating and 32% as having little or no change. Certainly, some pressures are reducing and some responses are improving. But outcome measures of the state of nature are either deteriorating or flatlining.

The latest statistics on the UK’s wild birds sadly make for grim reading. Nature in the UK is already known to be depleted, but the apparent acceleration of decline in birds is particularly alarming.

Trends are classified as “deteriorating” in most bird groups in the last five years; none are increasing. This nosedive is most evident in farmland birds (such as lapwing, yellow wagtail and starling) and seabirds (such as Arctic skua and Arctic terns).

It isn’t just birds, butterfly populations are in trouble, declining from steadily from 1976 when systematic monitoring began. These include the small tortoiseshell, adonis blue and small pearl-bordered fritillary.

The UK is a world leader in promoting biodiversity targets and indicators. The Environment Act, for example, includes a legally binding target to halt the decline of species abundance and reduce extinction risk, among wider environmental objectives.

Biodiversity indicators form the basis of much of the UK’s international reporting obligations on biodiversity. They are used to measure progress against targets set by the UN’s Convention on Biological Diversity in 2022. The groundbreaking agreement, known as the Kunming-Montreal global biodiversity framework, contains 23 action-oriented targets for 2030 and four overarching goals for biodiversity recovery by 2050.

Soberingly, government reporting earlier this year showed the UK was on track to meet just three of those 23 targets. For 19 targets, progress was being made but not fast enough. Progress for one target on the management and use of wild species couldn’t be assessed because the UK still lacks evidence on benefits to people.

Mixed signals

Protected areas of both land and sea are both vital for nature protection. The news on the area they cover and their condition sends mixed signals. While the total extent on land and sea protected has increased since the 1950s, the increase has been only at sea since the 1990s. The total area of protected land has flatlined and not changed since 2020.

Reliable information on the condition and quality of those sites is lacking, so whether they protect nature in a meaningful way remains open to question. Overall, the UK is way short of reaching the UN’s bold goal to protect 30% of the world’s land for nature by 2030. At sea, that 30% target has just been reached, according to the update, thanks to expanding marine protected areas around UK coasts.

Overall, more money is being spent on nature, both in the public sector and the non-governmental organisations and private sector. Whether that spending is in all the right places and up to the task of protecting nature is debatable. The current evidence on the state of nature says it is not because the loss of nature continues.

But at least with brilliant volunteers, monitoring schemes and comprehensive indicators, it will be easier to track and respond to any potentially insidious change around us.

Richard Gregory works for the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) as the Head of Monitoring Conservation Science.

articles.title: Could an erectile dysfunction drug offer a new way to treat Alzheimer’s?
articles.summary:
Orawan Pattarawimonchai/Shutterstock.com

A drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction might seem an unlikely treatment for Alzheimer’s disease. But researchers are increasingly interested in whether medicines such as Viagra could also help protect the brain.

These drugs affect blood flow and other processes that may play a role in brain health. An experimental drug called AR1001 has produced encouraging results in a large international clinical trial.

In one group of people with early Alzheimer’s, the drug was reported to slow the worsening of symptoms by 31% over a year, compared with a placebo.

AriBio, a South Korean biotechnology company, announced the results at the 19th Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston, US. A full scientific paper, reviewed by other researchers, has not yet been published.

The phase three trial – the final phase of testing in humans – involved 1,535 people with early Alzheimer’s in 13 countries. Participants took either 30mg of AR1001 or a placebo every day for a year.

Researchers measured changes in memory, thinking and everyday activities. They looked at two groups: everyone who took part in the trial and a smaller group of 604 people who were not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines to ease their symptoms, such as donepezil or memantine.

Only this smaller group saw a 31% reduction in worsening symptoms. Across the whole trial, AR1001 did not produce reliable benefits.

How could erectile dysfunction drugs affect the brain?

Erectile dysfunction drugs work by blocking an enzyme that normally breaks down a chemical messenger – called cGMP – in the body. This allows cGMP to build up, helping the muscles around blood vessels relax. The vessels widen, allowing more blood to flow through them. This is how the drugs help treat erectile dysfunction.

The same chemical messenger also helps brain cells communicate with each other. Researchers think that increasing its levels could help brain cells survive and maintain the connections they need to share information.

These connections are essential for learning and memory. Alzheimer’s gradually damages them, making it harder to remember things and think clearly. Researchers hope that AR1001 might help protect some of these connections and slow the damage caused by the disease.

However, this is still a theory. The clinical trial does not show that these biological changes explain the reported benefits in people.

Some laboratory and animal studies support the idea. In a 2022 study, mice with features of Alzheimer’s disease performed better in memory tests after receiving AR1001. The treatment also reduced levels of amyloid-beta and abnormal tau, two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s.

AR1001 belongs to the same family of drugs as Viagra.
artem evdokimov/Shutterstock.com

Other experimental research in mice has found that AR1001 can increase levels of cGMP and a protein that helps brain cells survive. However, results in animals do not always translate into benefits for humans.

Interest in this family of drugs has also grown following research in people. A 2024 study followed more than 269,000 men with erectile dysfunction. It found that men prescribed these drugs were 18% less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s than men who were not prescribed them.

But this was an observational study, which means it cannot show that the drugs themselves reduced the risk of Alzheimer’s. The two groups may have differed in other ways that influenced the results.

A complicated relationship

The relationship between erectile dysfunction and Alzheimer’s is complicated. Erectile dysfunction can be associated with conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, which can damage blood vessels. These same conditions are also linked to poorer brain health and a higher risk of dementia.

This means that some of the apparent link between erectile dysfunction, its treatments and dementia could be down to shared risk factors affecting blood vessels, rather than a direct effect of the drugs.

Erectile dysfunction drugs are not an established treatment for Alzheimer’s, and nothing in these results suggests people should take them to protect their memory.

The latest trial does, however, keep alive an interesting possibility: that drugs that improve blood flow and help brain cells communicate might also slow the damage caused by Alzheimer’s.

Whether this is the case will depend on the full trial results and further research in people, including studies looking at why the apparent benefit was seen only among those not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines.

Rahul Sidhu does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Resistance training could help boost brain health and confidence in older adults
articles.summary:
As you practise lifting weights, your nervous system gets better at coordinating the muscles you use. Lucigerma/Shutterstock

Think about the last time you stood up from a chair or lifted a heavy shopping bag from the floor. These movements might feel automatic, but they take a surprising amount of coordination between your brain and your muscles.

As you lift the bag, your brain sends signals that tell your muscles when to tighten and how hard to pull. At the same time, signals from your body help your brain tell where your limbs are and whether you’re starting to lose your balance. If the bag is heavier than you expected, you can adjust your grip and shift your weight as you lift.

A recent study involved 162 adults aged 65 and over who showed signs of mild cognitive impairment. This means having more difficulty with memory or thinking than is usual at that age while still being able to manage most everyday tasks.

The researchers compared gentle exercise with a 24-week programme of resistance training, in which muscles work against a weight or against the body’s own weight. The strength exercises gradually became harder. In the second half of the programme, participants began doing some of them on surfaces such as foam pads, which made it harder to keep their balance.

By the end of the programme, the strength-training group scored slightly higher than the gentle-exercise group on two tasks: repeating a string of numbers immediately after hearing it and naming as many words as possible beginning with the letter A in one minute. The groups scored similarly when asked to remember details from a story, both immediately and half an hour later. It’s unclear whether the small differences on the two tests would make a difference in daily life. Whether the programme affects the chances of developing dementia, where changes in memory or thinking interfere with daily life, remains an open question.

Learning to move

When someone first starts strength training, they can get stronger before their muscles grow noticeably. One reason is that the brain and nerves get better at activating the muscles needed for the movement. Think of it as developing a “muscle map”. With practice, it becomes easier to sense where your body is and adjust how much effort you need.

An exercise that challenges your balance may also demand more attention. Whether that extra effort benefits other thinking skills is less clear. In the 24-week study, the researchers compared the whole training programme with gentler exercise, so they couldn’t tell how much the balance challenge itself contributed to the results.

Much of the research on exercise and thinking skills in older age looks at memory or at skills such as planning and switching between tasks. Those tests can tell us how someone performs on a particular task. Other measures are needed to see whether exercise helps someone move more confidently or manage everyday activities on their own.

Practising one task can make a similar task easier. For example, doing squats can help you stand up from a chair because both movements use many of the same muscles. The same principle applies to thinking skills. Strength training might give you practice at remembering the order of your exercises, while a programme designed to improve memory gives you more direct practice at learning new information and recalling it later.

How strength training might affect the brain

Strength training may also affect the brain through changes elsewhere in the body. It can lower blood pressure and help the body respond better to insulin, the hormone that helps control blood sugar. Both high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes are linked to a higher risk of dementia.

Strength training can make everyday tasks, such as carrying the shopping, easier as people get older.
Mangkorn Danggura/Shutterstock

Strength training may also reduce some signs of long-lasting inflammation, which can occur when the body’s immune defences stay active over time. Researchers are still investigating what that might mean for the brain.

Other studies have looked at whether strength training changes the levels of proteins that help brain cells work and form connections. Some have found higher levels of these proteins in the blood after training, but results in people have varied. When muscles tighten during exercise, they also release substances called myokines, which can send signals to other parts of the body. Researchers are exploring whether some of those signals affect the brain.

Beyond the gym

Strength training can help some older adults who have difficulty getting around to move more easily. That might make it easier to walk to the shops or get to a regular social activity. Over time, those outings could provide more opportunities to stay active and see other people. Being physically inactive and being socially isolated are both linked to a higher risk of dementia. What someone can do with their improved strength also depends on practical things, such as how easy it is to get somewhere and how confident they feel going out.

More women than men live with dementia worldwide, yet women are less likely to do regular strength exercises. A review drawing on studies involving more than 2.6 million adults estimated that fewer than one in four did muscle-strengthening exercises at least twice a week. In interviews with women who trained regularly, some described feeling unsure of their abilities or feeling that strength training was seen as something for men.

Having the chance to build strength and confidence earlier in life can help people stay independent as they get older. The benefits can show up in ordinary ways, whether it’s carrying the shopping home or getting out of a chair without help.

Hannah Campbell receives funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.

articles.title: Weight-loss drugs could free up an area of farmland larger than Italy – new study
articles.summary:
Greta Rosati / shutterstock

GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land – an area slightly larger than Italy – for other uses.

The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift towards healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable and more appealing.

About 100 million people already use GLP-1 weight-loss medications worldwide.
IM Imagery / shutterstock

The food system could respond in unexpected ways

Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.

It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease”, blaming individual people for not having enough willpower. But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.

The UK government commissioned national food strategy, finalised in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.

Our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.

Changing the food system alongside medicine

A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use and the environment.

Rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.

GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.

The remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with new clarity, just how closely human health, food production and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.

Peter Alexander receives funding from UKRI and Wellcome.

Roslyn Henry does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Was Anthropic’s record US$81 billion listing a vote of confidence in AI – and what’s next?
articles.summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant behind Claude, has just pulled off the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history. The company raised US$81 billion by listing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market, beating the previous all-time record of US$75 billion set by SpaceX earlier this year.

Initially set at $US83, Anthropic’s share price soared to US$111 after its debut, briefly nudging the company’s value past US$2 trillion, before falling again as investors took profits.

The blockbuster stock market listing comes at a nervous moment in the AI sector. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the huge sums of money being poured into the AI boom are justified, and many are reducing their exposure to technology stocks.

Adding to this shakiness has been the shock departure of chipmaker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, following an affair scandal.

Anthropic’s debut certainly sets a benchmark for rival OpenAI, which still plans to go public.

But we shouldn’t mistake investor enthusiasm in one company for a broader vote of confidence in the global AI industry.

What does Anthropic’s performance tell us?

One thing we can learn from this week’s result is that there is a huge amount of demand for Anthropic itself.

Strong revenue was one factor. At the end of October, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate (an estimate of yearly revenue based on the previous month) was US$81 billion.

But the company’s popularity likely also played a role. Claude is one of the most widely used AI tools around the globe. “Familiarity bias” is a well known phenomenon in investing.

Intense demand meant many smaller investors missed out on getting shares ahead of the official listing. Last week, Bloomberg reported the share offering was about six times oversubscribed.

According to the Wall Street Journal, only about 15% of available shares were ultimately allocated to retail investors.

Is Anthropic’s huge valuation justified?

Anthropic’s share price closed the day at US$97.17, up 17% from its IPO price, which values the company at US$1.76 trillion. That’s slightly less than where SpaceX landed at the end of its first day, at US$2.1 trillion.

But it’s still a colossal figure, even accounting for the fact that Anthropic beat OpenAI to generating a quarterly operating profit earlier this year (before returning to an operating loss the following quarter).

For Anthropic, like any company, going public should make it easier to raise large amounts of capital. That could be important for a company which has already made about US$900 billion in future spending commitments – mostly on computing infrastructure – between now and 2045.

However, it’s important to look at how these commitments play out in the short and long term.

About half of this spending is due by 2030. The near-term bill over the next 12 months is about US$70 billion, which is manageable with its current revenue run rate of US$81 billion.

Other concerns may be more pressing. Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 47% – which is strong – but this compares to a growth rate of 144% in the second quarter. This suggests a sharp slowdown in growth overall.

Token prices have also been falling, driven in part by more competition from cheaper AI models.

Also on revenue, the company has warned that some of its customers – “particularly early-stage and high-growth companies” – rely on external financing. This could reduce their spending with Anthropic if that financing dries up.

What to watch after this public listing

For any company, listing on a public stock exchange introduces much more scrutiny.

Previously, the focus on Anthropic has centred on its technology and growth potential. Now, there’ll be a renewed focus on corporate governance.

Beyond the financial metrics of revenue growth, profitability, cash flow and more, investors will now more closely scrutinise how management balances commercial returns with AI safety, privacy and social responsibility.

Speaking just before the Nasdaq listing, Chief Executive Dario Amodei acknowledged people’s serious safety concerns:

We have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems.

But he expressed faith in Anthropic’s ability to get the balance right:

If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same.

Protesters staged major rallies outside the Nasdaq exchange’s New York headquarters and outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters. They called for stronger government regulation and a slowdown or total pause on AI development.

What does this mean for rival OpenAI?

Another of the world’s major AI companies, OpenAI, had initially planned its own public listing this year. However, it has now ruled this out until 2027, citing safety concerns around the technology.

Anthropic’s IPO creates both opportunities and challenges for its rival.

On the plus side, Anthropic’s performance gives OpenAI and potential investors a yardstick – including financial performance benchmarks and lots of other useful information.

But now that Anthropic has become a publicly listed company, this industry is about to come under even more intense scrutiny.

If public sentiment about AI worsens between now and when OpenAI launches its IPO, it could pay a steep price.

articles.title: The most iconic sports film of all time taught us winning isn’t everything: 50 years of Rocky
articles.summary:
IMDB

By all measures, Rocky (1976) is the most successful sport film of all time. Half a century on from its release, the story of small-time boxer Rocky Balboa – who rises to square up against heavyweight champion Apollo Creed — continues to capture our imagination.

Directed by John G. Avildsen, the film won the prestigious Best Picture and Best Directing Oscars in 1977. And the broader franchise, consisting of five sequels and three Creed spin-offs, has generated more than US$1 billion at the global box office.

Rocky resonates because it is the ultimate underdog story. The hero is flawed, yet faithful to his dreams – working to overcome his self-doubt. His final victory is not a boxing title, but in proving his worth.

Standing your ground

The story of Rocky, written by Sylvester Stallone himself, was inspired by a real-life match between heavy weight champion Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner.

Wepner was a little known boxer from New Jersey at the time. While he didn’t win the fight, he held his own, becoming one of few boxers in history to be able to knock Ali down.

As Stallone recalled in an interview:

for one brief moment, this supposed stumblebum turned out to be magnificent. And he lasted and knocked the champ down. I thought: ‘if this isn’t a metaphor for life.’

Hollywood lore tells how Stallone wrote the script in just three days after seeing Ali and Wepner’s fight. Stallone later admitted that 90% of this original script was terrible, but the “germ of the idea was there”. He says it took about 25 rewrites to get it right.

When interested producers wanted a famous name to take on the eponymous role, Stallone declined. He was determined to play Rocky.

It was a big risk, since Stallone was broke – so broke he was forced to sell his dog, Butkus, for US$40. But like Rocky he had faith in himself, and persisted until the studio, United Artists, agreed to cast him in the role.

When paid his advance, Stallone was able to buy Butkus back for $15,000. The hound went on to feature in several Rocky films.

Butkus, Stallone’s bullmastiff, died in 1981 from a heart attack.
IMDB

Rocky was filmed on a budget of just US$1 million, a small budget for a film, even in those days.

Many of the scenes were shot in public, including those in the famous training montage, in which curious members of the public watch on as Rocky jogs through the streets.

In one unscripted moment, a street seller throws Rocky an orange as he jogs past. This detail adds charm to the scene, instilling the sense of Rocky as the everyday man.

The training montage also doubles as a metaphor for the American dream, which promises that hard work and persistence will lead to success.

Such montages have since become commonplace in sports films, from Karate Kid (1984) to Million Dollar Baby (2004). But Stallone is often credited as having pioneered the format.

Rocky represents a powerful ethos

There has been much discussion about just what Rocky captured in the American psyche that led to its success.

Rocky wasn’t simply a fairytale about the American dream, although this was part of it. The film reflected the neglected working class at a time of growing “ethnic” pride – and local audiences connected with this.

The film’s global success, however, arguably comes down to its core message: recognition of the self.

As film academic Eric Lichtenfeld argues, Rocky is not just training to become a better boxer – he is searching for respect, both internally and externally.

By taking on Apollo Creed, and proving himself to be a worthy opponent, he demonstrates his worth in the world – even if he doesn’t win the final fight.

The appeal of this kind of underdog story transcends cultural boundaries.

It also goes to the heart of sport, as we’ve seen with Olympians like Eddy the Eagle and Eric the Eel.

As Pierre de Courbertin, founder of the Olympics, said:

the most important thing […] is not winning, but taking part. The essential thing in life is not conquering but fighting well.

Adding to the mystique is the fact that the protagonist’s underdog story is in many ways also Stallone’s story. Rocky was the small-time fighter seizing the opportunity of a lifetime; Stallone was the struggling actor trying to make it big in Hollywood.

Rocky’s revival

The release of the upcoming film I Play Rocky (2026), a biographical film marking the 50th anniversary, is testament to our enduring fascination with the entwined legends of character and star.

Featuring Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone, I Play Rocky portrays the story of how the original film was made. Many of the most beloved elements will return, including the very loyal Butkus, and a recreation of the training montage.

The Rocky franchise also continues to grow. Creed IV, the 10th film in the franchise, is currently listed as being in pre-production on IMDB.

Lisa J. Hackett does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Xi-Putin-Trump summit was heavy on symbolism, light on substance – and not exactly a Yalta II
articles.summary:
China's Xi Jinping places himself firmly in the center of the trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. Doug Mills/Getty Images

It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.

Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.

But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver?

As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance.

At an eagerly anticipated summit, the leaders of China, Russia and US discussed nuclear weapons – but not much else.

What were the key takeaways from the meeting?

The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order.

And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi. Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.

And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.

A rare airport hug from Xi Jinping.
Mandel Ngan/Getty Images

It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen.

In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds.

So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body.

And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls. In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985: “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.”

All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter.

President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping looks on in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026.
Iori Sagisawa/AFP via Getty Images

What wasn’t discussed?

The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations.

For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged.

But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting.

At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi.

Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings.

British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin sit together at the Yalta Conference.
AP Photo

This was touted as Yalta II – was it?

There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table.

Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years.

Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed.

Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary.

What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that.

Rana Mitter does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Myanmar genocide ruling is a watershed moment in international justice – with huge ramifications for other cases
articles.summary:
International Court of Justice President Iwasawa Yuji reads the court's judgment in The Hague on Nov. 19, 2026. Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP via Getty Images

The International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not.

The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar.

But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have important effects on the court’s other ongoing genocide cases, particularly the case of South Africa v. Israel.

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling on a screen at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. 19, 2026.
Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images

What the court ruled

Gambia’s case focused on actions that Myanmar’s military government called “clearance operations” in the course of its decades-long violent persecution of the country’s Muslim Rohingya minority.

The Tatmadaw, as the Myanmar military is known, justified these actions as a counterinsurgency operation. Yet in the course of those attacks, soldiers were found to have destroyed hundreds of Rohingya villages, and to have committed widespread rapes, torture and summary killings.

While the precise death toll of the 2017 attacks may never be known, at least 10,000 Rohingya civilians are thought to have died, and roughly 750,000 Rohingya fled to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined other Rohingya in what is now the world’s largest refugee camp of over 1.2 million people, comprised of those who had already fled years of the Myanmar government’s persecution and attacks.

The court’s ruling that the Tatmadaw’s attacks amounted to genocide rested on its interpretation of the crime of genocide in the 1948 U.N. Genocide Convention, the first major international treaty approved by the United Nations General Assembly.

For an attack to be genocidal, it must be directed against an ethnic, religious, racial or national group, and must include at least one of five prohibited acts: killing members of a group; inflicting serious physical or mental harm on members; deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about its destruction; imposing measures intended to prevent births; or forcibly transferring children from the group.

Beyond these factual requirements, genocide requires that the perpetrator specifically intended these acts to destroy the group, in whole or in part.

In its ruling, the court agreed that the facts of Myanmar’s attacks met the legal definition of genocide. For the notoriously difficult and demanding requirement for proving the “special intent” to destroy a group, the court determined that the pattern, selective targeting and lethality of the attacks on Rohingya villages could not plausibly be explained as a counterinsurgency operation.

Instead, the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the military’s actions, the court determined, was the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya ethnic minority.

A series of historic firsts

The court’s decision is unprecedented in many important respects.

In an influential previous ruling on violations of the Genocide Convention, in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro in 2007, the court found only that Serbia had not met its legal duty to prevent genocide by failing to use its influence to restrain the Bosnian Serb army in the Srebrenica massacre of 1995.

In the Myanmar ruling, by contrast, the court ruled for the first time that a country is legally responsible for committing genocide – not merely failing to prevent it.

Further, the court ruled for the first time that a country that has committed genocide also has multiple obligations toward the victim group. Those include designing and implementing a comprehensive program of reparations and compensation for victims; creating conditions where Rohingya can make a safe, voluntary and dignified return to their homes; and restoration of their citizenship status after national legislation from 1982 rendered them stateless.

Rohingya Refugees cross a river at Tambru, a no-man’s land on the Bangladesh-Myanmar border.
Majority World/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

Finally, the court also demanded that Myanmar take steps to investigate all those involved in the genocide to determine individual criminal responsibility. Since the International Court of Justice is not a criminal court and only hears cases between states, this order explicitly connects the ruling to other courts where individual perpetrators can be held accountable.

These include the International Criminal Court – which had already requested an arrest warrant for Tatmadaw leader Min Aung Hlaing – as well as national courts that may pursue prosecution according to the doctrine of universal jurisdiction.

The ruling’s broader implications

The court’s ruling in Gambia vs. Myanmar is also likely to have huge ramifications far beyond the case itself.

In filing its complaint, Gambia appealed to an innovative argument to establish that it had legal standing. It argued for what’s known as “erga omnes partes,” roughly translated as “toward all parties to a treaty.” According to this line of reasoning, the Genocide Convention imposes such strong legal duties to prevent and punish the crime of genocide that any state, even one that has not in any way been directly harmed, has the standing – in fact, the obligation – to seek legal remedies.

In accepting Gambia’s “erga omnes partes” approach, the court opened a pathway for other cases centering on violations of the Genocide Convention. Of these, the most significant by far is the ongoing case of South Africa v. Israel, which charges the Israeli government and the Israeli military of committing genocide against Palestinian civilians in the Gaza Strip. Going forward, other nations would now also have a legal tool for holding perpetrator states accountable for committing the most serious international crimes.

The International Court of Justice has no enforcement arm. As such, the Myanmar government cannot be compelled to abide by its rulings, whether to cease any further attacks or persecution on the Rohingya, make efforts to repatriate them or design a comprehensive reparation and compensation plan.

But even if Myanmar chooses to ignore the court’s specific orders, the ruling is a major defeat. The reputational damage of being the first country found guilty of state-sponsored genocide is likely to be considerable. Further, the ruling will support claims that other nations have a duty not to assist Myanmar in any way that might support or enable further attacks on Rohingya.

While that doesn’t automatically mean other countries will fulfill their duties under international law, many are nonetheless likely to use the ruling to bolster multilateral efforts to impose political, economic and social costs on the Tatmadaw. That could include targeted economic sanctions, financial restrictions, prohibitions on arms sales and other forms of cooperation with Myanmar’s government. The ruling thus comes with a potentially hefty price tag for the military junta.

Given the general weakening of international legal institutions over the past 20 years, a dysfunctional U.N. Security Council and an International Criminal Court under siege by the Trump administration, the court’s ruling is a rare victory for international justice and opens new routes for international genocide prevention and accountability efforts.

Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice at a camp in Bangladesh’s Cox’s Bazar on Nov. 19, 2026.
Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP via Getty Images

Before all else, though, it is also a victory for the Rohingya – a people who have suffered decades of persecution.

Thousands gathered in their Bangladeshi refugee camps to watch and cheer as the court’s president, Judge Iwasawa Yuji, read the court’s judgment. Camp inhabitants held aloft signs and chanted a simple message as the verdict came down: “Thank you Gambia.”

Max Pensky does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Switching devices off standby can save £45 a year – practical advice on energy bills from an expert
articles.summary:
Simple changes at home can save pounds. Nanci Santos Iglesias/Shutterstock.

As the weather turns colder and with energy bills predicted to rise, it’s the time of year when we look for ways to heat our homes more cost-effectively.

Gas and electricity bills for a typical UK home are predicted to rise by 26% from January. Some financial support is promised by the government, including the household energy payment of £100 to many households in England and a VAT cut on electricity bills until July. In most cases, though, these measures will not offset the increase in bills, which is projected to be around £443 for a typical household.

The UK has a high proportion of older properties, with 78% having been built before 1980. This means UK homes are often not as energy efficient as they could be, making them expensive to heat. Heat pumps, batteries, solar panels and full retrofit projects may ultimately reduce energy bills, but are expensive. Just 1.1% of homes in England and Wales reach an energy performance certificate score of A, and the vast majority (around 72%) score C or D, so there opportunities for all of us to improve our homes.

Reduce draughts

Draughts (cold air entering the house from outside, or entering a warm room from a colder one) dilute the warm air in the room with colder air, meaning our heating has to work harder to replace it. What’s more, draughts can make us feel cold even in a warm room, because air movement across our skin has a cooling effect.

The most common sources of draughts are windows, doors and letterboxes. Walking around your home on a cold or windy day will highlight any draughts. In many cases, draught-proofing can be a relatively cheap DIY job. Guidance from charity the Centre for Sustainable Energy explains how to go about it. A DIY draught excluder for the bottom of the door can be quite easy to make, and cut out some of the cold. A curtain behind the door is also effective, but make sure it’s wide enough to cover gaps around and below the door.

How to make a DIY draught excluder.

Energy advice charity the Energy Saving Trust suggests that professional window and door draught-proofing could save around £55 per year, and a chimney draught excluder could save another £45 per year.

Insulate

If the heat in our homes escapes, our heating has to replace it, which uses energy and costs money. Insulation stops this happening. Our homes should be insulated on all sides. This means the floor, walls, and roof.

In homes with a loft, this is often the easiest place to insulate. Loft insulation helps reduce heat loss through the roof. Insulating a loft now will reduce bills for years to come. This can be a DIY job, or can be done by a professional. Organisations such as the National Insulation Association can help find an installer.

If your loft is already insulated, you can add more insulation. The current minimum recommendation for new properties is 270mm, and increasing yours from 120mm to this level could save around £17-£20 per year. If you currently have less insulation, the saving will be much greater.

If you have a hot water cylinder, it’s also worth checking its insulation and adding or improving it. Insulating an uninsulated cylinder could save £200.

In properties with single glazing, heat loss from windows will be large. While installing double glazing is a big job, long term benefits are large.

Heat to suit your home

It is sometimes suggested that leaving your heating on at a low level can lead to lower total energy use than turning it on and off. Whether or not this is true depends on your house, your heating, and you.

A detached house with thick stone walls will take a long time to become warm, but will stay warm for longer (this is also true in summer, and is the reason churches and old buildings remain cool in summer). A newer house with brick and plasterboard walls will heat up more quickly, but also loses heat more quickly.

It’s often better to maintain temperature in the thick walled older house, so here it might be better to adopt the “low and slow” method, particularly if you have a heat pump or a modern boiler. If you have a newer house, turning the heating on and off is likely to be the cheaper option in the long run. Using a smart meter, it’s possible to test both options for a week or so, then adopt the best option.

Not just heating

Heating is a major contributor to energy use, but it’s not the only one. Cooking, lighting, hot water and appliances all play a part. If you have any old-fashioned light bulbs, swapping them for LEDs immediately can save around £45-£55 a year. Using lids on pans, only boiling the water you need, turning off your oven and letting food finish cooking in the leftover heat, and avoiding the tumble dryer wherever possible are all good ways to save energy and money.

There are many other practical options, such as reflecting film behind your radiators, to reduce your energy bills without too much hard work. Just switching devices off standby could save £45 annually. Then of course there’s also looking at changing your energy supplier or making the most of cheaper electricity overnight. We haven’t included every option here, but energy advice services such as the Energy Saving Trust and charity the Fuelbank foundation can all help.

Bigger projects

If you’re considering a bigger project and want to really understand how your house loses heat and prepare yourself for the winter, there are charities and organisations across the UK who offer surveys, or may have infrared cameras available to borrow.

A survey will tell you where your house is losing heat so you can target your efforts in the right place. Some are available for free, and even if you’re not planning major work can provide useful information on cold spots and missing insulation. You could start with charity the National Energy Action.

Stuart Walker is affiliated with the Grantham Centre for Sustainable Futures, University of Sheffield, and Hope Valley Climate Action.

articles.title: Paramedics need time and support to recover between emergency calls
articles.summary:
Paramedics can go straight from one emergency to the next, with little time to take in what happened on the last call. Rawpixel.com/Shutterstock

When a paramedic arrives at your door, they may have come straight from someone else’s emergency. “I don’t know how you do your job,” people often tell me. I think about how little time there can be to take in what’s happened on one call before the next one comes in.

I’m a paramedic and an academic specialising in paramedic science. Ambulance staff deal with death and serious injury, and they can encounter violence on the job. There are pressures between calls, too. A review of research on ambulance work describes how long shifts, unpredictable work and limited time to recover can add to the strain.

In a separate UK study carried out during the COVID-19 pandemic, ambulance staff reported worsening shortages and raised concerns about having too little time to do the job. In ambulance work, there’s an expectation that we’ll be resilient and raise a hand if we’re struggling. I find that second part difficult, and I doubt I’m the only one.

Researchers describe resilience as a process of adapting in the face of serious adversity. When I hear that we’re expected to be resilient, I think of something springing back into shape. I’m uneasy about applying that image to people. I can be ready to help the next patient and find, at the end of my shift, that I’m still thinking about the previous call. If getting on with the job is taken as a sign that we’ve recovered, it falls to us to say when the strain is getting too much.

I prefer to think about fortitude – the strength and courage it takes to face the demands of the work. That can include telling someone when a call has stayed with you. What interests me is where that strength comes from. Having a colleague you trust and time to talk can make it easier to say how you’re doing before the strain builds any further.

When it’s hard to give patients the care they need

Paramedics describe caring well for patients as one of the most rewarding parts of the job. That same commitment could make some calls especially painful. When staff felt unable to give a patient the care they believed was needed, they described a strain known as moral distress. It’s what you can feel when something prevents you from doing what you believe is right.

A separate study looked at how paramedics decide when to stop trying to revive a patient whose heart has stopped. Some described following guidelines that required them to keep going even when they believed further attempts would do no good. The guidelines are there to protect patients. Following them can still be difficult when a paramedic’s judgement about the person in front of them pulls in a different direction.

A conversation after a difficult call can help a crew make sense of what happened. If staff keep raising the same problem and see little change, it can be hard to see the point of speaking up again.

In interviews at one ambulance service in England, staff described feeling that senior managers put pressure on crews to work faster while giving too little attention to their wellbeing. When crews repeatedly flag something that makes it harder to give patients the care they need, managers should look into what’s causing it and tell staff what they’re doing about it.

Support crews feel able to use

Talking to someone they trusted helped people in my interviews make sense of difficult calls. That might be a colleague or someone outside work. In another interview study, paramedics said they wanted time to talk privately after a call, often with the colleague they worked with regularly.

An ambulance service can offer counselling, but staff still have to feel able to use it. Staying composed is often part of caring for a patient in an emergency. If people feel expected to appear unaffected once the call is over, it can be harder to say they’re struggling.

An ambulance service might offer extra support after a major incident. A crew can also reach the end of a shift worn down by a series of calls, even if none on its own would prompt that kind of follow-up.

Training is one place to start. A trial involving 570 student paramedics tested an online programme that taught students how to manage distressing memories and spend less time dwelling on difficult experiences. A year later, students offered the programme were less likely to meet the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder or major depression than those who continued with their usual training.

I’d also like students to hear, before they start taking calls, how the effects of difficult shifts can build up and who they can turn to when that happens.
Once crews are on the road, support should feel like part of an ordinary shift. That could mean making time to talk privately after a difficult call.

I see that as part of helping staff develop fortitude. It takes trust to say that a call has got to you, especially when you’re still working out what you need. The way a service responds when someone does speak up can make it easier for the next person to do the same.

Rebekah Haimes does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors
articles.summary:
Despite the countless books, podcasts, TV miniseries and documentaries, people continue to be fascinated by the fall of Elizabeth Holmes and her health-tech startup Theranos. We are now being offered a new insight into the founder through the much-hyped documentary, You Can See Everything.

The initial drama of the documentary takes places 34 days before Holmes started her 11-year prison sentence for investor fraud in 2023. In our research, we examined how Holmes was presented across promotional materials, tweets, talks and interviews over the ten year period from her initial appearance on the public stage in 2013 to the same period in which the documentary begins.

Valued at around US$9 billion (£7 billion) at its peak in 2014, Theranos claimed to have built a device that could run hundreds of lab tests from just a few drops of blood. Holmes and co-founder Sunny Balwani hid that the device could not in fact do what they said, leading to its 2018 shutdown and their convictions for investor fraud (and, in Balwani’s case, defrauding patients as well).

For many, the fascination in Holmes’s story lies in the hubris and deception of this young woman who set out to upend the multi-billion dollar diagnostic industry. But popular perspectives on Holmes obscure something important about how we view entrepreneurs, who we celebrate (or vilify) and whose interests this serves. This is something our research explores.

A highly sellable female entrepreneur

In our analysis, we found that gendered stereotypes helped create an attractive female narrative around Theranos and Holmes between 2013 and 2015 that served (predominantly male) investor interests.

Holmes was introduced as a very specific kind of woman entrepreneur – confident, ambitious, authoritative. The prominent venture capitalist Tim Draper, who made his name backing companies like Tesla and was an early investor in Theranos, praised what he saw as Holmes’s entrepreneurial instincts in 2014. He said she was the first entrepreneur he know who kept quiet about her business “so that the competition wouldn’t get a chance to start … She had a winner and knew it”.

In 2015, Theranos board member and longtime Holmes supporter former US secretary of state Henry Kissinger talked about her as combining “fierce and single-minded dedication with great charm”.

Much was also made of her looks, with the media often noting she was a “young, blond, and blue-eyed” woman. She was a refreshing change from the usual men the industry pinned all its hopes on.

Holmes did present a highly sellable vision of a new Silicon Valley that welcomed and celebrated female entrepreneurs. In her 2019 book The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, tech historian Margaret O’Mara noted that Holmes’s rise coincided with growing public scrutiny of Silicon Valley’s lack of diversity, and the “tech-bro” homogeneity of the early-to-mid 2010s. At the time, the Valley was also beset by high profile gender discrimination cases.

For investors, Holmes was an attractive answer to a media problem the tech industry had and the media coverage of her rise certainly helped counter some of critics of the Valley’s “brotopia”.

But Holmes’s brand of female founder was not totally new and this also served investors. In many articles she was portrayed as the female reincarnation of the stereotypical “tech bro” – a Mark Zuckerberg with a heart or a Steve Jobs with a social consciousness.

Then there was her intentional self styling, which the media played up as symbols central to her status as a female tech-visionary. Holmes’s signature black turtle necks seemed to be a homage to the uniform of Jobs, who regularly wore an Issey Miyake black turtleneck. She was asked about it again and again, admitting in an interview with Glamour that she owned 150 of them.

Holmes’s founder uniform combined with the fact that she had dropped out of university to pursue her vision, like Jobs, Zuckerberg and Bill Gates, gave her many of the recognisable characteristics of a successful tech founder. She was like all these visionaries but with the added bonus of being a woman. This portrayal fed straight into investor interests by making Holmes at once both familiar and novel, helping her company Theranos’s value to climb to unprecedented heights.

However, when things started to turn sour, our research found that much less flattering gendered stereotypes were quickly deployed. These narratives framed Holmes’ downfall as female weakness in order to protect powerful men.

An ousted ‘villain’

Holmes was vilified, not only as a failed entrepreneur, but also as a seductress who had used specifically female charms to lead competent men astray.

According to Rolling Stone, she “lured” male investors into her fraudulent schemes. Meanwhile, the Evening Standard reported her as having “wooed” the men on her board to do her bidding. Financial journalists described how Holmes “dazzled” normally sober leaders at supermarket chains Walgreens and Safeway who then invested in her scheme.

Holmes’s board of directors – once portrayed as the “most illustrious board in US corporate history” – along with the other powerful men she was seen as having duped could now be presented as innocent victims of malicious female magic.

For investors, this villification of Holmes could help them spin their own narratives in order to preserve public trust in their abilities. They could argue that her monstrous supernatural abilities to bamboozle and manipulate were too strong for them to overcome. In this media framing, the fact that investors appeared not to have conducted basic due diligence before investing hundreds of millions of dollars was neither their fault nor a reflection of their real talent for investment. They were simply good men who wanted to help people but had been fooled by a woman playing on an emotional blind spot. They were credulous rather than gullible.

To be clear, we don’t excuse Holmes or seek to diminish the seriousness of what she did. But her story tells us something interesting about the wider system surrounding tech entrepreneurs, and how we can remain blind to the ways capital interests can fuel – and exploit – popular and idolised archetypes.

You Can See Everything provides a new intimate portrait of Holmes, which will add, change or warp ideas we already have about her. But we also need to turn the focus back onto ourselves and think about the ways in which we idolise or judge people in her position – and the gendered stereotypes we would rather not admit to holding.

In the past ten years Susi Geiger has receive funding from the following public bodies: European Research Council (ERC Grant 2018-2024); Research Ireland (SFI Pathway grant 2024-2029); Horizon Europe MSCA Actions (2023-2026). Susi Geiger is an Ambassador to the European Research Council (voluntary and unpaid role) and a member of the WHO Technical Advisory Group on Pharmaceutical Pricing Policies (voluntary and unpaid role).
